# Regularity and compactness theory of stable free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces

**Authors:** Costante Bellettini Address: Department of Mathematics, University College London, London WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom Email address: c.bellettini@ucl.ac.uk , Martin Man-chun Li Address: Department of Mathematics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, N.T., Hong Kong Email address: martin.li@cuhk.edu.hk , Davide Parise Address: Department of Mathematics, Zeeman Building, University of Warwick, Gibbet Hill Road, Coventry CV4 7AL, UK Email address: Davide.Parise@warwick.ac.uk and Lorenzo Sarnataro Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Toronto, 40 St George Street, Toronto, ON M5S 2E4, Canada Email address: lorenzo.sarnataro@utoronto.ca

## Abstract

We study stable free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in a complete $(n+1)$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold-with-boundary $(M,\partial M)$ , and establish the free-boundary version of the well-known (interior) Schoen–Simon regularity and compactness theory from [38]. Our approach follows the intrinsic PDE scheme introduced by the first-named author in [4].

In the key step towards the compactness and regularity, we identify and address the two possible scenarios in which local weak flatness (of a stable free-boundary minimal hypersurface) is verified near a point on $\partial M$ : first, weak flatness with respect to $\partial M$ ; second, weak flatness with respect to a reference hypersurface-with-boundary that meets $\partial M$ almost orthogonally. In both flatness regimes we prove sheeting theorems, i.e. a graphical decomposition (possibly in the multi-valued sense) and estimates for the stable minimal hypersurface.

The sheeting theorems are obtained, in their most basic analytic form, as $\varepsilon$ -regularity theorems (where smallness of $\varepsilon$ reflects regimes with weak flatness). The starting point is a careful identification of geometrically adapted tilt functions. We choose them so that they quantify flatness and keep track of the ambient geometry, and we show that they solve appropriate non-linear elliptic PDEs on the free-boundary minimal hypersurface. These PDEs are amenable to an intrinsic analysis (of the tilt functions) via iteration à la De Giorgi, using stability to obtain weak Caccioppoli-type inequalities that make the iteration viable, and leading to the $\varepsilon$ -regularity.

The two $\varepsilon$ -regularity results (and consequent sheeting theorems) are valid for immersed hypersurfaces that are allowed to have a small singular set (a priori of locally finite $(n-2)$ -Hausdorff measure). When specialised to embeddings, they yield (in combination with soft classical tools) the compactness and regularity theorem: a sequence of stable free-boundary embedded minimal hypersurfaces with uniformly bounded area (possibly with a singular set of locally finite $(n-2)$ -measure) admits a subsequence converging to a free-boundary minimal hypersurface that is smoothly embedded away from a set of Hausdorff dimension at most $n-7$ (its singular set). The convergence is smooth and graphical (possibly with multiplicity) away from this (singular) set.

As an application of the compactness and regularity, we extend the free-boundary Almgren–Pitts existence theory of [29] to arbitrary dimension. In every compact Riemannian manifold-with-boundary of dimension $n+1$ , there exists a free-boundary minimal hypersurface, smoothly embedded except possibly for a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most $n-7$ .

## 1. Introduction

Let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold-with-boundary. A smooth hypersurface-with-boundary $(\Sigma,\partial\Sigma)\subset(M,\partial M)$ is a free-boundary minimal hypersurface if its mean curvature vanishes and it meets $\partial M$ orthogonally along $\partial\Sigma$ . This characterises stationarity with respect to area for compactly supported deformations that preserve the constraint $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial M$ . The purpose of this paper is to develop a regularity and compactness theory for stable free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces with a small singular set, and to apply it to the existence of optimally regular11 1 i.e. smoothly embedded away from a codimension 7 singular set. free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in compact Riemannian manifolds-with-boundary, in arbitrary dimension.

The analogous interior problem ( $\partial M=\emptyset$ ) found its resolution in the Schoen–Simon theory, a cornerstone of the field. In [38], they proved that a stable minimal hypersurface (without boundary), smoothly and properly embedded outside a closed set of locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure, extends to one that is smooth and embedded away from a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most $n-7$ , and established compactness of this class in the varifold topology under uniform mass bounds. The main efforts in [38] are devoted to the proof of a sheeting theorem, which, combined with a slicing argument, establishes the aforementioned compactness theorem. Finally, they used these results to obtain the existence of an optimally regular closed minimal hypersurface in every closed Riemannian manifold, extending the low-dimensional Almgren–Pitts theory [36], which was based on the Schoen–Simon–Yau curvature estimates in [37].

The Schoen–Simon theory also underpins Wickramasekera’s influential work [50], which (among other merits) has been fundamental in the development of an Allen–Cahn min-max approach to the existence of closed minimal hypersurfaces in compact Riemannian manifolds [23, 44, 20]. By analogy, a (future) free-boundary theory in the spirit of [50] (i.e. for free-boundary stationary stable integral varifolds without classical singularities) would most likely have to rely on the sheeting results that we provide here. Such developments would further lead to the completion of an Allen–Cahn min-max approach to the existence of free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, cf. [27].

The low-dimensional Almgren–Pitts theory was recently extended to the free-boundary setting by the second-named author in collaboration with X. Zhou in [29]. The missing ingredient for the higher-dimensional theory was a comprehensive free-boundary analogue of Schoen–Simon’s compactness for stable hypersurfaces with a singular set of locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure. A partial adaptation of the techniques of [38] to the free-boundary setting was carried out in [17] for surfaces ( $n=2$ ) in Euclidean domains with strictly uniformly convex boundary. Subsequently, [9] noted that the same arguments carry over in arbitrary dimension and for Riemannian domains with strictly uniformly convex boundaries. A noticeable effect of the convexity assumption in [17] and [9] is that it prevents interior touching of $\Sigma$ with $\partial M$ (by interior touching we mean that $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M\neq\emptyset$ ). Our results confirm a posteriori that (in the convex case) touching is also ruled out under a limit procedure. Touching behaviour can on the other hand arise when $\partial M$ is not convex, as easy examples show, and may happen in the limit even if we start from a sequence that presents no touching. Handling this possibility (especially in the limit) is crucial for the development of a compactness theory, as well as an existence theory. Indeed, [29] deal with this situation in low dimensions by means of curvature estimates [18] (in the spirit of Schoen–Simon–Yau [37]), while the compactness theory developed here permits its handling in all dimensions.

An intrinsic PDE approach to the Schoen–Simon theory was recently introduced by the first-named author in [4], where the key $\varepsilon$ -regularity result for the classical tilt function (in Euclidean space, with respect to a hyperplane) is obtained by direct (non-linear elliptic) PDE analysis, carried out on the hypersurface. Our proof follows this intrinsic paradigm: rather than linearising the minimal surface equation in an ambient coordinate system (as in [38, 17]), we derive differential inequalities directly on the immersed hypersurface for geometrically adapted tilt functions. Our tilt functions retain information about the Riemannian geometry of $M$ and of $\partial M$ , which turns out to be crucial for the success of the method, and particularly useful at the boundary (see Section 1.2.1 below). The $\varepsilon$ -regularity result is the key ingredient to obtain a sheeting theorem, from which the compactness theory will follow via soft classical geometric measure theory arguments.

Another advantage of the intrinsic PDE method lies in the fact that (unlike [38]) it allows us to prove $\varepsilon$ -regularity and sheeting theorems for stable immersed (rather than embedded) free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces with a sufficiently small (non-immersed) singular set. Both sheeting theorems are new in the case of stable immersions, with the boundary-parallel one new even in the embedded setting.

### 1.1. Main result

Our main result is the following free-boundary counterpart of the Schoen–Simon compactness theory.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Compactness theory).

Let $n\geq 2$ and let $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth complete Riemannian manifold-with-boundary. Consider a sequence of smooth (up to the boundary) embedded two-sided hypersurfaces-with-boundary $\{(\Sigma_{k},\partial\Sigma_{k})\}_{k}$ . Assume the following, for each $k$ .

- (i) (a priori control on the singular set) $\mathcal{S}_{k}=\overline{\Sigma}_{k}\setminus\Sigma_{k}$ has locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure, where the closure is taken in $M$ , and the embedding is proper in $M\setminus\mathcal{S}_{k}$ .

- (ii) (free boundary condition) $\partial\Sigma_{k}\subset\partial M$ .

- (iii) (stationarity) $\Sigma_{k}$ is minimal in its interior $\Sigma_{k}\setminus\partial\Sigma_{k}$ , in the sense that its mean curvature vanishes; for every $p\in\partial\Sigma_{k}$ the tangent half-plane to $\Sigma_{k}$ at $p$ is orthogonal to $T_{p}\partial M$ .

- (iv) (stability) for every $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Sigma_{k})$ the stability inequality holds on $\Sigma_{k}$ , namely (1.1)

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{k}}|\nabla_{\Sigma_{k}}\varphi|^{2}-\int_{\Sigma_{k}}\big(|A_{\Sigma_{k}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\nu_{\Sigma_{k}},\nu_{\Sigma_{k}})\big)\varphi^{2}-\int_{\partial\Sigma_{k}}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\nu_{\Sigma_{k}},\nu_{\Sigma_{k}})\varphi^{2}\geq 0, $$

where $\nu_{\Sigma_{k}}$ is a continuous determination of a unit normal to $\Sigma_{k}$ .

- (v) (mass bounds) For every compact set $K\subset M$ we have $\sup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma_{k}\cap K)<+\infty$ .

Then $\Sigma_{k}$ converges locally subsequentially in $M$ to a smooth embedded hypersurface-with-boundary $\Sigma$ such that $\mathcal{S}=\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\Sigma$ has $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{S})\leq n-7$ ; in addition, if $n=7$ the set $\mathcal{S}$ is discrete. The convergence is locally smooth and graphical (possibly with multiplicity) on $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ . Moreover, the hypersurface $\Sigma$ is a free-boundary minimal hypersurface (i.e. it satisfies (ii)-(iii) with $\Sigma$ in place of $\Sigma_{k}$ ) and, when taken with multiplicity, $\Sigma$ is the image of a two-sided stable free-boundary minimal immersion.

#### Remark 1.2 (Stability properties of the limit hypersurface $\Sigma$ ).

More precisely, $\Sigma$ in Theorem 1.1 (while not being necessarily two-sided) satisfies:

- • If $\Gamma$ is a two-sided connected component of $\Sigma$ , with unit normal $\nu_{\Gamma}$ , then it satisfies the stability inequality (1.1) with $\Gamma$ in place of $\Sigma_{k}$ .

- • If $\Gamma$ is a one-sided connected component of $\Sigma$ , then the inclusion $\Gamma\xhookrightarrow{}M$ lifts to a two-to-one immersion $\tilde{\iota}:\widetilde{\Gamma}\to M$ of the orientable double cover $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ in the normal bundle $N\Gamma$ , with image $\Gamma$ . Then $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ endowed with the pullback metric $\tilde{\iota}^{*}\mathrm{g}$ has a globally-defined unit normal $\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}$ and the following stability inequality holds

$$ \int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|\nabla_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\phi|^{2}-\int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\big(|A_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\big)\phi^{2}-\int_{\partial\widetilde{\Gamma}}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\phi^{2}\geq 0, $$

for all $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ .

See Section 5.6 for more details.

#### Remark 1.3.

Convergence aspects of Theorem 1.1 are naturally formulated in the language of varifolds. Indeed, under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, each $\Sigma_{k}$ defines a free-boundary stationary integral varifold $|\Sigma_{k}|\coloneqq\mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k},\mathds{1}_{\Sigma_{k}})$ . (We show this in Appendix B, as a consequence of the size assumption on $\mathcal{S}_{k}$ , see also Section 1.2.6.) We then prove that, up to a subsequence, the varifolds $|\Sigma_{k}|$ converge to the varifold $V=\theta|\Sigma|$ , where $\Sigma$ is as in Theorem 1.1, and $\theta$ is a locally constant integer-valued locally summable positive function on $\Sigma$ . In particular, the density function $\theta$ is constant on each connected component of $\Sigma$ . Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is a one-sided connected component of $\Sigma$ , then $\theta$ is necessarily an even positive integer on $\Gamma$ . Finally, $V$ is free-boundary stationary and stable, i.e. for every vector field22 2 $\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M)=\{X\in C^{1}_{c}(M,TM):X(x)\in T_{x}(\partial M)\text{ for all }x\in\partial M\}$ . $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M)$ , we have $\delta V(X)=0$ and $\delta^{2}V(X)\geq 0$ . See Section 5 for details.

#### Remark 1.4.

We emphasise that, throughout this paper, every reference to smoothness or smooth convergence of hypersurfaces-with-boundary should be interpreted as smoothness up to the boundary and smooth convergence up to the boundary respectively.

#### Remark 1.5.

Notice that the limit hypersurface $\Sigma$ in Theorem 1.1 may still touch the boundary in its interior, namely it is possible that $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M\neq\emptyset$ . However, since the convergence to $\Sigma$ is smooth and graphical, the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ vanishes on $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M$ . This constrains the possible behaviours. For example, by the maximum principle, if $\partial M$ is strictly mean-convex (namely $H_{\partial M}>0$ ), then necessarily $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M=\emptyset$ . Similarly, if $U\subset\partial M$ is a relatively open set and $U\subset(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M$ , then, again by the maximum principle, $H_{\partial M}\equiv 0$ on $U$ .

It is also possible that $(\overline{\Sigma}\setminus(\overline{\partial\Sigma}\cup\Sigma))\cap\partial M\neq\emptyset$ , namely that $\overline{\Sigma}$ touches the boundary at an interior singular point (see Example 1.16).

#### Remark 1.6.

Notice that, as in the interior case, the dimension bound $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{S})\leq n-7$ is sharp, as one can see by considering e.g. one half of the Simons cone, namely the area-minimising (and therefore stable) singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma^{+}=\bigl\{\sum_{j=1}^{4}x_{j}^{2}=\sum_{j=5}^{8}x_{j}^{2};\ x_{8}\geq 0\bigr\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{8}_{+}$ , which can be obtained as a smooth (away from its singular set $\mathcal{S}=\{0\}$ ) limit of a sequence of stable smooth free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma^{+}_{k}$ . Indeed, it is well-known that the complement $\mathbb{R}^{8}\setminus\Sigma$ of the full Simons’ cone consists of two connected components $E_{+},E_{-}$ , and each of $E_{\pm}$ is foliated by rescalings $\{\lambda\Gamma_{\pm}\}_{\lambda>0}$ of a smooth area-minimising hypersurface $\Gamma_{\pm}$ such that $\lambda\Gamma_{\pm}\to\Sigma$ as $\lambda\to 0^{+}$ both in the sense of varifolds, and locally smoothly away from the origin. Since each $\Gamma_{\pm}$ is smooth and invariant under reflection in $\{x_{8}=0\}$ , then $\Sigma^{+}_{k}\coloneqq k^{-1}(\Gamma_{+}\cap\{x_{8}\geq 0\})$ is an area-minimising (hence stable) smooth free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{8}_{+}$ and $\Sigma^{+}_{k}\to\Sigma^{+}$ (which has a codimension 7 singular set) as $k\to\infty$ .

#### Remark 1.7.

In dimensions $3\leq n+1\leq 7$ , where the singular set is empty, the compactness theory can equivalently be expressed as a curvature estimate. More precisely, our Theorem 1.1 implies [18, Theorem 1.1] under the additional assumption that the stable free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ is embedded. We note that the original theorem [18, Theorem 1.1] can now be strengthened, due to the first-named author’s extension of the Schoen–Simon–Yau estimates to ambient dimension $n+1=7$ and to the recent progress on the stable Bernstein problem. In particular, as a consequence of [4, Theorem 2], the curvature estimate of [18, Theorem 1.1] holds for immersed stable free boundary minimal hypersurfaces in the full dimensional range $3\leq n+1\leq 7$ , and, as a consequence of [6, 5, 32, 22], the constant $C_{1}$ in [18, Theorem 1.1] can be taken to be independent of the area bound $C_{0}$ .

As announced above, replacing the low-dimensional compactness input in [29] by Theorem 1.1 gives the following existence theorem, which is new for $n\geq 7$ .

#### Theorem 1.8.

For any given compact Riemannian manifold-with-boundary $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ with $n\geq 2$ , there exists a smooth embedded hypersurface-with-boundary $\Sigma$ that satisfies the following properties.

- • $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial M$ .

- • $\Sigma$ is minimal in its interior $\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma$ (in the sense that its mean curvature vanishes) and for every $p\in\partial\Sigma$ the tangent half-plane to $\Sigma$ at $p$ is orthogonal to $T_{p}\partial M$ .

- • $\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\Sigma$ has Hausdorff dimension at most $n-7$ .

#### Remark 1.9.

Similarly to Remark 1.3, in the language of varifolds, the varifold $V=|\Sigma|$ induced by the free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ in Theorem 1.8 is free-boundary stationary, namely its first variation $\delta V$ vanishes along every vector field $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M)$ . Moreover, the singular set $\operatorname{sing}V$ of $V$ has Hausdorff dimension at most $n-7$ .

#### Remark 1.10.

Note that in Theorem 1.8 the set $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M$ might be empty, i.e. $V$ might be supported on an optimally regular closed minimal hypersurface contained in the interior of $M$ (see Section D.1). However, under additional geometric assumptions on $(M^{n+1},\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ , for example if $\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}\geq 0$ on $M$ and $\partial M$ is strictly mean-convex, it is possible to guarantee that $V$ is supported on an optimally regular free-boundary minimal hypersurface with non-empty boundary. See Section D.2 for a proof.

### 1.2. Ideas of the proof

Let us now explain the overall structure of the argument for Theorem 1.1, and the various intermediate results of independent interest we obtain en route to the compactness theorem. As we mentioned at the very beginning of this introductory section, the approach is based on the method developed in [4], which relies on intrinsic PDE analysis on immersed minimal hypersurfaces. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is organised around two sheeting theorems (Theorem 1.12 and Theorem 1.15), which characterise stable singular free-boundary hypersurfaces that are $L^{2}$ -close to certain almost-flat models as unions of minimal graphs over these models. Although the compactness theorem (Theorem 1.1) only deals with stable embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces (see Section 1.2.5 for more on this aspect), the sheeting results can be proven with barely any additional effort in the larger class of stable immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces (see Definition 2.6 for a precise definition of the class of hypersurfaces we consider).

Our first step in the free-boundary setting is to identify the two almost-flat models. In the first, we use as reference hypersurface a geodesic ball in the boundary $\partial M$ (leading to the boundary-parallel sheeting result in Theorem 1.12); in the second, the reference hypersurface is a smooth embedded half-disc meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally (leading to the boundary-orthogonal sheeting result in Theorem 1.15).

The analytic architecture is the same in the two cases: the sheeting theorem is obtained as a consequence of an $\varepsilon$ -regularity theorem (Theorem 1.11 and Theorem 1.14 respectively) for an appropriately chosen scale-invariant tilt excess, which is supposed to measure closeness to the model. Once the correct geometrically adapted tilt function is identified for each case, the proof of the $\varepsilon$ -regularity formally follows the same steps as in [4]: first, a differential inequality is derived for the tilt function; secondly, by using a truncation of the tilt function as a test function in the stability inequality, an intrinsic weak Caccioppoli inequality on $\Sigma$ is obtained; finally, by using an appropriate Sobolev inequality to relate the $L^{2}$ energies of successive truncations on nested cylinders, an iteration à la De Giorgi can be set up to yield an $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{\infty}$ estimate for the tilt function at a smaller scale. This $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{\infty}$ estimate under the assumption of initial smallness is the essence of our $\varepsilon$ -regularity. Once the tilt is uniformly small, projection onto the model is locally invertible; so properness and the smallness of the projected singular set promote local graphs to a finite multigraph structure.

In order to highlight the common abstract structure of the arguments, we will present the common ingredients (such as the Sobolev inequalities in Section 2.2.4 or the iteration lemmas in Section 2.3) as stand-alone results in Section 2.

#### 1.2.1. Geometric choice of the tilt functions

Two considerations determine the comparison hypersurfaces and tilt functions used in this argument. The first concerns the metric in which the differential identities are derived. In their boundary curvature estimates, Grüter–Jost [17, Section 3] flatten the boundary by a local diffeomorphism and treat the transformed area integrand as a perturbation of Euclidean area, following the framework of Schoen–Simon [38]. In doing so, the exact variational information is inevitably lost: stationarity and stability conditions become approximate conditions (for the Euclidean area), and the PDE for the tilt will feature differentiation of the Euclidean mean-curvature, a term that admits no natural estimate and is not amenable to the PDE methods we use. Instead, the tilt functions that we use here are naturally induced by the Riemannian metric, and this permits us to preserve all variational information.

The second consideration is compatibility with the boundary geometry, which affects the choices of both the reference for flatness, and the tilt function to measure flatness (with respect to said reference). This issue persists even when $M$ is the closure of a smooth domain in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ equipped with the Euclidean metric, and the $n$ -area is already Euclidean. As the proof of the compactness and regularity theorem proceeds via tangent cone analysis, it might be very tempting to aim for sheeting theorems where flatness is captured by the standard Euclidean tilt function with respect to either the hyperplane $T_{x}\partial M\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ , or a half-hyperplane orthogonal to $T_{x}\partial M$ . In both cases, however, we would run into trouble with the PDE analysis for the tilt, because Euclidean tilt functions introduce terms arising from the free boundary that, in general, are not controlled by the estimates used in our iteration. We consequently adapt both the comparison hypersurface and the reference normal field to the curved boundary. In the boundary-parallel case, we compare with a local portion of $\partial M$ itself and define the tilt $g$ using its distance function. In the boundary-orthogonal case, we use a comparison half-disc meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally and define the tilt $\tau$ using a smooth unit extension $Z$ of its normal that is tangent to $\partial M$ along the ambient boundary. These choices yield the boundary identities needed to eliminate or control the conormal terms in the Caccioppoli inequalities.

#### 1.2.2. Boundary-parallel sheeting theorem

Let $d_{\partial M}$ be the distance to the boundary in a collar neighbourhood, and define

$$ g:=|\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}|. $$

This will be our tilt function when the comparison hypersurface is chosen to be a geodesic ball in $\partial M$ : it measures the tangential component of the boundary-normal direction, and hence the deviation of $T\Sigma$ from the tangent spaces to the parallel hypersurfaces of the collar. A crucial feature is that

$$ g=1\qquad\text{on }\partial\Sigma, $$

while it satisfies a PDE in $\Sigma$ thanks to Bochner’s formula. Thus an $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{\infty}$ estimate which ensures $g<1$ in a smaller domain automatically shows that there are no free-boundary points there. The subsequent sheeting is therefore by interior minimal graphs over $\partial M$ . In particular, boundary-parallel $L^{2}$ closeness rules out a degeneration in which boundary components collapse into a boundary-parallel limit through flatter and flatter half-catenoidal necks.

#### Theorem 1.11 (Boundary-parallel $\varepsilon$ -regularity for the tilt).

Let $M$ be as above, $p\in\partial M$ , and let $P$ be a geodesic ball in $\partial M$ centred at $p$ . Assume $\rho_{0}>0$ is such that $P$ has a $\rho_{0}$ -collar neighbourhood $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P)$ in $M$ , and

$$ |\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|+|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|\leq\Lambda^{2}\quad\text{ in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P)$,} $$

where $d_{\partial M}$ denotes the distance function from $\partial M$ . There exist $\varepsilon_{0}>0,R_{0}>0$ depending only on the dimension $n$ and the geometric constant $\Lambda$ such that the following holds. Let $\delta\in(0,\rho_{0}/2)$ , $R\in(0,R_{0})$ , $\sigma\in(0,1)$ , and let $P_{R}=B_{R}^{\partial M}(p)\subset P$ . Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R})$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ and $\partial\Sigma\subset P_{R}$ . If

$$ \mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{2}\coloneqq R^{-n}\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}|^{2}<(1-\sigma)^{n}\varepsilon^{2}\quad\text{for some $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}$}, $$

then

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}|<C_{0}(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}},\quad\text{on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{\sigma R})$}, $$

where the constant $C_{0}=C_{0}(n,\Lambda)$ only depends on the dimension $n$ and the constant $\Lambda$ .

#### Theorem 1.12 (Boundary-parallel sheeting).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.11, we further conclude that $\partial\Sigma\cap P_{R/2}=\emptyset$ , and that there exist an integer $Q\geq 1$ and ordered Lipschitz functions

$$ 0\leq u_{1}\leq u_{2}\leq\cdots\leq u_{Q},\qquad u_{j}\colon P_{R/2}\to[0,\delta), $$

such that

$$ \overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u_{j})\bigr), $$

where $F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u_{j})\bigr)\coloneqq\{F_{\partial M}(y,u_{j}(y)):y\in P_{R/2}\}$ and $F_{\partial M}\colon P\times[0,\rho_{0})\rightarrow M$ is the normal exponential map of $\partial M$ (as defined in Section 2) restricted to $P$ . Furthermore,

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{P}(u_{j})\leq C(n,\Lambda)\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}, $$

for every $j=1,\ldots,Q$ , where the constant $C(n,\Lambda)$ only depends on the dimension $n$ and the geometric constant $\Lambda$ in (1.2). Moreover,

- (i) If we further assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ , then there exist smooth functions $v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{Q}\colon P_{R/2}\rightarrow[0,\delta)$ such that

$$ \overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(v_{j})\bigr), $$

and with

$$ \|\nabla^{2}v_{j}\|_{C^{0}(P_{R/2})}+R^{\alpha}[\nabla^{2}v_{j}]_{\alpha,P_{R/2}}\leq C(n,\alpha,\Lambda)\left(R^{-1}\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+1\right) $$

for all $j=1,2,\ldots,Q$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . In particular, $R|A_{\Sigma}|\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+R\right)$ on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})$ .

- (ii) If, on the other hand, we assume that $\Sigma$ is embedded, then $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})=\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})$ and $0\leq u_{1}<u_{2}<\ldots<u_{Q}$ are smooth with estimates

$$ \|\nabla^{2}u_{j}\|_{C^{0}(P_{R/2})}+R^{\alpha}[\nabla^{2}u_{j}]_{\alpha,P_{R/2}}\leq C(n,\alpha,\Lambda)\left(R^{-1}\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+1\right) $$

for all $j=1,2,\ldots,Q$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . Lastly, $R|A_{\Sigma}|\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+R\right)$ on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})$ .

#### 1.2.3. Boundary-orthogonal sheeting theorem

The second model is a smooth two-sided $n$ -dimensional half-disc $P$ meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally. We need to define a tilt function that quantifies deviation from this model. Directly extending the unit normal to $P$ as the gradient of $d_{P}$ is not suitable for the boundary calculation: the normal derivative of the associated tilt would contain the uncontrolled component $A(\eta,\eta)$ , where $\eta$ is the free-boundary conormal. We instead construct a unit vector field $Z$ on a neighbourhood of $P$ in $M$ such that

$$ Z|_{P}=\nu_{P},\qquad Z\in T(\partial M)\quad\text{along }\partial M. $$

Its flow preserves $\partial M$ , and we measure tilt by

$$ \tau:=|Z^{T}|, $$

where $Z^{T}$ is the projection of $Z$ onto $T\Sigma$ . Tangentiality of $Z$ converts the boundary derivative of $\tau$ into terms involving only the second fundamental form of $\partial M$ and derivatives of $Z$ (see Lemma 4.9), so the boundary contribution can be handled by the trace inequality.

#### Remark 1.13.

Our boundary-orthogonal sheeting theorem includes, as a special case, the result in [17, Section 3]. Our construction of $Z$ replaces, in some sense, the flattening of $\partial M$ performed in [17]. While $M$ is therein locally described in coordinates as a half ball $B^{n+1}_{+}(0)$ , with $\partial M$ identified with $B^{n}(0)\times\{0\}$ , we use (flow lines of) $Z$ and $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ to reach a neighbourhood of $P$ in $M$ (adapted neighbourhood, using our terminology in Section 4.4), noting that $Z$ preserves $\partial M$ and $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ is orthogonal to it. Crucially, we keep the ambient metric and the variational information, while [17] work with the Euclidean metric in $B^{n+1}_{+}(0)$ (following [38]). That choice would not work for our method, since the Euclidean mean curvature of the transformed hypersurface becomes nonzero and its gradient inevitably appears in the estimates, producing error terms that are not controlled by the available hypotheses. On the other hand, the tilt function $\tau$ , being built from $Z$ , reflects the Riemannian geometry of the ambient boundary; moreover, with the ambient metric and variational hypotheses left unaltered, $\tau$ satisfies a PDE that allows us to successfully carry out the approach of [4] in our setting. We note that $Z$ and $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ play a similar role, in flavour, to the construction of a so-called orthogonal foliation in [28], used in the context of a maximum principle for free-boundary minimal submanifolds.

More precisely, let $P$ be a smooth two-sided embedded $n$ -dimensional half-disc, let $\partial_{0}P=P\cap\partial M$ , and assume that $P$ meets $\partial M$ orthogonally along $\partial_{0}P$ . Such a $P$ can be constructed locally, for instance by taking the half-disk in Fermi coordinates centred at $p\in\partial M$ . See Section 4.1 for further details. If $p\in\partial_{0}P$ , write $P_{R}=B_{R}^{P}(p)$ . The adapted field $Z$ has a flow map $F_{Z}$ , and we set

$$ N_{\delta}^{Z}(P_{R}):=F_{Z}\bigl(P_{R}\times(-\delta,\delta)\bigr). $$

#### Theorem 1.14 (Boundary-orthogonal $\varepsilon$ -regularity for the tilt).

Let $M$ be as above and let $P$ be a smooth two-sided, embedded, $n$ -dimensional half-disc in $M$ meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally along $\partial_{0}P$ . Let the vector field $Z$ be as above, and let $p\in\partial_{0}P=P\cap\partial M$ . Assume $\rho_{1}>0$ is such that the flow map $F_{Z}$ is a diffeomorphism from $P_{\rho_{1}}\times(-\rho_{1},\rho_{1})$ onto the relatively open neighbourhood $\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P)$ of $P$ in $M$ . Assume that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{P_{\rho_{1}}}|A_{P}|^{2}+\sup_{P_{\rho_{1}}}|\nabla_{P}A_{P}|+\sup_{P_{\rho_{1}}}|\nabla^{2}_{P}A_{P}|^{2/3}\leq\Lambda^{2}, \displaystyle\sup|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+\sup|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|+\sup|\nabla^{4}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2/3}\leq\Lambda^{2}, \displaystyle\sup|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|+\sup|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|^{2/3}+\sup|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|^{1/2}\leq\Lambda^{2}, $$

in $\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P)$ , where $d_{\partial M}$ denotes the distance to $\partial M$ in $M$ , and $A_{P}$ denotes the second fundamental form of $P$ in $M$ . Then there exist $\varepsilon_{1}>0$ , $\delta_{1}\in(0,\rho_{1})$ and $R_{1}>0$ depending only on the dimension $n$ and the geometric constant $\Lambda$ such that the following holds. Let $\delta\in(0,\delta_{1})$ , $R\in(0,R_{1})$ , $\sigma\in(0,1)$ . Assume $\Sigma$ is a stable singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ and $\partial\Sigma\subset(\partial M\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P))$ . If we let $Z^{T}$ denote the orthogonal projection of $Z$ onto $T\Sigma$ , we have that if

$$ \mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{2}\coloneqq R^{-n}\int_{\Sigma}|Z^{T}|^{2}<(1-\sigma)^{n}\varepsilon^{2}\quad\text{for some $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{1}$,} $$

then

$$ |Z^{T}|\leq C_{1}(n,\Lambda)(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\quad\text{on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{\sigma R})$}, $$

where the constant $C_{1}=C_{1}(n,\Lambda)$ only depends on the dimension $n$ and the constant $\Lambda$ .

#### Theorem 1.15 (Boundary-orthogonal sheeting).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.14, there exist an integer $Q\geq 1$ and ordered Lipschitz functions

$$ u^{Z}_{1}\leq u^{Z}_{2}\leq\ldots\leq u^{Z}_{Q},\qquad u^{Z}_{j}\colon P_{R/2}\rightarrow(-\delta,\delta), $$

such that

$$ \overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{Z}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u^{Z}_{j})\bigr), $$

where $F_{Z}(\operatorname{graph}(u^{Z}_{j}))=\{F_{Z}(y,u^{Z}_{j}(y)):y\in P_{R/2}\}$ and $F_{Z}\colon P_{R/2}\times(-\delta,\delta)\rightarrow M$ is the flow map of the vector field $Z$ . Furthermore,

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{P}(u^{Z}_{j})\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\delta+\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\right), $$

for every $j=1,\ldots,Q$ , where the constant $C(n,\Lambda)$ only depends on the dimension $n$ and the geometric constant $\Lambda$ in (1.3). Moreover,

- (i) If we further assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ , then there exist smooth functions $v^{Z}_{1},v^{Z}_{2},\ldots,v^{Z}_{Q}\colon P_{R/2}\rightarrow(-\delta,\delta)$ such that

$$ \overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{Z}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(v^{Z}_{j})\bigr), $$

and with

$$ \|\nabla^{2}v^{Z}_{j}\|_{C^{0}(P_{R/2})}+R^{\alpha}[\nabla^{2}v^{Z}_{j}]_{\alpha,P_{R/2}}\leq C(n,\alpha,\Lambda)\left(R^{-1}\left(\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+\delta\right)+1\right) $$

for all $j=1,2,\ldots,Q$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . In particular,

$$ R|A_{\Sigma}|\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\delta+R+\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\right) $$

on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})$ .

- (ii) If, on the other hand, we assume that $\Sigma$ is embedded, then $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})=\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})$ , $u^{Z}_{1},\ldots u^{Z}_{Q}$ are smooth and

$$ u^{Z}_{1}<u^{Z}_{2}<\dots<u^{Z}_{Q}\quad\text{on $P_{R/2}$}. $$

Moreover, the $u^{Z}_{j}$ satisfy estimates

$$ \|\nabla^{2}u^{Z}_{j}\|_{C^{0}(P_{R/2})}+R^{\alpha}[\nabla^{2}u^{Z}_{j}]_{\alpha,P_{R/2}}\leq C(n,\alpha,\Lambda)\left(R^{-1}\left(\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}+\delta\right)+1\right) $$

for all $j=1,2,\ldots,Q$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . Lastly, $R|A_{\Sigma}|\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\delta+R+\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\right)$ on $\Sigma\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R/2})$ .

#### 1.2.4. Examples

We now construct two examples showing that, in the immersed setting, when $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S})>0$ genuine singular points of branch type may be present both in $\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\overline{\partial\Sigma}$ (and may possibly lie on $\partial M$ ) and in $\overline{\partial\Sigma}$ . By abuse of terminology, we will refer to these two situations as interior branch points of $\Sigma$ , and boundary branch points of $\Sigma$ , respectively. Neither stability nor the existence of a flat tangent cone implies regularity at a point of contact with $\partial M$ . Example 1.16 exhibits an interior branch point lying on $\partial M$ , at which the surface is tangent to $\partial M$ and has a multiplicity-two planar tangent cone. The product construction in Example 1.17 produces a genuine free-boundary stable minimal immersion whose codimension-two branch set reaches the boundary and whose tangent cone there is a multiplicity-two half-hyperplane meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally. Thus, both types of flat cone appearing in our boundary sheeting theory can occur at branch points and therefore cannot, for immersed hypersurfaces, yield regularity. On the other hand, the sheeting theorems imply the uniqueness of the flat tangent cone, as recorded in Corollary 1.18.

#### Example 1.16 (Interior branch point touching the boundary).

We will now exhibit a branched minimal immersion with an interior branch point touching the boundary $\partial M$ . Consider $x_{3}=u_{\pm}(x)$ , where $x=(x_{1},x_{2})$ , satisfying $|u(x)|\leq C|x|^{\alpha}$ . Let $b_{R}(x)=-R+\sqrt{R^{2}-|x|^{2}}=-\frac{|x|^{2}}{2R}+O(|x|^{4})$ be the upper half-sphere centred at $-Re_{3}$ . If $\alpha>2$ , then

$$ u_{\pm}(x)\geq-c|x|^{\alpha}>-\frac{|x|^{2}}{2R}+O(|x|^{4})=b_{R}(x), $$

for $|x|$ sufficiently small. In particular, $u=\pm c\Re(z^{5/2})$ satisfies this property, but it is harmonic, not minimal. We will use the Weierstrass–Enneper parametrization to circumvent this. Consider $\Phi(\zeta)=(\zeta(1-\zeta^{6}),\mathrm{i}\zeta(1+\zeta^{6}),2\zeta^{4}),$ and note that $\Phi\cdot\Phi\equiv 0$ . In particular,

$$ X(\zeta)=\Re\int\Phi(\zeta)\,d\zeta=\Re\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}}{2}-\frac{\zeta^{8}}{8},\mathrm{i}\frac{\zeta^{2}}{2}+\mathrm{i}\frac{\zeta^{8}}{8},\frac{2\zeta^{5}}{5}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

The Weierstrass–Enneper theorem (cf. [8, p. 33]) shows that $X$ is a branched minimal immersion, and that $\zeta=0$ is an isolated branch point. Furthermore, writing $X=(X^{\prime},X_{3})$ with $X^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , we have

$$ X^{\prime}(\zeta)=\frac{1}{2}(\Re(\zeta^{2}),-\Im(\zeta^{2}))+O(|\zeta|^{8})\qquad\text{and}\qquad X_{3}(\zeta)=\frac{2}{5}\Re(\zeta^{5}), $$

so that $|X^{\prime}(\zeta)|\simeq|\zeta|^{2}$ , while $|X_{3}(\zeta)|\leq C|\zeta|^{5}\leq C|X^{\prime}(\zeta)|^{5/2},$ so that $X_{3}\simeq\pm c\Re((x_{1}+\mathrm{i}x_{2})^{5/2})$ as required. Now, for small enough $\zeta$ , there holds

$$ |X(\zeta)+Re_{3}|^{2}-R^{2}=|X^{\prime}(\zeta)|^{2}+X_{3}(\zeta)^{2}+2RX_{3}(\zeta)\geq c|\zeta|^{4}-C_{R}|\zeta|^{5}>0, $$

with equality holding at $\zeta=0$ . This is a smooth stable immersion $f:S\coloneqq D\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , where $D$ is a sufficiently small disc centred at the origin in $\mathbb{R}^{2}=\mathbb{C}$ . Stability follows from Barta’s theorem (cf. [8, Lemma 1.36]). More precisely, if $\nu(\zeta)$ denotes the upward pointing unit normal, then $\langle\nu(\zeta),e_{3}\rangle$ gives a positive Jacobi field. Take then as manifold-with-boundary $\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus B_{R}(-Re_{3})$ . We refer to [39] for more examples of stable branched minimal immersions.

#### Example 1.17 (Boundary branch point).

Let $f\colon S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$ be as in Example 1.16, so that in particular $f$ is a two-sided stable branched minimal immersion, with $\partial\Sigma=\emptyset$ and discrete branch set $\mathcal{B}$ . Set $\Sigma=f(S)$ , $N=\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , and $F:S\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}^{4}_{+}$ , as well as

$$ \widehat{\Sigma}\coloneqq\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}_{+},\qquad\widehat{M}\coloneqq N\times\mathbb{R}_{+}=\mathbb{R}_{+}^{4},\qquad F(x,y,s)\coloneqq(f(x),s), $$

where $\mathbb{R}_{+}=[0,\infty)$ and $\widehat{g}=g+ds^{2}$ . Then $\partial\widehat{\Sigma}=\Sigma\times\{0\}$ and $F(\partial\widehat{\Sigma})\subset\partial\widehat{M}.$ For $X\in T_{x}\Sigma$ , and $a\in\mathbb{R}$ , $dF(X,a)=(df(X),a)$ so that $\operatorname{rank}dF=\operatorname{rank}df+1.$ Hence

$$ \widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{reg}}=(\Sigma\setminus\mathcal{B})\times\mathbb{R}_{+},\qquad\mathcal{B}_{F}=\mathcal{B}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}. $$

Thus $\dim\mathcal{B}_{F}=1$ , so $\mathcal{B}_{F}$ has codimension $2$ , and its boundary part is $\mathcal{B}\times\{0\}$ . On the parameter manifold $S\times\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , $F^{*}\widehat{g}=f^{*}g+ds^{2}.$ If $\nu$ is a unit normal to $f$ , then $\widehat{\nu}=(\nu,0)$ is a unit normal to $F$ , and the product connection gives $A_{F}\bigl((X,a),(Y,b)\bigr)=A_{f}(X,Y).$ All mixed and Euclidean-factor terms vanish; hence $\operatorname{tr}A_{F}=\operatorname{tr}A_{f}=0,$ so that $F$ is minimal. Along $\partial\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ , the outward conormal of $F$ and the outward normal to $\partial\widehat{M}$ are both $-\partial_{s}$ . Thus $F$ is free-boundary, see also Lemma C.2. Since $\partial\widehat{M}$ is totally geodesic, $|A_{F}|^{2}=|A_{f}|^{2},$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_{\widehat{M}}(\widehat{\nu},\widehat{\nu})=\operatorname{Ric}_{N}(\nu,\nu).$ Therefore, for $\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{reg}})$ , writing $\varphi_{s}(x)\coloneqq\varphi(x,s)$ ,

$$ Q_{F}(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}Q_{f}(\varphi_{s})\,ds+\int_{\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{reg}}}|\partial_{s}\varphi|^{2}\,d\mu_{F}\geq 0. $$

By splitting a variation into odd and even components with respect to reflection in the totally geodesic boundary, we see that $F$ is free-boundary stable. Stability extends across $\mathcal{B}_{F}$ by logarithmic cutoff. Lastly, if the tangent varifold of $f$ at $p$ is $Q|P|$ , then that of $F$ at $F(p,0)$ is $Q|P\times\mathbb{R}_{+}|,$ a multiplicity- $Q$ half-hyperplane meeting $\partial\widehat{M}$ orthogonally.

#### Corollary 1.18 (Uniqueness of flat tangent cones).

Let $(\Sigma,\partial\Sigma)$ be as in Definition 2.12, and let $x\in\overline{\Sigma}$ be such that a tangent cone (to the stationary varifold $|\Sigma|$ at $x$ ) is either a half-hyperplane orthogonal to $T_{x}\partial M$ , or the hyperplane $T_{x}\partial M$ (in both cases, a constant integer multiplicity may be present). Then the tangent cone is unique.

#### 1.2.5. From the sheeting theorems to the compactness theory

We finally indicate how the local estimates yield Theorem 1.1. The local mass bounds, together with the corresponding local first-variation bounds, give subsequential varifold compactness. In the present class, the required support convergence follows directly from a uniform lower density estimate obtained by combining the usual interior monotonicity formula with the boundary-centred monotonicity formula of [18]. In particular, no reference to the (computationally heavy) monotonicity of reflected density is needed.

Let $V$ be a limit varifold and consider a tangent cone at a boundary point. After doubling in the tangent half-space, a cone with an $n$ -dimensional spine is flat and falls into one of the two models above: either a multiple of $T_{x}\partial M$ , or a multiple of an orthogonal half-hyperplane. Varifold convergence gives height closeness to the relevant model. The height-to-tilt inequalities of Section 5.1 turn this into small $L^{2}$ tilt, and Theorems 1.12 and 1.15 then give smooth graphical convergence at a fixed scale. This proves regularity at every flat tangent cone and, at the same time, uniqueness of that cone.

Up to here, no distinction between embeddings and immersions is needed. The next step, on the other hand, uses embeddedness in an essential way. The Schoen–Simon slicing argument, adapted to the boundary, excludes stationary classical cones with an $(n-1)$ -dimensional spine. For immersed hypersurfaces, sheets may branch or pass through one another, as Examples 1.16 and 1.17 illustrate, and this exclusion mechanism is no longer available in the same form (see Question 1.19 for recent progress).

Once the $(n-1)$ -dimensional stratum is excluded, the standard dimension-reduction argument for stable cones gives $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\operatorname{sing}V\leq n-7$ , by adapting the usual argument to the case of free-boundary stationary varifolds. At this stage as well we do not need to introduce a reflected density or reflected monotonicity formula: the ordinary interior monotonicity formula and the boundary monotonicity formula of [18] suffice. Reflection is used only at the tangent-cone level, where it becomes straightforward, as the manifold-with-boundary has become a half-space and the boundary has become a Euclidean hyperplane.

#### 1.2.6. On the smallness assumption and the stationarity condition

Our assumptions on the singular set are also novel, and less restrictive than in other previous works on stable immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, such as [49]. Indeed, we only require the set of non-immersed singular points to have locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ measure, and only impose stationarity away from this set. In order to be able to use the consequences of global stationarity, such as monotonicity of area ratios, we then show that stationarity extends across sets of locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ measure by constructing a function that blows up on the exceptional set and is superharmonic along every $n$ -dimensional tangent plane (this part is inspired by a construction of Harvey–Lawson in [21]); a logarithmic Caccioppoli estimate then yields cutoff functions of vanishing tangential energy. See Appendix B for details.

### 1.3. Open questions and future directions

We finish this introduction by mentioning some questions and open problems that arose during the preparation of this work.

#### Question 1.19.

Is there a compactness theory for stable singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces with a singular set of locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure? This seems likely given the present work and the recent substantial advances in the interior theory in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ : in [45], Wang–Zhang produce a tilt function that allows them to extend the methods and conclusions of [4], leading to a sharp $(n-3)$ -dimensional bound for the non-branch singular set, and establish a branched sheeting theorem near cones that are unions of hyperplanes with a spine of dimension $n-1$ and $n-2$ . At the free boundary one must additionally understand boundary branch points and their interaction with the touching set.

#### Question 1.20.

Can the boundary-orthogonal $\varepsilon$ -regularity and sheeting theorems (Theorems 1.14 and 1.15) be proven under the weaker notion of stability away from the touching set used in [19, Definition 2.2]? The present proof uses the analytic stability inequality for all compactly supported scalar test functions, including across the touching set, and it is not immediate how to recover the same Caccioppoli estimate from the weaker hypothesis.

Notice that, on the other hand, the tilt function used in the boundary-parallel case naturally vanishes on the touching set, and it is an admissible test function for the stability inequality under the weaker notion of stability away from the touching set.

#### Question 1.21.

Can the sheeting and compactness theorems above be generalised to the capillary setting? This appears to be promising, in light of the present work and of very recent or simultaneous progress on related aspects. A theory for stable minimal hypersurfaces-with-boundary with a given capillary angle in a Euclidean half-space is developed in [46]. Moreover, in the forthcoming work [2], a regularity and compactness theory is established, for stable hypersurfaces whose mean curvature is prescribed by an ambient function on a Riemannian manifold. A combination of the three works is likely to lead to a compactness and regularity theory for capillary hypersurfaces in the presence of a wetting energy and a potential energy.

#### Question 1.22.

Let $V$ be an $n$ -dimensional rectifiable varifold which is stationary away from a relatively closed set $S$ satisfying $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(S)=0$ . Must $V$ be stationary across $S$ ? Proposition B.5 gives a positive answer when $S$ has locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure. Its proof is critical at that exponent and the construction used there no longer has the required properties under the weaker assumption $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(S)=0$ .

#### Question 1.23.

What structural hypothesis gives an optimal regularity and compactness theory for free-boundary stationary integral varifolds whose regular part is stable? The desired statement would be a free-boundary counterpart of Wickramasekera’s interior theory [50], allowing stable regular parts without an a priori $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ bound on the singular set and excluding the appropriate boundary classical singularities. This question is the subject of ongoing work.

## 2. Preliminaries and Notation

### 2.1. Inequalities and constants

We shall use the convention that $C(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\dots)$ denotes a positive constant (which may change from line to line) and depends only on the parameters $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\dots$ unless we specify otherwise.

### 2.2. Geometric setup

We refer to [24, pp. 24–29] for the definition of a (smooth) $(n+1)$ -dimensional manifold-with-boundary $M$ . We stress that $\partial M$ is itself a (smooth) $n$ -dimensional manifold, and that $M$ contains it. The interior of $M$ , i.e. $M\setminus\partial M$ , is a (smooth) $(n+1)$ -dimensional manifold33 3 The notions of boundary and interior in this setting are not to be understood with respect to the topology of an ambient space in which we realise $M$ as a subset..

A Riemannian manifold-with-boundary $(M,\mathrm{g})$ is obtained from $M$ by endowing it with a smooth Riemannian metric $\mathrm{g}$ , with smoothness required up to the boundary44 4 In local charts, this means that the metric is smooth in the interior and all of its derivatives extend continuously to the boundary.. Let $\nabla$ denote the Levi-Civita connection on $M$ induced by $\mathrm{g}$ . We will sometimes stress the dependence on the metric by writing $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}$ .

We denote by $\mathbf{n}$ the inward unit normal of $\partial M$ , and we use the following notation for the (scalar-valued) second fundamental form of $\partial M$ in $M$ :

$$ \mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(Y,Z)\coloneqq\mathrm{g}(\nabla_{Y}Z,\mathbf{n})=-\mathrm{g}(\nabla_{Y}\mathbf{n},Z), $$

for vector fields $Y$ and $Z$ tangent to $\partial M$ .

#### Remark 2.1.

We note that, essentially by the collar neighbourhood construction ([24, Theorems 9.25 and 9.26]), in the case $\partial M\neq\emptyset$ , the manifold $M$ can be realised as a proper (i.e. strict) closed subset $\iota(M)\subsetneq\Omega$ of a smooth $(n+1)$ -manifold $\Omega$ , with $\iota\colon M\rightarrow\Omega$ a smooth proper embedding. In other words, $M$ can be seen as a closed subset $M\subset\Omega$ with smooth boundary $\partial M$ . Additionally, $\Omega$ can be taken to be smoothly homotopic to the interior of $M$ . Furthermore, $\Omega$ admits a (smooth) Riemannian metric that restricts on $M$ to the given one55 5 This follows essentially from a lemma of Borel, showing that a function is smooth up to the boundary, in the sense defined earlier, if and only if it admits a smooth extension across the boundary, see [24, p.27]..

Roughly speaking, the collar neighbourhood (which is a subset of $M$ diffeomorphic to $\partial M\times[0,1)$ , with $\partial M\times\{0\}$ identified with $\partial M$ ) can be doubled, reflected and smoothly attached outside of $M$ along $\partial M$ , thus creating $\Omega$ .

By Remark 2.1 and [25, Theorem 5.25 and Corollary 6.39(d)], whenever $P\subset\partial M$ is a relatively compact smooth submanifold of $\partial M$ , then there exists some $\rho_{P}>0$ such that the normal exponential map $F_{\partial M}$ of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $P\times[0,\rho_{P})$ onto its image $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{P}}(P)\coloneqq F_{\partial M}(P\times[0,\rho_{P}))$ of $P$ in $M$ .

#### 2.2.1. Free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces

We will be interested in the following class of codimension one submanifolds-with-boundary, inside a smooth complete, Riemannian manifold-with-boundary $(M^{n+1},\mathrm{g})$ .

#### Definition 2.2 (Free-boundary minimal immersions and embeddings).

Given a smooth $n$ -dimensional manifold-with-boundary $N$ and a relatively open set $U\subset M$ , a smooth immersion $\iota:(N,\iota^{*}\mathrm{g})\to U\subset(M,\mathrm{g})$ is a free-boundary minimal immersion in $U$ if

- (1) $\iota(\partial N)\subset\partial M\cap U$ ,

- (2) its mean curvature vanishes on the interior $N\setminus\partial N$ of $N$ ,

- (3) for all $z\in\partial N$ , the inward conormal of $\partial N$ in $N$ at $z$ is mapped to $\mathbf{n}(\iota(z))$ .

We shall denote the image $\iota(N)$ of $\iota$ by $\Sigma$ , and let $\partial\Sigma\coloneqq\iota(\partial N)$ . Then $(\Sigma,\partial\Sigma)$ is said to be a smooth immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $(M,\partial M)$ . If, furthermore, $\iota$ is a homeomorphism of $N$ onto its image, we will say that $(\Sigma,\partial\Sigma)$ is a smooth embedded free-boundary hypersurface in $(M,\partial M)$ .

In what follows we shall often simplify the notation and write “ $\Sigma$ is a smooth immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface”, without explicitly referring to the manifold-with-boundary $N$ or the map $\iota:N\to M$ . Similarly, we shall often drop the more cumbersome notation $(M,\partial M,\mathrm{g})$ , $(\Sigma,\partial\Sigma)$ for (Riemannian) manifolds-with-boundary and immersed/embedded hypersurfaces with boundary, in favour of the simpler $(M,\mathrm{g})$ , $\Sigma$ .

#### Remark 2.3.

Note that the intersection of the interior of $\Sigma$ and $\partial M$ is not necessarily empty as easy examples show. We stress that the orthogonality between $\Sigma$ and $\partial M$ is only imposed at points in $\partial\Sigma$ .

#### Remark 2.4.

Notice that the conditions in Definition 2.2 imply that the immersion $\iota:N\to M$ is stationary for area with respect to compactly supported variations $(\iota_{t}\colon N\rightarrow M)_{t\in(-\delta,\delta)}$ which preserve the inclusion $\iota_{t}(\partial N)\subset\partial M$ for all $t$ , as is easily seen from the first variation formula for area66 6 Notice that the conditions in Definition 2.2 are stronger than stationarity with respect to compactly supported variations which map $\partial N$ into the boundary $\partial M$ . Indeed stationarity only implies the vanishing of the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ away from the touching set $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M$ , which is not assumed to be empty, as observed in Remark 2.3..

#### Notation 2.5.

From now on, whenever for $A\subset M$ we write an integral $\int_{\Sigma\cap A}f$ , we shall always implicitly assume it is shorthand for the integral $\int_{\iota^{-1}(A)}f\circ\iota\,d\mathcal{H}^{n}_{\iota^{*}\mathrm{g}}$ over $\iota^{-1}(A)$ with respect to the induced metric $\iota^{*}\mathrm{g}$ . Similarly quantities such as the second fundamental form $A_{\Sigma}$ or a unit normal $\nu_{\Sigma}$ are to be understood implicitly as quantities on $N$ .

#### 2.2.2. Singular free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces

We will be concerned with the class of stable immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces (see Definition 2.12 below). It is well-known that allowing a small singular set is unavoidable for a comprehensive theory in this class (e.g. for regularity, compactness, existence). We shall do so by introducing the notion of singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, where we impose some a priori size constraint on the singular set.

#### Definition 2.6 (Singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces).

Let $\iota:N\to M$ be a free-boundary minimal immersion as in Definition 2.2 with image $\Sigma=\iota(N)$ , and let $\mathcal{S}=\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\Sigma$ , where the closure is taken in $M$ . We shall say that $\Sigma$ (or, more precisely, $\overline{\Sigma}$ ) is a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ if:

- (1) The immersion $\iota$ is proper in $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , i.e. for every compact set $K\subset M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ the inverse image $\iota^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $N$ .

- (2) The measure $\mathcal{H}^{n}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma$ is locally finite, in the sense that for any compact $K\subset M$ we have $\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma\cap K)<\infty$ .

- (3) The set $\mathcal{S}\coloneqq\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\Sigma$ has locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -measure (in $M$ ), i.e. for any compact $K\subset M$ we have $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S}\cap K)<\infty$ .

We shall refer to $\mathcal{S}$ as the singular set of $\Sigma$ .

Notice that by (2), a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ defines an integral $n$ -varifold $V=|\Sigma|$ in $M$ with weight measure $\|V\|=\mathcal{H}^{n}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|=\overline{\Sigma}$ . Moreover, by definition of a smooth free boundary minimal immersion, $V$ is free-boundary stationary in $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ in the sense of Section C.1.

#### Remark 2.7.

Under the hypotheses of Definition 2.6 the varifold $V=|\Sigma|$ is free-boundary stationary in $M$ in the sense of Section 5.2. More precisely, under those assumptions one can extend stationarity from $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ to $M$ (thus giving e.g. area-ratio estimates on balls centred on $\mathcal{S}$ by the monotonicity formula), see the discussion in Appendix B (Proposition B.5 in particular).

#### Remark 2.8.

As stated, in Definition 2.6 we may have points in $\mathcal{S}$ that are not genuinely singular, e.g. we take $\Sigma$ to be a punctured equatorial disc in $\mathbb{B}^{3}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ to be the missing point. Strictly speaking, one should define the singular set $\operatorname{sing}(\Sigma)$ as the set of all $x\in M$ such that for every $r>0$ the intersection of $\overline{\Sigma}$ with the geodesic ball $B_{r}(x)$ in $\Omega$ is not the image of a smooth free-boundary immersion in $M$ which is proper in $B_{r}(x)$ , that is, $\operatorname{sing}(\Sigma)$ is the set of points across which $\Sigma$ cannot be smoothly extended as a proper free-boundary immersion77 7 The set $\operatorname{sing}(\Sigma)$ corresponds to the (non-immersed) singular set of the varifold $|\Sigma|$ induced by $\Sigma$ , in the definition of [49].. However, clearly $\operatorname{sing}(\Sigma)\subset\mathcal{S}$ and, after extending $\Sigma$ across its removable singularities, one may take $\mathcal{S}=\operatorname{sing}(\Sigma)$ .

#### Remark 2.9.

We will speak of a smooth properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface when $\mathcal{S}=\emptyset$ . In this case the notion reduces to Definition 2.2 with the additional assumption of properness in $M$ .

#### Remark 2.10.

In our main compactness theorem, cf. Theorem 1.1, we specialise to (possibly) singular embeddings, in which case the immersion in Definition 2.6 is assumed to be an embedding. We also recall that a proper injective immersion with closed image is necessarily an embedding.

#### Remark 2.11.

When we refer to a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface as being two-sided we shall always mean that there exists a continuous global determination of a unit normal (more precisely, that the pullback normal bundle on $N$ is trivial, and a global unit normal is a continuous section of the pullback unit normal bundle on $N$ ).

In what follows, we shall often simply write “ $\Sigma$ is a singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ ”. This is always to be interpreted as shorthand for “ $\Sigma$ is a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ ” in the sense of Definition 2.6, unless we specify otherwise.

#### 2.2.3. Stability

We shall take the following analytic inequality as our notion of stability for singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces. We shall restrict ourselves to two-sided hypersurfaces, as we make clear in the following definition.

#### Definition 2.12 (Stable free-boundary minimal hypersurface).

Let $\Sigma=\iota(N)$ be a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in the sense of Definition 2.6. Further assume $\Sigma$ to be two-sided, with unit normal $\nu_{\Sigma}$ and second fundamental form $A_{\Sigma}$ 88 8 More precisely, $\nu_{\Sigma}$ and $A_{\Sigma}$ are tensor fields on $N$ along $\iota$ , see Notation 2.5.. We say that $\Sigma$ is stable if the following inequality holds

$$ \int_{N}|\nabla_{N}\varphi|^{2}-(|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\nu_{\Sigma},\nu_{\Sigma}))\varphi^{2}-\int_{\partial N}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\nu_{\Sigma},\nu_{\Sigma})\varphi^{2}\geq 0 $$

for all $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(N)$ , where $N$ is endowed with $\iota^{*}\mathrm{g}$ .

#### Remark 2.13.

It turns out (see Definition 2.6 and the discussion in Appendix B) that the assumptions in Definition 2.6 imply that the singular set $\mathcal{S}$ has vanishing relative 2-capacity in $\Sigma$ , denoted $\operatorname{cap}_{2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ . Thus, (2.1) extends to any test function of the form $\varphi=\phi\circ\iota$ for $\phi\in C^{1}_{c}(M)$ . The proof is by approximation using the cutoff functions provided by Corollary B.6 (see Lemma 2.14 for a similar argument).

From now on, following the convention laid out in Notation 2.5, when we want to plug a test function of the form $\varphi=\phi\circ\iota$ for $\phi\in C^{1}_{c}(M)$ into (2.1), we shall always write integrals directly on $\Sigma$ ; that is, we shall write $\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi|^{2}$ in place of $\int_{N}|\nabla_{N}(\phi\circ\iota)|^{2}$ .

#### 2.2.4. Trace and Sobolev inequality

Fix a relatively compact open set $U\subset M$ such that the distance function $d_{\partial M}$ to $\partial M$ is smooth on $U$ . Let $\Sigma$ be a two-sided singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset U$ . Then, appropriate versions of the classical trace inequality and Sobolev inequality hold for $\Sigma$ .

In this subsection, functions on $\Sigma$ are understood on the parameter manifold $N$ , as in Notation 2.5.

#### Lemma 2.14.

Let $\Sigma$ be a two-sided singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset U$ . Then if $f$ is a non-negative compactly supported Lipschitz function in $U$ , we have

$$ \int_{\partial\Sigma}f\leq\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}f|+\left(\sqrt{n}\sup_{U}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|\right)\int_{\Sigma}f. $$

For simplicity, write $C_{\mathrm{tr}}=C_{\mathrm{tr}}(n,U)\coloneqq\sqrt{n}\sup_{U}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|$ .

#### Proof.

Let us first give a one-line proof in the case $f$ is supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ (see also [11, Lemma 2.1]), and then extend it to the more general case of $f$ compactly supported in $U$ by a (more or less standard) excision argument based on Corollary B.6.

Suppose $f$ is supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ . Then by the divergence theorem on the immersed hypersurface $\Sigma$ we have

$$ \int_{\partial\Sigma}f=\int_{\partial\Sigma}\mathrm{g}(f\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M},\eta)=-\int_{\Sigma}\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}(f\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M})=-\int_{\Sigma}\mathrm{g}(\nabla_{\Sigma}f,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M})+f\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}(\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}), $$

where in the last equality we used that the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ vanishes identically. Equation (2.2) follows directly.

For a general $f$ , let $K\Subset U$ be such that $\operatorname{spt}f\subset K$ . By Corollary B.6, there exist cutoffs $\chi_{j}\in C_{c}^{0,1}(U)$ such that $0\leq\chi_{j}\leq 1$ , $\operatorname{spt}\chi_{j}\subset U\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , $\chi_{j}\to 1$ locally on $\Sigma$ , and $\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|^{2}\to 0$ . Apply (2.2) to $f_{j}\coloneqq\chi_{j}f\circ\iota$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\partial\Sigma}f_{j} \displaystyle\leq\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(\chi_{j}f)|+C_{\mathrm{tr}}\int_{\Sigma}f_{j}\leq\int_{\Sigma}(\chi_{j}|\nabla_{\Sigma}f|+f|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|)+C_{\mathrm{tr}}\int_{\Sigma}f_{j}. $$

Notice that by (ii) of Definition 2.6, $\Sigma$ 99 9 or, more precisely, the measure $\mathcal{H}^{n}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma$ . has locally finite mass, so by the properties of the cutoffs $\chi_{j}$ we have

$$ \int_{\Sigma}f|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|\leq\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma\cap K)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\Sigma\cap K}|\nabla\chi_{j}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\to 0. $$

The other terms on the right hand side converge by dominated convergence, and

$$ \int_{\partial\Sigma}f\leq\liminf_{j}\int_{\partial\Sigma}f_{j} $$

by Fatou’s lemma. This concludes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 2.15.

Notice that by taking $f\equiv 1$ in (2.2), we obtain an upper bound for $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial\Sigma)$ in terms of the geometry of $U$ and $\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma)$ .

The trace inequality turns out to be very useful in dealing with stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, because it allows us to absorb the boundary term in the stability inequality into an interior term.

#### Lemma 2.16.

Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset U$ . For every $\alpha>0$ there is a finite constant $C(n,\alpha,U)$ depending on $n,\alpha$ , $\sup_{U}|\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}|,\sup_{U}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|$ such that

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|A|^{2}\zeta^{2}\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\zeta|^{2}+C(n,\alpha,U)\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2} $$

for all bounded compactly supported Lipschitz functions $\zeta$ on $U$ . More precisely, $C(n,\alpha,U)$ can be taken to be $\sup_{U}|\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}|+(4\alpha^{-1}+\sqrt{n})\sup_{U}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let us first consider the case where $\zeta$ is supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ . Then (2.1) holds. Therefore, by Lemma 2.14 and Young’s inequality

$$ \left|\int_{\partial\Sigma}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\nu,\nu)\zeta^{2}\right|\leq\alpha\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\zeta|^{2}+\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}\|_{L^{\infty}}\left(\alpha^{-1}\|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}\|_{L^{\infty}}+C_{\mathrm{tr}}\right)\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2}. $$

This proves the result for compactly supported bounded Lipschitz functions $\zeta$ with $\operatorname{spt}\zeta\subset U\setminus\mathcal{S}$ .

For the general case, it is enough to apply the estimate we have just obtained to $\zeta_{j}\coloneqq\chi_{j}\zeta\in C_{c}^{0,1}(U\setminus\mathcal{S})$ , where $\chi_{j}$ is as in the proof of Lemma 2.14. ∎

Finally, we are going to need to use the following Sobolev inequality, which follows from Edelen’s Michael–Simon inequality for smooth free-boundary hypersurfaces in [11, Theorem 2.2].

#### Lemma 2.17.

Let $\Sigma$ be a two-sided singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset U$ . There are a dimensional constant $C_{\mathrm{Sob}}=C_{\mathrm{Sob}}(n)>0$ and a geometric constant $K_{\mathrm{Sob}}=K_{\mathrm{Sob}}(n,U)$ depending on $n$ and $\sup_{U}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|>0$ such that for all compactly supported Lipschitz functions $\zeta$ on $U$ , we have

$$ \left(\int_{\Sigma}|\zeta|^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{n}}\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\zeta|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2}\right)\quad\text{for $n\geq 3$}, $$

and

$$ \left(\int_{\Sigma}|\zeta|^{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\zeta|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\quad\text{for $n=2$}. $$

#### Proof.

For $\zeta$ supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ , this follows from the free-boundary Michael-Simon inequality in [11, Theorem 2.2] and the trace inequality (2.2) applied to $f=|\zeta|^{\frac{2(n-1)}{n-2}}$ for $n\geq 3$ and $f=\zeta^{2}$ for $n=2$ , followed by Young’s inequality.

The general case then follows from the same approximation argument as in Lemma 2.16 using Corollary B.6. ∎

### 2.3. Iteration à la De Giorgi

Now let $\Sigma$ be a free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ . In what follows we shall be interested in the situation where $\Sigma$ is weakly close, in a sense to be made precise later, to a smooth embedded two-sided hypersurface $P\subset M$ of one of the following two types:

- • $P$ is a geodesic ball $B^{\partial M}_{R}(p)$ in $\partial M$ centred at a point $p\in\partial M$ and $0<R<\operatorname{inj}_{p}(\partial M)$ (see Section 3);

- • $P$ is an $n$ -dimensional free-boundary half-disc in $M$ intersecting $\partial M$ orthogonally (see Section 4).

As explained in the Introduction, the central idea in the proofs of both Theorem 1.11 and Theorem 1.14 is an $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{\infty}$ estimate for the tilt relative to $P$ , which is obtained via a non-linear adaptation of De Giorgi’s iteration technique following [4].

The overall strategy in both cases is very similar: first, we introduce a tilt function to measure the deviation of the normal of $\Sigma$ from the normal of $P$ , and show that this function satisfies a differential inequality involving the norm $|A|^{2}$ of the second fundamental form of $\Sigma$ ; then by using truncations of this tilt as appropriate test functions in the stability inequality, we obtain an intrinsic Caccioppoli-type inequality on $\Sigma$ ; finally, thanks to the differential inequality satisfied by the tilt and the Sobolev inequality in Section 2.2.4, we set up a De Giorgi-style iterative scheme which results in a nonlinear recurrence equation for the $L^{2}$ -norm of successive truncations of the tilt function on smaller and smaller cylinders. The superlinear nature of the recurrence (see e.g. [4, Lemma B.1]) implies that, provided the $L^{2}$ -norm of the tilt is sufficiently small at the original scale, then the $L^{2}$ -norm of successive truncations on shrinking cylinders must go to 0, thereby providing an $L^{\infty}$ estimate for the tilt function at a smaller scale.

We now formulate this procedure abstractly, in a framework that applies to both tilt functions we shall use in Section 3 and Section 4.

#### 2.3.1. Setup

Let $\Sigma$ be a two-sided singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and assume $\overline{\Sigma}\subset U$ , where $U$ is a relatively compact open subset of $M$ . Let $\sigma\in(0,1)$ , $R>0$ and let $\{U_{r}\}_{0<r\leq R}$ be a nested family (increasing in $r$ ) of relatively open subsets of $\Sigma$ . Assume that for all $\sigma R\leq r<r^{\prime}\leq R$ , there exists a compactly supported Lipschitz function $\phi_{r,r^{\prime}}$ on $\Sigma$ such that

$$ 0\leq\phi_{r,r^{\prime}}\leq 1,\quad\phi_{r,r^{\prime}}\equiv 1\text{ on }U_{r},\quad\operatorname{spt}\phi_{r,r^{\prime}}\subset U_{r^{\prime}},\quad|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi_{r,r^{\prime}}|\leq\frac{C_{c}}{r^{\prime}-r} $$

for some constant $C_{c}$ independent of $r,r^{\prime}$ .

Let $u:\Sigma\to[0,1]$ be a locally Lipschitz function on $\Sigma$ and assume that there are constants $k_{*}\in(0,1]$ , $C_{\mathrm{Cac}},K_{\mathrm{Cac}}>0$ such that for every $k\in[0,k_{*}]$ and every compactly supported Lipschitz function $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Sigma)$ , the following Caccioppoli-type inequality is satisfied

$$ \int_{\{u>k\}}\left(1-\frac{k}{u}\right)|\nabla_{\Sigma}u|^{2}\phi^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{Cac}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}(u-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Cac}}^{2}\int_{\{u>k\}}\phi^{2}\right), $$

where as usual all integrals should more precisely be understood on $N$ (see 2.5). Finally, let $K_{*}\coloneqq\max\{K_{\mathrm{Sob}},K_{\mathrm{Cac}}\}$ .

#### Lemma 2.18 (De Giorgi iteration).

Let $\Sigma$ , $u$ be as above and let $\sigma\in(0,1)$ be fixed. There exists $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}(n,k_{*},C_{\mathrm{Sob}},C_{\mathrm{Cac}},C_{c})>0$ with the following property. Let $\mathcal{d}\in(0,k_{*}]$ . If $K_{*}R\leq 1$ and

$$ R^{-n}\int_{U_{R}}u^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}^{2}(1-\sigma)^{n}\mathcal{d}^{n+2}, $$

then

$$ \sup_{U_{\sigma R}}u\leq\mathcal{d}. $$

#### Proof.

Define

$$ k_{\ell}=\mathcal{d}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{\ell}}\right),\quad r_{\ell}=\sigma R+2^{-\ell}(1-\sigma)R $$

for $\ell\geq 0$ . Hence $k_{0}=0$ and $k_{\ell}\uparrow\mathcal{d}\leq k_{*}$ , $r_{0}=R$ and $r_{\ell}\downarrow\sigma R$ .

Since $k_{\ell}\leq k_{*}$ , we can apply (2.5). Let $U_{\ell}\coloneqq U_{r_{\ell}}$ , $u_{\ell}\coloneqq(u-k_{\ell})_{+}$ , and $D_{\ell}\coloneqq U_{\ell}\cap\{u>k_{\ell}\}$ . Then let

$$ G_{\ell}\coloneqq\int_{\Sigma\cap U_{\ell}}u_{\ell}^{2}. $$

Notice that, by definition (since both the cylinders and the truncations decrease),

$$ G_{\ell+1}\leq G_{\ell}. $$

Now let $\phi_{\ell}\coloneqq\phi_{r_{\ell+1},r_{\ell}}$ , so that

$$ 0\leq\phi_{\ell}\leq 1,\quad\phi_{\ell}\equiv 1\text{ on }U_{\ell+1},\quad\operatorname{spt}\phi_{\ell}\subset U_{\ell},\quad|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi_{\ell}|\leq\frac{C_{c}}{(1-\sigma)R}2^{\ell+1}, $$

where $C_{c}$ is the fixed constant from the setup.

On $D_{\ell+1}$ , by definition, we have $u>k_{\ell+1}$ , so that

$$ 1-\frac{k_{\ell}}{u}\geq\frac{k_{\ell+1}-k_{\ell}}{k_{\ell+1}}\geq 2^{-\ell-1}\quad\text{on $D_{\ell+1}$}. $$

Therefore,

$$ 2^{-\ell-1}\int_{\Sigma}\phi_{\ell}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}|^{2}=2^{-\ell-1}\int_{U_{\ell}\cap\{u>k_{\ell+1}\}}\phi_{\ell}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}u|^{2}\leq\int_{D_{\ell}}\left(1-\frac{k_{\ell}}{u}\right)|\nabla_{\Sigma}u|^{2}\phi_{\ell}^{2}, $$

and, by (2.5), since $|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi_{\ell}|^{2}\leq C^{2}_{c}4^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}$ and $\operatorname{spt}\phi_{\ell}\subset U_{\ell}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma}\phi_{\ell}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}|^{2} \displaystyle\leq 2^{\ell+1}C_{\mathrm{Cac}}\left(C^{2}_{c}\,4^{\ell+1}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}G_{\ell}+K^{2}_{\mathrm{Cac}}\,\mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell})\right) \displaystyle\leq C_{0}8^{\ell}\left(((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}G_{\ell}+K^{2}_{\mathrm{Cac}}\,\mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell})\right), $$

where, throughout this proof, $C_{0}$ denotes a constant which is allowed to change from line to line depending on $n,k_{*},C_{\mathrm{Cac}},C_{\mathrm{Sob}},C_{c}$ only.

Since $|\nabla_{\Sigma}(\phi_{\ell}u_{\ell+1})|^{2}\leq 2\phi^{2}_{\ell}|\nabla_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}|^{2}+2u^{2}_{\ell+1}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\phi_{\ell}|^{2}$ , then

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|\nabla(\phi_{\ell}u_{\ell+1})|^{2}\leq C_{0}8^{\ell}\left(((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}G_{\ell}+K^{2}_{\mathrm{Cac}}\,\mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell})\right). $$

Notice that on $D_{\ell}$ we have $u_{\ell-1}=u-k_{\ell-1}>k_{\ell}-k_{\ell-1}\geq\mathcal{d}2^{-\ell}$ , so that by Markov’s inequality

$$ \mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell})\leq\left(\frac{2^{\ell}}{\mathcal{d}}\right)^{2}\int_{D_{\ell}}u_{\ell-1}^{2}\leq\left(\frac{2^{\ell}}{\mathcal{d}}\right)^{2}\int_{U_{\ell-1}}u_{\ell-1}^{2}\leq 4^{\ell}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}, $$

as $D_{\ell}\subset U_{\ell}\subset U_{\ell-1}$ . Since $u_{\ell+1}\leq u_{\ell}$ , $G_{\ell}\leq G_{\ell-1}$ and $\mathcal{d}\leq 1$ , by (2.8) and (2.9), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(u_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell})|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}u^{2}_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell}^{2} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}8^{\ell}\left(((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}G_{\ell}+4^{\ell}\mathcal{d}^{-2}K_{*}^{2}G_{\ell-1}\right)+K_{*}^{2}G_{\ell} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}, $$

where in the last inequality we used the condition $K_{*}R\leq 1$ .

Case $n\geq 3$ : Assume $n\geq 3$ , and apply the Sobolev inequality in Lemma 2.17 to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\left(\int_{\Sigma}|u_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell}|^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{n}} \displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(u_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell})|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}^{2}\phi_{\ell}^{2}\right) \displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(u_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell})|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}G_{\ell}\right). $$

Since $u_{\ell+1}\leq u_{\ell}$ and $\operatorname{spt}\phi_{\ell}\subset U_{\ell}$ and $\phi_{\ell}\equiv 1$ on $U_{\ell+1}$ , then, by (2.10)

$$ \left(\int_{U_{\ell+1}}u_{\ell+1}^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{n}}\leq C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}. $$

By Hölder’s inequality and (2.9)

$$ \displaystyle G_{\ell+1}=\int_{D_{\ell+1}}u_{\ell+1}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{U_{\ell+1}}u_{\ell+1}^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{n}}\mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell+1})^{\frac{2}{n}} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}(4^{\ell+1}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell})^{\frac{2}{n}} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}128^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}\mathcal{d}^{-2-\frac{4}{n}}G_{\ell-1}^{1+\frac{2}{n}}. $$

Case $n=2$ : For $n=2$ , the Sobolev inequality in Lemma 2.17 gives

$$ \displaystyle\left(\int_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}^{4}\phi_{\ell}^{4}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}\left(\int_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}^{2}\phi_{\ell}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(u_{\ell+1}\phi_{\ell})|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Sob}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}u_{\ell+1}^{2}\phi_{\ell}^{2}\right)^{1/2} $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\int_{U_{\ell+1}}u^{4}_{\ell+1}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Sob}}G_{\ell}^{1/2}\left(C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-2}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-1}\mathcal{d}^{-1}G_{\ell-1}. $$

By Hölder’s inequality,
