$$ \displaystyle G_{\ell+1} \displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{U_{\ell+1}}u_{\ell+1}^{4}\right)^{1/2}\mathcal{H}^{n}(D_{\ell+1})^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\left(C_{0}32^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-1}\mathcal{d}^{-1}G_{\ell-1}\right)\left(4^{\ell+1}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq C_{0}128^{\ell}((1-\sigma)R)^{-1}\mathcal{d}^{-2}G_{\ell-1}^{3/2}. $$

Notice that (2.12) and (2.13) are of the same form. More concretely, if we set

$$ p_{n}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\frac{2}{n}&\text{if $n\geq 3$,}\\
\frac{1}{2}&\text{if $n=2$,}\end{cases} $$

and $S_{j}\coloneqq((1-\sigma)R)^{-n}\mathcal{d}^{-n-2}G_{2j}$ , then by letting $\ell=2j+1$ in (2.12) and (2.13) respectively, we obtain

$$ S_{j+1}\leq C_{0}128^{2j+1}S^{1+p_{n}}_{j} $$

for $j\geq 0$ . The standard nonlinear iteration lemma (see [4, Lemma B.1]) implies that there exists a constant $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}(n,k_{*},C_{\mathrm{Sob}},C_{\mathrm{Cac}},C_{c})>0$ such that $S_{j}\to 0$ as $j\to\infty$ provided $S_{0}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}^{2}$ . Since $\{G_{\ell}\}_{\ell}$ is a non-increasing sequence, this means that

$$ G_{\ell}\to 0\,\text{as $\ell\to\infty$, provided that }G_{0}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}^{2}((1-\sigma)R)^{n}\mathcal{d}^{n+2}, $$

as required. ∎

We shall always apply Lemma 2.18 in the following form.

#### Corollary 2.19.

Under the assumptions of Lemma 2.18, let

$$ \mathrm{E}(R)\coloneqq\left(R^{-n}\int_{U_{R}}u^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Then there exist $\varepsilon_{*}=\varepsilon_{*}(n,k_{*},C_{\mathrm{Sob}},C_{\mathrm{Cac}},C_{c})>0$ and $C_{*}=C_{*}(n,k_{*},C_{\mathrm{Sob}},C_{\mathrm{Cac}},C_{c})>0$ such that if

$$ K_{*}R\leq 1\quad\text{and }\mathrm{E}(R)\leq\varepsilon_{*}(1-\sigma)^{n/2}, $$

then $\displaystyle{\sup_{U_{\sigma R}}u\leq C_{*}(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}}$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from Lemma 2.18. Indeed, let $\varepsilon_{*}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}k_{*}^{\frac{n+2}{2}}$ and $C_{*}\coloneqq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}^{-\frac{2}{n+2}}$ . Then, if $\mathrm{E}(R)\leq\varepsilon_{*}(1-\sigma)^{n/2}$ , take $\mathcal{d}\coloneqq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DG}}^{-\frac{2}{n+2}}(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}$ and apply Lemma 2.18. ∎

## 3. Boundary-parallel sheeting

### 3.1. Geometric setup

Throughout this section, let us fix $p\in\partial M$ , and let $\rho_{0}>0$ be such that

- • the intrinsic geodesic balls $P_{R}=B^{\partial M}_{R}(p)$ are smooth and relatively compact in $\partial M$ for $0\leq R\leq 2\rho_{0}$ ;

- • the normal exponential map $F_{\partial M}$ of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $P_{2\rho_{0}}\times[0,2\rho_{0})$ onto a relatively open set.

For $0\leq\delta\leq 2\rho_{0}$ , $0<R\leq 2\rho_{0}$ , define $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})\coloneqq F_{\partial M}\bigl(P_{R}\times[0,\delta)\bigr)$ . In particular, the distance function $d_{\partial M}$ to $\partial M$ is smooth on $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}(P_{2\rho_{0}})$ .

Let $\Lambda\geq 0$ be such that

$$ |\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|+|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|\leq\Lambda^{2}\quad\text{ in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}(P_{2\rho_{0}})$}. $$

Now let us assume as in Theorem 1.11 that $\Sigma$ is a two-sided free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R})$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ for some $\delta\in(0,\rho_{0}),R\in(0,R_{0})$ , where $R_{0}\in(0,\rho_{0})$ is to be specified later depending on $n$ and $\Lambda$ only.

#### Definition 3.1 (Tilt function).

Let $X\coloneqq\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}$ , $g=|X|_{\mathrm{g}}$ , and $\theta\coloneqq\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M})$ . We shall refer to $g$ as the tilt function on $\Sigma$ with respect to $\partial M$ .

We start by computing the partial differential inequality satisfied by the tilt on $\Sigma$ .

#### Lemma 3.2 (Differential inequalities for the tilt).

Let $(M,\mathrm{g})$ and $P_{R}$ be as above. Additionally, let $\Sigma$ be a smooth two-sided free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ as in Section 2 and assume that $\Sigma\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Let $\nu$ be a choice of unit normal to $\Sigma$ , $A$ its second fundamental form, and let $X,g,\theta$ be as in Definition 3.1. Then $g^{2}+\theta^{2}=1$ . Set $B\coloneqq\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|_{T\Sigma}$ . Then the following hold.

First, on $\{g>0\}$ , if $v\coloneqq X/g$ , then

$$ \nabla_{\Sigma}g=\theta A(\cdot,v)+B(\cdot,v) $$

and, for every $\gamma>0$ ,

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)(1-g^{2})|A(\cdot,v)|^{2}+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}. $$

Second, assuming that (3.1) holds, then for every $\gamma>0$ on $\{g>0\}$

$$ \displaystyle g\Delta_{\Sigma}g \displaystyle\geq(1-\gamma)|A|^{2}(1-g^{2})-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}+\gamma\right)|A|^{2}-\gamma|A|^{2}g^{2}-C(n,\gamma)\Lambda^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $d_{\partial M}$ is the signed $\mathrm{g}$ -distance to $P$ in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P)$ , we have $|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|_{\mathrm{g}}=1$ in the tubular neighbourhood. Thus $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}=X+\theta\nu$ along $\Sigma$ , and so $g^{2}+\theta^{2}=1$ .

The identity $\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}=B+\theta A$ follows from the relation between ambient and intrinsic Hessians. Indeed, for $Y,Z\in T\Sigma$ ,

$$ \nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}(Y,Z)=\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}(Y,Z)+\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M},\nu)A(Y,Z)=B(Y,Z)+\theta A(Y,Z). $$

By taking $Z=X$ in this identity, we immediately obtain that

$$ g\,Yg=\frac{1}{2}Y(g^{2})=\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}(Y,X)=B(Y,X)+\theta A(Y,X). $$

On $\{g>0\}$ , writing $X=gv$ , this becomes $Yg=\theta A(Y,v)+B(Y,v)$ as required.

Moreover, taking norms and using $\theta^{2}=1-g^{2}$ , we obtain

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}|^{2}=|A|^{2}(1-g^{2})+2\theta\langle A,B\rangle+|B|^{2}. $$

The classical Bochner formula on $\Sigma$ gives

$$ \Delta_{\Sigma}\frac{g^{2}}{2}=|\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\Delta_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M},X\rangle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(X,X). $$

Since $\Delta_{\Sigma}(g^{2}/2)=g\Delta_{\Sigma}g+|\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}$ , we get

$$ g\Delta_{\Sigma}g=|\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\Delta_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M},X\rangle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(X,X)-|\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}. $$

The contracted Gauss equation gives, since $H=0$ ,

$$ \operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(X,X)=\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,X)-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,\nu,X,\nu)-|A(\cdot,X)|^{2}. $$

Combining this with the expansion of $|\nabla_{\Sigma}^{2}d_{\partial M}|^{2}$ yields the exact Bochner identity.

Now let $\gamma>0$ . From the identity $\nabla_{\Sigma}g=\theta A(\cdot,v)+B(\cdot,v)$ and Young’s inequality, we obtain

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)(1-g^{2})|A(\cdot,v)|^{2}+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}. $$

By definition, $|A(\cdot,X)|^{2}=g^{2}|A(\cdot,v)|^{2}$ , so that

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}+|A(\cdot,X)|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma(1-g^{2}))|A(\cdot,v)|^{2}+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}. $$

Since $H=0$ , $A$ is trace-free. Hence, for every unit vector $v$ , we have $|A(\cdot,v)|^{2}\leq\frac{n-1}{n}|A|^{2}$ . Therefore,

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}+|A(\cdot,X)|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{n-1}{n}+\gamma\right)|A|^{2}+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}. $$

Again using Young’s inequality, we also bound

$$ 2|\theta\langle A,B\rangle|\leq\gamma|A|^{2}\theta^{2}+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}=\gamma|A|^{2}(1-g^{2})+C(\gamma)|B|^{2}, $$

so that, after substituting into the exact Bochner identity, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle g\Delta_{\Sigma}g \displaystyle\geq(1-\gamma)|A|^{2}(1-g^{2})-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}+\gamma\right)|A|^{2}-C(\gamma)|B|^{2} \displaystyle+\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\Delta_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M},X\rangle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,X)-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,\nu,X,\nu). $$

Finally, since $\Sigma$ is minimal, $\Delta_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}=\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}-\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}(\nu,\nu)$ . Differentiating this expression tangentially gives terms involving $\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ , $\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ , and one derivative of $\nu$ , hence one factor of $|A|$ , namely

$$ \left|\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\Delta_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M},X\rangle\right|\leq(C(n)|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|+2|A||\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|)g. $$

By Young’s inequality, $2|A||\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|g\leq\gamma|A|^{2}g^{2}+C(\gamma)|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}$ . The curvature terms can be estimated by

$$ \left|\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,X)-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(X,\nu,X,\nu)\right|\leq C(n)|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|g^{2}. $$

Assuming (3.1) holds, this gives the final estimate, since $0\leq g\leq 1$ by definition. ∎

Next we compute the normal derivative of the tilt function along $\partial M$ .

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $\Sigma,M$ , $d_{\partial M}$ , and $g$ be as in Lemma 3.2. Let $\eta$ be the inward unit conormal to $\partial\Sigma$ in $\Sigma$ . Then

$$ g=1\quad\text{and}\quad\partial_{\eta}g=0\quad\text{on $\partial\Sigma$}. $$

#### Proof.

By definition of a free-boundary minimal hypersurface, $\eta$ coincides with the normal $\mathbf{n}$ to $\partial M$ along $\partial\Sigma$ . Since $P_{R}$ is a relatively open subset of $\partial M$ and $\partial\Sigma\subset P_{R}$ , then $\eta=\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|_{\partial\Sigma}$ .

Hence, $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}$ is tangential to $\Sigma$ along $\partial\Sigma$ and so, by definition, $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|_{\partial\Sigma}=\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}|_{\partial\Sigma}$ . In particular, then, for every $x\in\partial\Sigma$

$$ g(x)=|\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}(x)|=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}(x)|=1, $$

i.e. $g|_{\partial\Sigma}\equiv 1$ . Since $g^{2}+\theta^{2}=1$ everywhere on $\Sigma$ , then $\theta|_{\partial\Sigma}\equiv 0$ . Thus, on $\partial\Sigma$

$$ \partial_{\eta}g=g\partial_{\eta}g=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\eta}g^{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\eta}\theta^{2}=-\theta\partial_{\eta}\theta=0 $$

as $\theta$ vanishes on $\partial\Sigma$ . ∎

### 3.2. Caccioppoli-type inequality

We shall now prove the intrinsic (weak) Caccioppoli inequality that will be used later to implement the iteration scheme à la De Giorgi.

#### Lemma 3.4 (Caccioppoli inequality).

Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and assume that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Assume that (3.1) holds. Then there exists a positive dimensional constant $C(n)>0$ such that for every $k\in[0,1/(4n)]$ and every $\varphi\in C_{c}^{0,1}(\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R}))$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\{g>k\}}|A|^{2}\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n)\left(\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+\Lambda^{2}\int_{\{g>k\}}\varphi^{2}\right). $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\{g>k\}}|\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n)\left(\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+\Lambda^{2}\int_{\{g>k\}}\varphi^{2}\right). $$

#### Proof.

We shall first prove (3.2) and (3.3) for test functions $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Sigma)$ , and then extend to compactly supported ambient Lipschitz functions by an excision argument, similar to the one in Lemma 2.14.

Let $\Omega_{k}\coloneqq\{g>k\}$ . By Lemma 2.16 for every compactly supported Lipschitz function $\zeta$ on $\Sigma$ and a fixed $\alpha>0$ to be determined later, we have

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|A|^{2}\zeta^{2}\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\zeta|^{2}+C(n,\alpha)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Sigma}\zeta^{2} $$

where $C(n,\alpha)$ only depends on $n,\alpha$ . Let now $\zeta=(g-k)_{+}\varphi$ to get

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|A|^{2}(g-k)_{+}^{2}\varphi^{2}\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}((g-k)_{+}\varphi)|^{2}+C(n,\alpha)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)_{+}^{2}\varphi^{2}. $$

After integration by parts, we have

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}((g-k)_{+}\varphi)|^{2}=-\int_{\Omega_{k}}(g-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}g\,\varphi^{2}+\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}, $$

and the boundary term vanishes by Lemma 3.3. Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Omega_{k}}|A|^{2}(g-k)^{2}\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq-(1+\alpha)\int_{\Omega_{k}}(g-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}g\,\varphi^{2}+(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2} \displaystyle+C(n,\alpha)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)^{2}_{+}\varphi^{2}. $$

Notice that on $\Omega_{k}$ , one has

$$ (g-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}g=\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)g\Delta_{\Sigma}g, $$

so we can use the differential inequality for the tilt in Lemma 3.2 to obtain for $\gamma>0$ to be determined later

$$ \displaystyle-(g-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}g\leq-\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\left[\left((1-\gamma)(1-g^{2})-\frac{n-1}{n}-\gamma-\gamma g^{2}\right)|A|^{2}-C(n,\gamma)\Lambda^{2}\right]. $$

Thus, after moving all the terms containing $|A|^{2}$ to the left hand side and using the obvious inequality $0\leq(g-k)_{+}\leq 1$ , we get

$$ \int_{\Omega_{k}}\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha,\gamma}|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+(C(n,\alpha)+C(n,\gamma))\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}, $$

where

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\alpha,\gamma}\coloneqq(g-k)^{2}+(1+\alpha)\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\left((1-\gamma)(1-g^{2})-\frac{n-1}{n}-\gamma-\gamma g^{2}\right). $$

By direct computation,

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\alpha,\gamma}=\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\left(\frac{1+\alpha}{n}-kg-\alpha g^{2}-2(1+\alpha)\gamma\right). $$

We can choose $\alpha=\alpha_{n}\coloneqq 1/(8n)$ and $\gamma=\gamma_{n}\coloneqq 1/(16n(1+\alpha_{n}))$ to obtain

$$ \frac{1+\alpha}{n}-kg-\alpha g^{2}-2(1+\alpha)\gamma\geq\frac{1}{2n} $$

since $k\in[0,1/(4n)]$ and $0\leq g\leq 1$ by definition. Inequality (3.2) then follows.

As for (3.3), recall by Lemma 3.2 on the open set $\{g>0\}$ we have $\nabla_{\Sigma}g=\theta A(v,\cdot)+B(v,\cdot)$ for the unit vector $v=g^{-1}X$ . Therefore, on $\Sigma\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R})$

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}g|^{2}\leq 2\theta^{2}|A|^{2}+2|B|^{2}\leq 2|A|^{2}+2|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}\leq 2|A|^{2}+2\Lambda^{2}, $$

and (3.3) then follows from (3.2).

Finally, apply Corollary B.6 on a compact neighbourhood of $\operatorname{spt}\varphi$ : there exist Lipschitz cutoff functions $\chi_{j}$ , each supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ , such that $0\leq\chi_{j}\leq 1$ , $\chi_{j}\to 1$ locally on $\Sigma$ , and $\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|^{2}\to 0$ . We can then apply the smooth inequality (3.2) with test function $\chi_{j}\varphi$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\{g>k\}}|A|^{2}\left(1-\frac{k}{g}\right)\chi_{j}^{2}\varphi^{2}\leq C(n)\int_{\Sigma}(g-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(\chi_{j}\varphi)|^{2}+C(n)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\{g>k\}}\chi_{j}^{2}\varphi^{2}. $$

Since

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}(\chi_{j}\varphi)|^{2}\leq 2\chi_{j}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+2\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|^{2}, $$

and $0\leq(g-k)_{+}\leq 1$ , the contribution of the second term is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|^{2}$ , which tends to zero. All other terms pass to the limit by Fatou’s lemma, the dominated convergence theorem, and the local area bound, cf. Remark 2.7. Thus, letting $j\to\infty$ , we obtain the asserted estimate with $|A|^{2}$ on the left-hand side. Then (3.3) follows exactly as above. ∎

### 3.3. Proof of Theorem 1.11

We are now able to prove Theorem 1.11 by applying the iteration lemma in Section 2.3.

Let us assume that (3.1) holds. Define $K_{0}(n,\Lambda)\coloneqq\max\{K_{\mathrm{Sob}}(n,\Lambda),K_{\mathrm{Cac}}(n,\Lambda)\}$ , and set

$$ \delta_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\rho_{0},\quad R_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\min\bigl\{\rho_{0},K_{0}^{-1}\bigr\}. $$

Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ for some $\delta\in(0,\delta_{0}),R\in(0,R_{0})$ .

Then, for $0<r\leq R$ define the Fermi cylinder $C_{r}$ by

$$ C_{r}\coloneqq F_{\partial M}\bigl(P_{r}\times[0,2\delta)\bigr)=\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\delta}(P_{r}), $$

and consider the following tilt excess quantity:

$$ \mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(r)\coloneqq\left(r^{-n}\int_{\Sigma\cap C_{r}}g^{2}\right)^{1/2} $$

where $g$ is the tilt function in Definition 3.1.

Let us apply Lemma 2.18 with $u=g$ and $k_{*}=1/(4n)$ . Notice that Lemma 3.4 provides the necessary Caccioppoli-type inequality (2.5). Therefore, by Corollary 2.19, there exist $\varepsilon_{0}=\varepsilon_{0}(n,\Lambda)>0$ and $C_{0}=C_{0}(n,\Lambda)>0$ such that

$$ \sup_{\Sigma\cap C_{\sigma R}}g\leq C_{0}(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}} $$

provided $\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{0}^{2}(1-\sigma)^{n}$ , which is the desired statement.

### 3.4. Proof of Theorem 1.12

We shall now prove our first sheeting theorem, Theorem 1.12. The proof is similar to [4, Section 5], to which we shall often refer.

Assume $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})=F_{\partial M}(P_{R}\times[0,\delta))$ , and recall that $F_{\partial M}$ is a diffeomorphism $P_{R}\times[0,\delta)\to\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Let the inverse map $F_{\partial M}^{-1}:\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})\to P_{R}\times[0,\delta)$ be given by $(\pi_{\partial M},d_{\partial M})|_{\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})}$ , where $\pi_{\partial M}$ is the nearest point projection map onto $\partial M$ .

By Theorem 1.11 with $\sigma=3/4$ , we have that

$$ \sup_{\Sigma\cap C_{3R/4}}g\leq C_{0}(n,\Lambda)\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}. $$

By decreasing $\varepsilon_{0}$ if necessary, we may assume $\sup_{\Sigma\cap C_{3R/4}}g\leq\frac{1}{4}$ .

Step 0: $\partial\Sigma\cap P_{3R/4}=\emptyset$ . Suppose $x\in\partial\Sigma\cap P_{3R/4}$ . By definition, the inner conormal $\eta(x)$ of $\partial\Sigma$ at $x$ equals $\mathbf{n}(x)=\nu_{P}(x)$ . Hence, $\nu_{P}(x)\in T_{x}\Sigma$ and $g(x)=|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}\Sigma}_{\mathrm{g}}\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}(x)|=|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}\Sigma}_{\mathrm{g}}\nu_{P}(x)|=1$ , contradicting (3.7).

Step 1: Local graphicality. Let $\iota:N\to M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ parametrise $\Sigma$ . At every point of $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ ,

$$ \operatorname{Ker}D\pi_{\partial M}=\operatorname{span}\{\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}\}. $$

By (3.7) and (3.8), the differential of $\pi_{\partial M}\circ\iota$ is invertible at every $z\in N$ such that $\iota(z)\in C_{3R/4}$ . Thus the argument in [4, Proof of Theorem 6] shows that there is a neighbourhood of $z$ in $N$ the image of which is a smooth Fermi graph over an open subset of $P_{3R/4}$ .

Step 2: Finite covering away from the projected singular set. Let

$$ \Gamma\coloneqq\pi_{\partial M}(\mathcal{S}\cap\overline{\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}}(P_{3R/4}))\subset\bar{P}_{3R/4},\quad B\coloneqq P_{3R/4}\setminus\Gamma. $$

Since $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S}\cap\overline{\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}}(P_{3R/4}))<\infty$ and $\pi_{\partial M}$ is a Lipschitz map in $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R})$ , then $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma)=0$ . Since $\mathcal{S}$ is closed, it is easy to see that $\Gamma$ is relatively closed in $P_{3R/4}$ . Then $B$ is open in $P_{3R/4}$ and path connected (see [4, Proof of Theorem 5]). Define

$$ N_{0}\coloneqq\{z\in N:\iota(z)\in C_{3R/4},\ \pi_{\partial M}(\iota(z))\in B\} $$

and $\hat{\pi}\coloneqq\pi_{P}\circ\iota|_{N_{0}}:N_{0}\to B$ . By Step 1, $\hat{\pi}$ is a local diffeomorphism. Because of properness of $\iota$ as an immersion into $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , one can check that $\hat{\pi}$ is also proper. Since $B$ is connected, each connected component of $N_{0}$ is therefore mapped onto the whole of $B$ . When restricted to each connected component of $N_{0}$ , $\hat{\pi}$ is a proper local diffeomorphism between connected smooth manifolds, so it is a smooth covering map by [24, Proposition 4.46]. In particular, for each $y\in B$ , $\hat{\pi}^{-1}(y)$ is finite. Its cardinality is a locally constant function on $B$ , so it is constant as $B$ is connected. Let this cardinality be $Q$ .

Step 3: Lipschitz estimate and extension across $\Gamma$ . By Step 2, for each $y\in B$ the normal fibre $F(\{y\}\times[0,\delta))$ has exactly $Q$ preimages in $N_{0}$ . Order the heights of their images under $\iota$ counting repetitions, and write $0\leq u_{1}(y)\leq u_{2}(y)\leq\cdots\leq u_{Q}(y),$ for $y\in B$ , where the functions $u_{j}$ are locally Lipschitz. Then,

$$ \Sigma\cap\pi_{\partial M}^{-1}(B)=\cup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u_{j})\bigr). $$

Write $F_{\partial M}^{*}\mathrm{g}=dt^{2}+h_{t}$ , where $h_{t}$ is a smooth family of metrics on $P_{R}$ with $h_{0}=\mathrm{g}|_{P_{R}}$ . It is easy to check that for a smooth graph $G[u]=F_{\partial M}\bigl(\{(y,u(y)):y\in P_{R}\}\bigr)$ on $P_{R}$ with $|\nabla_{G[u]}d_{\partial M}|\leq c\in(0,1)$ , $|\nabla_{\partial M}u|\leq C_{\mathrm{Fermi}}(n,\Lambda)c(1-c^{2})^{-1/2}$ , where $C_{\mathrm{Fermi}}$ controls the uniform equivalence of the metrics $(h_{t})_{t\in[0,\delta]}$ and depends on $n$ and $\Lambda$ by (3.1).

Since we can approximate curves in $P_{3R/4}$ by curves avoiding $\Gamma$ , we conclude that

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{\partial M}(u_{j};B)\leq 2C_{\mathrm{Fermi}}\sup_{\Sigma\cap C_{3R/4}}g\leq C(n,\Lambda)\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}. $$

By density of $B$ in $P_{3R/4}$ , every $u_{j}$ extends uniquely to a Lipschitz function (still denoted $u_{j}$ ) on the whole of $P_{3R/4}$ , with the same bound on the Lipschitz constant, i.e.

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{\partial M}(u_{j})\leq C(n,\Lambda)\mathrm{E}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}. $$

By density of the regular set in $\overline{\Sigma}$ and of $B$ in $P_{3R/4}$ , we obtain

$$ \overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{3R/4})=\cup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u_{j})\bigr) $$

for the extended functions $u_{j}$ .

We can now prove (i) and (ii).

- (i) Assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ . Since $\pi_{\partial M}$ is Lipschitz on $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\rho_{0}}(P_{R})$ , then necessarily $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\Gamma)=0$ . By [40, Appendix A], then $B=P_{3R/4}\setminus\Gamma$ is simply connected. Therefore every connected component of the covering $\hat{\pi}:N_{0}\to B$ is one-sheeted. The components determine $Q$ globally defined, not necessarily ordered Lipschitz functions $v_{1},\dots,v_{Q}:B\to[0,\delta)$ such that

$$ \Sigma\cap\pi_{\partial M}^{-1}(B)=\cup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(v_{j})\bigr). $$

Arguing as above, for every $j\in{1,2,\ldots,Q}$ , we can extend $v_{j}$ to a Lipschitz function defined on the whole of $P_{3R/4}$ , preserving the Lipschitz constant. Clearly, $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma)=0$ . Since $\partial\Sigma\cap P_{3R/4}=\emptyset$ , the Lipschitz functions $v_{j}$ are weak solutions of the minimal surface equation on the bounded open set $B=P_{3R/4}\setminus\Gamma$ with a uniform bound on the Lipschitz constant. Since the metrics $(h_{t})_{t\in[0,\delta]}$ are uniformly equivalent, in local coordinates the area integrand $\mathcal{L}(y,z,q)=(\det h_{z}(y))^{1/2}(1+h_{z}^{ij}(y)q_{i}q_{j})^{1/2}$ is uniformly elliptic. Therefore, the removal of singularities result in Lemma A.2 applies, and $\mathcal{S}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{3R/4})=\emptyset$ . Finally, the gradient bound $\|\nabla v_{j}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(P_{R/2})}$ follows from the combination of De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory and Schauder theory.

- (ii) Assume instead $\Sigma$ is embedded. Then for every $y\in B$ the points of $\Sigma$ lying in the normal fibre are distinct, i.e. $0\leq u_{1}<\dots<u_{Q}$ on $B$ . Therefore, each $u_{j}$ is smooth on $B$ . Since $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma)=0$ , as above by Lemma A.2 each $u_{j}$ extends to a smooth solution of the minimal surface equation on the whole of $P_{3R/4}$ . Weak ordering is preserved, and, indeed, strict ordering by the strong maximum principle for the minimal surface equation. Thus $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{3R/4})$ is a union of pairwise disjoint smooth graphs. In particular $\mathcal{S}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{3R/4})=\emptyset$ . The gradient estimates then follow from standard elliptic theory as in (i).

## 4. Boundary-orthogonal sheeting

### 4.1. Geometric setup

Let $M$ be an $(n+1)$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold-with-boundary as in Section 2, and assume $\partial M\neq\emptyset$ . Let $P$ be a (smooth) two-sided, embedded, $n$ -dimensional manifold-with-boundary in $M$ that is diffeomorphic to a half-disc and whose boundary lies in $\partial M$ . In other words, $P$ is the image of a smooth embedding $e$ from $\mathbb{B}^{n}_{+}(0)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|x|<1,x_{n}\geq 0\}$ into $M$ and $\partial_{0}P=e(\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{n}_{+}(0))\subset\partial M$ , where $\partial_{0}\mathbb{B}^{n}_{+}(0)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|x|<1,x_{n}=0\}$ . We shall further assume that $P\cap\partial M=\partial_{0}P$ and $P$ meets $\partial M$ orthogonally along $\partial_{0}P$ . Let $\nu_{P}$ denote a smooth choice of unit normal on $P$ . Then by orthogonality to $\partial M$ along $\partial_{0}P$ , we have $\mathrm{g}(\nu_{P},\mathbf{n})=0$ on $\partial_{0}P$ .

Let $p\in\partial_{0}P$ , and, for $0<R<\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{inj}_{p}(P)$ , let $P_{R}$ denote the intrinsic half-ball $B^{P}_{R}(p)$ in $P$ centred at $p$ .

#### Definition 4.1 (Adapted $\rho$ -neighbourhood).

Let $\rho>0$ . An adapted $\rho$ -neighbourhood of $P_{R}$ in $M$ consists of a relatively open neighbourhood $U\subset M$ of $P_{2R}$ and a smooth function $z_{P}:U\to\mathbb{R}$ with the following properties:

- (i) $d_{\partial M}$ is smooth in $U$ ;

- (ii) $P\cap U=\{z_{P}=0\}$ and $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}$ is a positive multiple of $\nu_{P}$ on $P\cap U$ ;

- (iii) $\frac{1}{2}\leq|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|\leq 2$ in $U$ ;

- (iv) $\langle\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P},\mathbf{n}\rangle=0$ in $U\cap\partial M$ .

- (v) the flow $\Phi^{Z}_{t}$ of the vector field $Z=\frac{\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}}{|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|}$ defines a diffeomorphism $F_{Z}$ of $P_{2R}\times(-2\rho,2\rho)$ onto a relatively open (compactly contained in $U$ ) neighbourhood of $P_{2R}$ in $M$ by (4.1)

$$ F_{Z}(y,t)\coloneqq\Phi_{t}^{Z}(y)\quad\text{ for $(y,t)\in P_{2R}\times(-2\rho,2\rho)$.} $$

#### Remark 4.2.

The essential datum in an adapted neighbourhood is the vector field $Z$ . One could instead prescribe a smooth unit vector field on a relatively open neighbourhood $U$ of $P_{2R}$ , equal to $\nu_{P}$ on $P_{2R}$ and tangent to $\partial M$ along $\partial M\cap U$ , whose flow satisfies condition (v) of Definition 4.1. With the derivative bounds (4.6), the flow estimate (4.7)–(4.8), and the ambient geometric bounds used below, the $\varepsilon$ -regularity and sheeting arguments apply without requiring $Z$ to be a normalized gradient.

In particular, the tilt and Caccioppoli estimates involve only the first two derivatives of $Z$ , whereas deriving these bounds from $Z=\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}/|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|$ requires control of three derivatives of $z_{P}$ . The function $z_{P}$ therefore provides a convenient construction, rather than an essential ingredient of the argument.

We now show that for every $P$ as above, there exists $\rho>0$ such that the half disc $P_{\rho}$ has an adapted $\rho$ -neighbourhood.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $P\subset M$ be as above and let $p\in\partial_{0}P$ . Then there exists $0<\rho<\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{inj}_{p}(P)$ sufficiently small such that $P_{\rho}$ has an adapted $\rho$ -neighbourhood $U$ in the sense of Definition 4.1.

#### Proof.

Consider the smooth embedded relatively compact submanifold $\Gamma\coloneqq\partial_{0}P$ of $\partial M$ . By [15, Section 3.1], there exists $\varrho_{0}>0$ such that the normal exponential map $F_{\Gamma}$ of $\Gamma$ in $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $\Gamma\times(-\varrho_{0},\varrho_{0})$ onto an open set $O_{\Gamma}$ in $\partial M$ . Since $O_{\Gamma}$ has compact closure in $\partial M$ , then, as mentioned in Section 2, after shrinking $\varrho_{0}$ if needed, the normal exponential map of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $O_{\Gamma}\times[0,\varrho_{0})$ into a normal collar neighbourhood $U_{\Gamma}$ of $O_{\Gamma}$ in $M$ . In particular, the composition of the two normal exponential maps gives a diffeomorphism $\Psi$ of $\Gamma\times(-\varrho_{0},\varrho_{0})\times[0,\varrho_{0})$ onto $U_{\Gamma}\subset M$ by

$$ \Psi:(q,s,r)\mapsto F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{exp}^{\partial M}_{q}(s\nu_{P}(q)),r\bigr). $$

Let $\widehat{\Pi}$ be the map $(q,s,r)\mapsto(q,r)$ , and let $\Pi:P\cap U_{\Gamma}\to\Gamma\times[0,\varrho_{0})$ be defined by $\Pi=\widehat{\Pi}\circ\Psi^{-1}$ . Since $P$ meets $\partial M$ orthogonally along $\Gamma$ , for all $q\in\Gamma$ we have $\Pi(q)=(q,0)$ , and it is easy to check that $D\Pi_{q}|_{T_{q}P}$ is an isomorphism. By the implicit function theorem, there is $\varrho>0$ and an open set $U_{\varrho}\subset U_{\Gamma}$ such that for a neighbourhood $\Gamma_{p}$ of $p$ in $\Gamma$ we have a smooth function $\psi:\Gamma_{p}\times[0,\varrho)\to(-\varrho,\varrho)$ with the property that

$$ P\cap U_{\varrho}=\{\Psi(q,\psi(q,r),r):q\in\Gamma_{p},r\in[0,\varrho)\},\quad\psi(q,0)=0,\quad\partial_{r}\psi(q,0)=0. $$

Define the function $z_{P}$ on $U_{\varrho}$ by $z_{P}(\Psi(q,s,r))\coloneqq s-\psi(q,r)$ . We shall slightly abuse notation and write $z_{P}(q,s,r)=s-\psi(q,r)$ . Notice that on $U_{\varrho}\cap\partial M$ (corresponding to $\{r=0\}$ ) we have $\partial_{r}z_{P}=-\partial_{r}\psi(q,0)=0$ , so $\langle\nabla z_{P},\mathbf{n}\rangle=0$ on $U_{\varrho}\cap\partial M$ . Moreover, $\partial_{s}z_{P}=1$ everywhere, so that $\mathrm{d}z_{P}\neq 0$ . Since $z_{P}=0$ on $P\cap U_{\varrho}$ and $\mathrm{d}z_{P}\neq 0$ , then $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}$ is normal to $P$ on $P\cap U_{\varrho}$ . Also, by construction, $|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|=1$ on $U_{\varrho}\cap\partial M$ , so that, by shrinking $\varrho$ if necessary, we have $1/2\leq|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|\leq 2$ on $U_{\varrho}$ .

By the flowout theorem (see [24, Theorem 9.20 and Theorem 9.34]), there is $\rho\in(0,\varrho)$ such that (v) in Definition 4.1 is satisfied with $U=U_{\varrho}$ and $R=\rho$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.4.

For the compactness argument in Section 5.3, it suffices to consider reference half-discs obtained by restricting $F_{\partial M}(\Gamma\times[0,\varrho))$ to a neighbourhood of a point of $\Gamma$ . In the coordinates of the preceding proof, these are given by $s=0$ , so that $\psi\equiv 0$ and $z_{P}=s$ . By choosing $T_{p}\Gamma$ appropriately, such reference half-discs realize every tangent half-hyperplane at $p$ orthogonal to $\partial M$ . We nevertheless establish sheeting for arbitrary smooth two-sided reference half-discs meeting $\partial M$ orthogonally, since the argument applies in this greater generality.

Assume $\rho_{1}>0$ is such that $U_{1}$ is an adapted $\rho_{1}$ -neighbourhood of $P_{\rho_{1}}\subset P$ as in Lemma 4.3. Thus, for $\delta\in(0,2\rho_{1}]$ , $R\in(0,2\rho_{1}]$ , we can define

$$ \mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})\coloneqq F_{Z}\bigl(P_{R}\times(-\delta,\delta)\bigr). $$

Let the inverse map $F^{-1}_{Z}$ be given by $F^{-1}_{Z}=(\pi_{Z},\mathcal{t}_{Z})$ .

#### Remark 4.5.

Notice that, since $Z$ is tangential to $\partial M$ along $\partial M\cap U_{1}$ and does not vanish anywhere, then the flow preserves $\partial M$ and the interior of $M$ , i.e. $F_{Z}\bigl(\partial_{0}P_{2\rho_{1}}\times(-2\rho_{1},2\rho_{1})\bigr)=\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{2\rho_{1}}(P_{2\rho_{1}})\cap\partial M$ .

Let $\Lambda\geq 0$ be such that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|A_{P}|^{2}+\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|\nabla_{P}A_{P}|+\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|\nabla^{2}_{P}A_{P}|^{2/3}\leq\Lambda^{2}, \displaystyle\sup_{U_{1}}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2}+\sup_{U_{1}}|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|+\sup_{U_{1}}|\nabla^{4}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|^{2/3}\leq\Lambda^{2}, \displaystyle\sup_{U_{1}}|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|+\sup_{U_{1}}|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|^{2/3}+\sup_{U_{1}}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|^{1/2}\leq\Lambda^{2}, $$

where $A_{P}$ denotes the second fundamental form of $P$ in $M$ .

#### Lemma 4.6.

Let $P$ , $\rho_{1}$ , $U_{1}$ , $z_{P}$ and $Z$ be chosen as above, and suppose that (4.4) holds. There exists a constant $\delta_{1}=\delta_{1}(n,\Lambda,\rho_{1})>0$ such that for all $\delta,R\in(0,\delta_{1})$ the following estimates hold on $\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{2\delta}(P_{2R})$ :

$$ |\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|\leq C(n)\Lambda,\quad|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|\leq C(n)\Lambda^{2}, $$

$$ |\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}Z|\leq C(n)\Lambda,\quad|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}Z|\leq C(n)\Lambda^{2}. $$

Moreover, the flow map $F_{Z}$ restricted to $P_{2R}\times(-2\delta,2\delta)$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{2\delta}(P_{2R})$ and it satisfies

$$ |DF_{Z}|+|D(F_{Z}^{-1})|\leq C(n). $$

Finally, if $(y,t)\in P_{2R}\times(-2\delta,2\delta)$ and $x=F_{Z}(y,t)$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{v\in T_{y}P,|v|=1}\bigl|\langle Z(x),(D_{y}F_{Z})_{(y,t)}v\rangle\bigr|\leq C(n)\bigl(\sup|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|\bigr)|t|\leq C(n)\Lambda|t|. $$

#### Proof.

Recall the construction in the proof of Lemma 4.3, and the definition of the map $\Psi:\partial_{0}P_{2\rho_{1}}\times(-2\rho_{1},2\rho_{1})\times[0,2\rho_{1})\to U_{1}$ given by

$$ \Psi:(q,s,r)\mapsto F_{\partial M}\bigl(\operatorname{exp}^{\partial M}_{q}(s\nu_{P}(q)),r\bigr). $$

Let $(\overline{\mathrm{g}}_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n+1}$ denote the pullback metric tensor $\Psi^{*}\mathrm{g}$ and let $\theta=\theta(n,\Lambda,\rho_{1})\in(0,1/2)$ be a constant to be determined in the proof; then let $\rho_{\theta}\coloneqq 2\theta\rho_{1}$ . By the estimates of [29, Appendix A] and the Riccati equation, there exists a constant $c_{0}(n)$ such that, provided we choose $\theta>0$ small enough that $\rho_{\theta}\Lambda\leq c_{0}(n)$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}}\leq\overline{\mathrm{g}}\leq 2\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}},\quad|\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})|\leq C(n)\Lambda,\quad|\partial\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})|\leq C(n)\Lambda^{2} $$

on $\partial_{0}P_{\rho_{\theta}}\times(-\rho_{\theta},\rho_{\theta})\times[0,\rho_{\theta})$ , where by $\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})$ we denote the Christoffel symbols of the metric $\overline{\mathrm{g}}$ and with $\partial\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})$ the collection of their partial derivatives with respect to the coordinate vector fields. Moreover, since $D\psi=0$ on $\partial_{0}P_{\rho_{1}}$ , by shrinking $\theta$ if needed, we can assume $|D\psi|\leq 1$ on $\partial_{0}P_{\rho_{\theta}}\times[0,\rho_{\theta})$ . Therefore, using the graph representation in (4.2) together with the equation for the components of the second fundamental form of a graph, we obtain

$$ |D^{2}\psi|\leq C(n)\bigl(\textstyle\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|A_{P}|+|\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})|\bigr)\leq C(n)\Lambda $$

on $\partial_{0}P_{\rho_{\theta}}\times[0,\rho_{\theta})$ . Finally, differentiating the equation for the second fundamental form components in the tangential directions, we obtain

$$ |D^{3}\psi|\leq C(n)\bigl(\textstyle\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|\nabla_{P}A_{P}|+|\partial\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})|+\bigl(\sup_{P_{2\rho_{1}}}|A_{P}|+|\Gamma(\overline{\mathrm{g}})|+|D^{2}\psi|\bigr)^{2}\bigr)\leq C(n)\Lambda^{2} $$

after shrinking $c_{0}(n)>0$ further, if necessary.

Recall in the proof of Lemma 4.3, we defined the function $z_{P}$ by $z_{P}(\Psi(q,s,r))\coloneqq s-\psi(q,r)$ . By differentiating the definition and using (4.10)–(4.11), it is immediate to obtain the higher order estimates (4.5) in $\mathcal{N}_{\rho_{\theta}}(P_{\rho_{\theta}})$ . Finally, by definition of $Z$ , for every vector $X$ ,

$$ \nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{X}Z=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{-1}\left(\mathrm{Id}-Z\otimes Z\right)\left(\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}(X,\cdot)\right)^{\sharp}. $$

Therefore, (4.6) follows from (4.12) and (4.5).

By standard ODE theory, bounds on $|Z|,|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|,|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}Z|$ , together with (4.4), control the flow map $F_{Z}$ in $C^{2}$ . In particular, on $P_{\rho_{\theta}}\times(-\rho_{\theta},\rho_{\theta})$ , after shrinking $c_{0}(n)$ if needed, since $|t|\leq\rho_{\theta}$ and $\rho_{\theta}\Lambda\leq c_{0}(n)$ , we obtain (4.7) and (4.8). Thus, we can let $\delta_{1}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\theta\rho_{1}$ , which satisfies all the required properties. ∎

Now let us assume as in Theorem 1.14 that $\Sigma$ is a two-sided free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ for some $\delta\in(0,\delta_{1}),R\in(0,R_{1})$ , where $R_{1}\in(0,\delta_{1})$ is to be specified later depending on $n$ and $\Lambda$ only.

#### Definition 4.7 (Adapted tilt function).

Let $\mtxcal{X}\coloneqq\mathrm{proj}^{T\Sigma}_{\mathrm{g}}(Z)$ , $\tau=|\mtxcal{X}|_{\mathrm{g}}$ , and $\vartheta\coloneqq\mathrm{g}(\nu,Z)$ , where $Z$ is the vector field in Definition 4.1. Then $\tau$ is a tilt function on $\Sigma$ , with respect to $P$ , adapted to $\partial M$ . We will refer to it, for brevity, as the adapted tilt function.

We shall now compute the differential inequality satisfied by $\tau$ , and notice that it is very similar to the inequality in Lemma 3.2.

#### Lemma 4.8.

Let $P,\delta_{1},Z$ be as in Lemma 4.6. Additionally, let $\Sigma$ be a smooth two-sided free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and assume that $\Sigma\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Let $\nu$ be a choice of unit normal to $\Sigma$ , $A$ its second fundamental form, and let $\tau,\mtxcal{X},\vartheta$ be as in Definition 4.7. Then $\tau^{2}+\vartheta^{2}=1$ . Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the (0,2)-tensor on $\Sigma$ corresponding to $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|_{T\Sigma}$ . Then the following hold.

First, on $\{\tau>0\}$ , if $\mathcal{v}\coloneqq\mtxcal{X}/\tau$ , then

$$ \nabla_{\Sigma}\tau=\vartheta A(\cdot,\mathcal{v})+\mathcal{B}(\cdot,\mathcal{v}) $$

and, for every $\gamma>0$ ,

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)(1-\tau^{2})|A(\cdot,\mathcal{v})|^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2}. $$

Second, assuming that (4.4) holds, then for every $\gamma>0$ on $\{\tau>0\}$

$$ \displaystyle\tau\Delta_{\Sigma}\tau \displaystyle\geq(1-\gamma)|A|^{2}(1-\tau^{2})-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}+\gamma\right)|A|^{2}-\gamma|A|^{2}\tau^{2}-C(n,\gamma)\Lambda^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

We shall follow the outline of the proof of Lemma 3.2, and highlight the analogies and differences. Notice that $|Z|_{\mathrm{g}}=1$ and $Z=\mtxcal{X}+\vartheta\nu$ along $\Sigma$ , so that $\tau^{2}+\vartheta^{2}=1$ .

Analogously to Lemma 3.2, let $\mathcal{B}$ be the (0,2)-tensor on $\Sigma$ corresponding to $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|_{T\Sigma}$ , so that for $V,W\in T\Sigma$ , $\mathcal{B}(V,W)$ is defined by $\mathcal{B}(V,W)\coloneqq\langle\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}Z,W\rangle$ .

Notice that for $V\in T\Sigma$

$$ \nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}\mtxcal{X}=\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}Z-(V\vartheta)\nu-\vartheta\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}\nu=\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}Z-(V\vartheta)\nu+\vartheta A(V,\cdot)^{\sharp}. $$

If we take a tangential projection,

$$ \nabla^{\Sigma}_{V}\mtxcal{X}=(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}Z)^{T}+\vartheta A(V,\cdot)^{\sharp}. $$

Therefore for $V,W\in T\Sigma$ ,

$$ \mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\Sigma}_{V}\mtxcal{X},W)=\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{V}Z,W)+\vartheta A(V,W)=\mathcal{B}(V,W)+\vartheta A(V,W). $$

By taking $W=\mtxcal{X}$ in this identity, we immediately obtain that

$$ \tau V\tau=\frac{1}{2}V(\tau^{2})=\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\Sigma}_{V}\mtxcal{X},\mtxcal{X})=\mathcal{B}(V,\mtxcal{X})+\vartheta A(V,\mtxcal{X}). $$

On $\{\tau>0\}$ , writing $\mtxcal{X}=\tau\mathcal{v}$ , this becomes $V\tau=\vartheta A(V,\mathcal{v})+\mathcal{B}(V,\mathcal{v})$ , or, equivalently, $\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau=\vartheta A(\cdot,\mathcal{v})+\mathcal{B}(\cdot,\mathcal{v})$ . Taking norms, we obtain

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\mtxcal{X}|^{2}=\vartheta^{2}|A|^{2}+2\vartheta\langle A,\mathcal{B}\rangle+|\mathcal{B}|^{2}=|A|^{2}(1-\tau^{2})+2\vartheta\langle A,\mathcal{B}\rangle+|\mathcal{B}|^{2}. $$

It follows from Young’s inequality that for any fixed $\gamma>0$

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)\vartheta^{2}|A(\cdot,\mathcal{v})|^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}(\cdot,\mathcal{v})|^{2}. $$

Since $\vartheta^{2}=1-\tau^{2}$ and $|\mathcal{B}(\cdot,\mathcal{v})|\leq|\mathcal{B}|$ , we obtain

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)(1-\tau^{2})|A(\cdot,\mathcal{v})|^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2}. $$

Let $Y\in T\Sigma$ be a tangent vector field. Then we have the following Bochner identity (see [35, Theorem 9.4.1])

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{\Sigma}\frac{|Y|^{2}}{2} \displaystyle=|\nabla_{\Sigma}Y|^{2}+\langle Y,\nabla_{\Sigma}\divergence_{\Sigma}Y\rangle+\langle Y,\divergence_{\Sigma}((\nabla_{\Sigma}Y)-(\nabla_{\Sigma}Y)^{*})\rangle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(Y,Y). $$

As in the proof of Lemma 3.2, since $H=0$ , by the contracted Gauss equation

$$ \operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(Y,Y)=\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(Y,Y)-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(Y,\nu,Y,\nu)-|A(Y,\cdot)|^{2}. $$

Now, letting $Y=\mtxcal{X}$ in the Bochner formula, we notice that by (4.13),

$$ \divergence_{\Sigma}\mtxcal{X}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}(\mathcal{B}+\vartheta A)=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B}+\vartheta H=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B} $$

since $H=0$ by minimality of $\Sigma$ . Moreover, let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ -tensor on $\Sigma$ defined by $\mathcal{K}(V,W)=\langle\nabla^{\Sigma}_{V}\mtxcal{X},W\rangle-\langle\nabla^{\Sigma}_{W}\mtxcal{X},V\rangle$ for $V,W\in T\Sigma$ , and notice that this term does not appear in the proof of Lemma 3.2, since in that situation $\nabla_{\Sigma}X$ is symmetric, because $X$ is a gradient vector field.

Since $\tau=|\mtxcal{X}|_{\mathrm{g}}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\tau\Delta_{\Sigma}\tau+|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}=\Delta_{\Sigma}\frac{\tau^{2}}{2} \displaystyle=|\nabla_{\Sigma}\mtxcal{X}|^{2}+\langle\mtxcal{X},\nabla_{\Sigma}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B}\rangle+\langle\mtxcal{X},\divergence_{\Sigma}\mathcal{K}\rangle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\Sigma}(\mtxcal{X},\mtxcal{X}) \displaystyle=|A|^{2}(1-\tau^{2})+2\vartheta\langle A,\mathcal{B}\rangle+|\mathcal{B}|^{2} \displaystyle+\langle\mtxcal{X},\nabla_{\Sigma}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B}\rangle+\langle\mtxcal{X},\divergence_{\Sigma}\mathcal{K}\rangle \displaystyle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\mtxcal{X})-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\nu,\mtxcal{X},\nu)-|A(\cdot,\mtxcal{X})|^{2}, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\tau\Delta_{\Sigma}\tau \displaystyle=|A|^{2}(1-\tau^{2})-|A(\mtxcal{X},\cdot)|^{2}-|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}+2\vartheta\langle A,\mathcal{B}\rangle+|\mathcal{B}|^{2} \displaystyle+\langle\mtxcal{X},\nabla_{\Sigma}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B}\rangle+\langle\mtxcal{X},\divergence_{\Sigma}\mathcal{K}\rangle \displaystyle+\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\mtxcal{X})-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\nu,\mtxcal{X},\nu), $$

Because $H=0$ , $A$ is trace-free. Hence, for every unit vector $v$ , $|A(v,\cdot)|^{2}\leq\frac{n-1}{n}|A|^{2}$ , and

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\leq(1+\gamma)(1-\tau^{2})\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)|A|^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2}. $$

The same computations as in the proof of Lemma 3.2 also show that

$$ |A(\cdot,\mtxcal{X})|^{2}+|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{n-1}{n}+\gamma\right)|A|^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2} $$

and

$$ 2|\vartheta\langle A,\mathcal{B}\rangle|\leq\gamma|A|^{2}\vartheta^{2}+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2}=\gamma|A|^{2}(1-\tau^{2})+C(\gamma)|\mathcal{B}|^{2}. $$

For the remaining terms in (4.14), similarly to Lemma 3.2, we have

$$ |\nabla_{\Sigma}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\mathcal{B}|+|\divergence_{\Sigma}\mathcal{K}|\leq C(n)(|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}Z|+|A||\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|). $$

The bound in terms of $\Lambda$ then follows from (4.4) since

$$ |\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\mtxcal{X})-\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mtxcal{X},\nu,\mtxcal{X},\nu)|\leq C(n)|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|\tau^{2}. $$

∎

We also need to estimate the boundary normal derivative of the adapted tilt function along $\partial M$ .

#### Lemma 4.9.

Let $\eta$ be the inward unit conormal to $\partial\Sigma$ in $\Sigma$ . Along $\partial\Sigma\cap\{\tau>0\}$ we have $|\partial_{\eta}\tau|\leq|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}|+|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|$ pointwise.

#### Proof.

Let us differentiate the function $\vartheta$ in the direction of the unit conormal $\eta$ to $\partial\Sigma$ along $\partial\Sigma\cap\{\tau>0\}$ . Notice that $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}\nu\in T\Sigma$ , so that

$$ \partial_{\eta}\vartheta=\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}\nu,Z)+\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z)=\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}\nu,\mtxcal{X})+\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z)=-A(\eta,\mtxcal{X})+\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z). $$

By definition, $Z$ is tangent to $\partial M$ in $\partial M\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Therefore, along $\partial\Sigma\cap\{\tau>0\}\subset\partial M\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{g}(\mtxcal{X},\mathbf{n})=\mathrm{g}(Z-\vartheta\nu,\mathbf{n})=\mathrm{g}(Z,\mathbf{n})-\vartheta\mathrm{g}(\nu,\mathbf{n})=0, $$

and $\mtxcal{X}$ is also tangent to $\partial M$ along $\partial\Sigma$ . Hence, by symmetry of the second fundamental form and the free-boundary condition

$$ A(\eta,\mtxcal{X})=A(\mtxcal{X},\eta)=-\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\mtxcal{X}}\nu,\eta)=-\mathrm{g}(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\mtxcal{X}}\nu,\mathbf{n})=-\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\mtxcal{X},\nu) $$

and

$$ \partial_{\eta}\vartheta=\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\mtxcal{X},\nu)+\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z). $$

Clearly, $|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\mtxcal{X},\nu)|\leq|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}||\mtxcal{X}||\nu|=\tau|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}|$ . Moreover, since $|Z|_{\mathrm{g}}\equiv 1$ ,

$$ |\mathrm{g}(\nu,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z)|=|\mathrm{g}(\nu-\vartheta Z,\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}_{\eta}Z)|\leq|\nu-\vartheta Z||\eta||\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|=\tau|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|. $$

Finally,

$$ \tau|\partial_{\eta}\tau|=|\vartheta\partial_{\eta}\vartheta|\leq|\vartheta|\tau(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}|+|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|)\leq\tau(|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}|+|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|) $$

since $|\vartheta|\leq 1$ . This concludes the proof. ∎

### 4.2. Caccioppoli-type inequality

We shall now move to the weak intrinsic Caccioppoli inequality. As in Section 3, we start with the smooth case, and then extend it to the singular set using the vanishing 2-capacity assumption on $\mathcal{S}$ .

#### Lemma 4.10 (Caccioppoli inequality).

Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and assume that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Assume that (4.4) holds. Then there exist a positive dimensional constant $C(n)>0$ and a constant $K_{\mathrm{Cac}}=K_{\mathrm{Cac}}(n,\Lambda)>0$ depending on $n$ and $\Lambda$ such that for every $k\in[0,1/(4n)]$ and every $\varphi\in C_{c}^{0,1}(\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\rho_{1}}(P_{R}))$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\{\tau>k\}}|A|^{2}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n)\left(\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Cac}}^{2}\int_{\{\tau>k\}}\varphi^{2}\right). $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\{\tau>k\}}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n)\left(\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+K_{\mathrm{Cac}}^{2}\int_{\{\tau>k\}}\varphi^{2}\right). $$

#### Proof.

We shall first prove (4.15) and (4.16) for test functions $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Sigma)$ , and then extend to compactly supported ambient Lipschitz functions by an excision argument, similar to the one in Lemma 2.14.

Let $\Omega_{k}\coloneqq\{\tau>k\}$ , and apply Lemma 2.16 to $\zeta=(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi$ to obtain

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|A|^{2}(\tau-k)_{+}^{2}\varphi^{2}\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}((\tau-k)_{+}\varphi)|^{2}+C(n,\alpha)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}\varphi^{2}. $$

Let $J\coloneqq\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}((\tau-k)_{+}\varphi)|^{2}$ and integrate by parts to get

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|\nabla_{\Sigma}((\tau-k)_{+}\varphi)|^{2}=-\int_{\Omega_{k}}(\tau-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}\tau\,\varphi^{2}+\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}-\int_{\partial\Sigma\cap\Omega_{k}}(\tau-k)_{+}\partial_{\eta}\tau\varphi^{2}. $$

By Lemma 4.8, on $\Omega_{k}$ we have

$$ -(\tau-k)\Delta_{\Sigma}\tau\leq-\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)\left[\left((1-\gamma)(1-\tau^{2})-\frac{n-1}{n}-\gamma-\gamma\tau^{2}\right)|A|^{2}-C(n,\gamma)\Lambda^{2}\right]. $$

Then (4.17) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Omega_{k}} \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)\left(\tau(\tau-k)+(1+\alpha)\left(\frac{1}{n}-\tau^{2}-2\gamma\right)\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq(1+\alpha)\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+C(n,\alpha)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}\varphi^{2}+(1+\alpha)C(n,\gamma)\Lambda^{2}\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2} \displaystyle-(1+\alpha)\int_{\partial\Sigma\cap\Omega_{k}}(\tau-k)_{+}\partial_{\eta}\tau\varphi^{2}. $$

The same choices $\alpha=\alpha_{n},\gamma=\gamma_{n}$ (depending on $n$ only) as in Lemma 3.4 make the coefficient in front of $(1-k/\tau)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}$ bounded below by $1/(2n)+1/(8n^{2})>1/(2n)$ . Also, noticing that $0\leq(\tau-k)_{+}\leq 1$ and $(\tau-k)_{+}=0$ outside $\Omega_{k}$ , we can write the previous inequality as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\Omega_{k}}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n)\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2} \displaystyle-C(n)\int_{\partial\Sigma\cap\Omega_{k}}(\tau-k)_{+}\partial_{\eta}\tau\varphi^{2}. $$

Let us now deal with the boundary term. Let $B_{k}\coloneqq\int_{\partial\Sigma\cap\Omega_{k}}(\tau-k)_{+}\partial_{\eta}\tau\varphi^{2}$ . By Lemma 4.9,

$$ |B_{k}|\leq\left(\sup_{U_{1}}|\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}|+\sup_{\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})}|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|\right)\int_{\partial\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi^{2}\leq C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\partial\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi^{2} $$

where the second inequality follows from Lemma 4.6 and (4.4). By Lemma 2.14,

$$ \int_{\partial\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|+2\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|+C_{\mathrm{tr}}(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi^{2}. $$

For every $\lambda>0$ , by the weighted Young inequality

$$ \displaystyle C(n,\Lambda)\left(\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|+2\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|\right) \displaystyle\leq\lambda\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}+\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2} \displaystyle+C(\lambda)C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}. $$

Similarly, since $(\tau-k)_{+}\leq\mathds{1}_{\Omega_{k}}$ , we can write $\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}\varphi^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle|B_{k}| \displaystyle\leq\lambda\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\tau|^{2}+\int_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+C(\lambda)C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}. $$

Since $\varphi\nabla_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}=\nabla_{\Sigma}((\tau-k)_{+}\varphi)-(\tau-k)_{+}\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi$ , we have the obvious inequality $\int\varphi^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}(\tau-k)_{+}|^{2}\leq 2J+2\int(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}$ , so that

$$ |B_{k}|\leq 2\lambda J+C(n,\lambda)\mathcal{R}_{k} $$

where $\mathcal{R}_{k}\coloneqq\int(\tau-k)^{2}_{+}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\varphi^{2}$ .

Recall that by (4.18) and (4.19), we have

$$ J\leq C(n)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}+C(n)\mathcal{R}_{k}+|B_{k}|. $$

Therefore, by combining (4.20) and (4.21), we obtain

$$ |B_{k}|\leq 2\lambda\left(C(n)\int_{\Omega_{k}}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}+C(n)\mathcal{R}_{k}+|B_{k}|\right)+C(n,\lambda)\mathcal{R}_{k}, $$

i.e.

$$ |B_{k}|\leq\frac{2\lambda C(n)}{1-2\lambda}\int_{\Omega_{k}}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}+\frac{2\lambda C(n)+C(n,\lambda)}{1-2\lambda}\mathcal{R}_{k}. $$

By choosing $\lambda>0$ small enough (depending on $n$ only) that $\frac{2\lambda C(n)}{1-2\lambda}<\frac{1}{8n^{2}}$ , we can reabsorb the multiple of $\int_{\Omega_{k}}\left(1-\frac{k}{\tau}\right)|A|^{2}\varphi^{2}$ coming from (4.22) into the left hand side and obtain the desired inequality.

Finally, for an ambient test function $\varphi$ , first apply the inequality to $\chi_{j}\varphi$ , where $\chi_{j}$ are the cutoff functions of Corollary B.6, chosen to equal one in the limit on $\operatorname{spt}\varphi\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , then take the limit as in the proof of Lemma 3.4. ∎

### 4.3. Proof of Theorem 1.14

As in Section 3, we can now conclude the argument for Theorem 1.14 by applying the iteration lemma in Section 2.3.

Let us assume that (4.4) holds. Define $K_{1}(n,\Lambda)\coloneqq\max\{K_{\mathrm{Sob}}(n,\Lambda),K_{\mathrm{Cac}}(n,\Lambda)\}$ , let $\delta_{1}$ be as in Lemma 4.6, and set

$$ R_{1}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\min\bigl\{\delta_{1},K_{1}^{-1}\bigr\}. $$

Let $\Sigma$ be a stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ for some $\delta\in(0,\delta_{1}),R\in(0,R_{1})$ .

Then, for $0<r\leq R$ define the adapted cylinder $\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}$ by

$$ \mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}\coloneqq F_{Z}(P_{r}\times(-2\delta,2\delta))=\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{2\delta}(P_{r}), $$

and consider the following adapted tilt excess quantity:

$$ \mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(r)\coloneqq\left(r^{-n}\int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}}\tau^{2}\right)^{1/2} $$

where $\tau$ is the adapted tilt function in Definition 4.7.

Let us apply Lemma 2.18 with $u=\tau$ and $k_{*}=1/(4n)$ . Notice that Lemma 4.10 provides the necessary Caccioppoli-type inequality (2.5). Therefore, by Corollary 2.19, there exist $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{1}(n,\Lambda)>0$ and $C_{1}=C_{1}(n,\Lambda)>0$ such that

$$ \sup_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{\sigma R}}\tau\leq C_{1}(1-\sigma)^{-\frac{n}{n+2}}\,\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}} $$

provided $\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{1}^{2}(1-\sigma)^{n}$ , which is the desired statement.

### 4.4. Proof of Theorem 1.15

The proof of the second sheeting theorem, Theorem 1.15, is rather similar to the proof of Theorem 1.12.

Assume $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . By Theorem 1.14 with $\sigma=3/4$ , we have

$$ \sup_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}}\tau\leq C_{1}(n,\Lambda)\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}. $$

By decreasing $\varepsilon_{1}$ if necessary, we may assume $\sup_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}}\tau\leq\frac{1}{4}$ .

Step 0: $(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}=\emptyset$ . Let $\iota:N\to M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ parametrise $\Sigma$ . If $z\in N\setminus\partial N$ and $x=\iota(z)\in\partial M\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}$ , the function $d_{\partial M}\circ\iota$ has a local minimum at $z$ , and $\mathrm{d}(d_{\partial M}\circ\iota)_{z}=0$ , so that $T_{x}\Sigma\subset T_{x}\partial M$ . By dimension counting, $T_{x}\Sigma=T_{x}\partial M$ , which implies that $\tau(x)=1$ , contradicting (4.26).

Step 1: Local graphicality. Notice that

$$ \operatorname{Ker}(D\pi_{Z})_{x}=\operatorname{span}\{Z(x)\} $$

for every $x\in\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . As in the proof of Theorem 1.12 in Section 3.4, if $x=\iota(z)\in\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}$ for some $z\in N$ , we can show that $D(\pi_{Z}\circ\iota)_{z}$ is an isomorphism. If $z\in\partial N$ , the same argument and the identity $\pi_{Z}(\partial M)=P\cap\partial M$ show that in this case $\pi_{Z}\circ\iota$ is a local diffeomorphism of manifolds-with-boundary. In particular, similarly to Section 3.4, for every $z\in N$ such that $\iota(z)\in\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}$ there is a (relatively open) neighbourhood (in $N$ ) the image of which is a smooth graph over a relatively open subset of $P_{3R/4}$ via the map $F_{Z}$ .

Step 2: Finite covering away from the projected singular set. Let

$$ \Gamma_{Z}\coloneqq\pi_{Z}(\mathcal{S}\cap\overline{\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}}(P_{3R/4}))\subset\bar{P}_{3R/4},\quad B_{Z}\coloneqq P_{3R/4}\setminus\Gamma_{Z}. $$

As in the proof of Theorem 1.12, $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma_{Z})=0$ . By the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.12, $\Gamma_{Z}$ is relatively closed, and $B_{Z}$ is open, dense and path-connected in $P_{3R/4}$ . Define

$$ N_{Z}\coloneqq\{z\in N:\iota(z)\in\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4},\ \pi_{Z}(\iota(z))\in B_{Z}\}, $$

and $\hat{\pi}_{Z}\coloneqq\pi_{Z}\circ\iota|_{N_{Z}}:N_{Z}\to B_{Z}$ . By Step 1, $\hat{\pi}_{Z}$ is a local diffeomorphism of manifolds-with-boundary and, by properness of $\iota$ as an immersion into $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , it is also proper. Again, as in the proof of Theorem 1.12, it is a finite covering map of some degree $Q$ .

Step 3: Lipschitz estimate and extension across $\Gamma_{Z}$ . By Step 2, after ordering the preimages in the $Z$ -fibre $F_{Z}(\{y\}\times(-\delta,\delta))$ , we obtain locally Lipschitz functions $u^{Z}_{1},\dots,u^{Z}_{Q}$ such that $u^{Z}_{1}(y)\leq\dots\leq u^{Z}_{Q}(y)$ for all $y\in B_{Z}$ . Hence,

$$ \Sigma\cap\pi_{Z}^{-1}(B_{Z})=\cup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{Z}\bigl(\operatorname{graph}(u^{Z}_{j})\bigr). $$

For a smooth graph $G[w]=F_{Z}(\{(y,w(y)):y\in P_{R}\})$ on $P_{R}$ and $v\in T_{y}P$ , where $x=F_{Z}(y,w(y))$ , consider the vector

$$ V(x)=(D_{y}F_{Z})_{(y,w(y))}(v)+dw_{y}(v)Z(x)\in T_{x}G[w]. $$

Since $|Z|_{\mathrm{g}}=1$ , by taking the inner product with $Z$ , we have

$$ dw_{y}(v)=\langle V(x),Z(x)\rangle-\langle(D_{y}F_{Z})_{(y,w(y))}(v),Z(x)\rangle. $$

Thus, by Lemma 4.6,

$$ \displaystyle|dw_{y}(v)| \displaystyle\leq|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}G[w]}_{\mathrm{g}}Z(x)||V(x)|+|\langle(D_{y}F_{Z})_{(y,w(y))}(v),Z(x)\rangle| \displaystyle\leq|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}G[w]}_{\mathrm{g}}Z(x)|(C(n)|v|+|dw_{y}(v)|)+C(n)\Lambda\delta|v|. $$

If $|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}G[w]}_{\mathrm{g}}Z(x)|\leq 1/4$ (as is the case for our graphs $u^{Z}_{j}$ , where this is just $\tau$ ), then

$$ |dw_{y}(v)|\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(|\mathrm{proj}^{T_{x}G[w]}_{\mathrm{g}}Z(x)|+\delta\right)|v|. $$

Since we can approximate curves in $P_{3R/4}$ by curves which avoid $\Gamma_{Z}$ , by (4.26) we conclude that

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{P}(u^{Z}_{j};B_{Z})\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\delta+\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\right). $$

Similarly to the proof of Theorem 1.12, by density of $B_{Z}$ in $P_{3R/4}$ , every $u^{Z}_{j}$ extends uniquely to a Lipschitz function (still denoted $u^{Z}_{j}$ ) on the whole of $P_{3R/4}$ , with the same bound on the Lipschitz constant, namely

$$ \operatorname{Lip}_{P}(u^{Z}_{j})\leq C(n,\Lambda)\left(\delta+\mathrm{E}^{Z}_{\Sigma,P}(R)^{\frac{2}{n+2}}\right). $$

Finally, showing that $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{3R/4})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{Z}(\operatorname{graph}(u^{Z}_{j}))$ follows from the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.12.

As in Section 3, we can now prove (i) and (ii).

- (i) Assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ . Since $\pi_{Z}$ is Lipschitz on $\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{2\delta}(P_{3R/4})$ by (4.7), then $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\Gamma_{Z})=0$ . By reflecting across $\partial_{0}P_{R}$ and applying the result in [40, Appendix A], we see that $B_{Z}$ must then be simply connected, so every component of the covering $\hat{\pi}_{Z}:N_{Z}\to B_{Z}$ is one-sheeted. As in the proof of Theorem 1.12, this determines $Q$ globally defined, not necessarily ordered Lipschitz functions $v^{Z}_{1},\dots,v^{Z}_{Q}:B_{Z}\to(-\delta,\delta)$ such that

$$ \Sigma\cap\pi_{Z}^{-1}(B_{Z})=\cup_{j=1}^{Q}F_{Z}(\operatorname{graph}(v^{Z}_{j})), $$

each of which extends to a Lipschitz function (still denoted $v^{Z}_{j}$ ) on the whole of $P_{3R/4}$ , preserving the Lipschitz constant. As in the proof of Theorem 1.12, $\Gamma_{Z}$ is relatively closed and $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma_{Z})=0$ . Notice that the flow of $Z$ preserves $\partial M$ , so the vertical variation $v^{Z}_{j}+t\varphi$ is admissible on $B_{Z}$ up to the boundary $\partial_{0}P_{3R/4}$ . Therefore, the Lipschitz functions $v^{Z}_{j}$ are weak solutions of the minimal surface equation (with a uniform bound on the Lipschitz constant) for test functions compactly supported in $B_{Z}$ . By direct computation, the area integrand $\mathcal{L}(y,z,q)$ in the local coordinates induced by the diffeomorphism $\Psi$ (in Lemma 4.3) is uniformly elliptic by Lemma 4.6. Therefore, Lemma A.2 applies and the $v^{Z}_{j}$ extend smoothly across $\Gamma_{Z}$ all the way to the boundary, so that $\mathcal{S}\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R/2})=\emptyset$ , as required. The bound on $\|\nabla v^{Z}_{j}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(P_{3R/4})}$ follows from standard elliptic regularity theory as in the proof of Theorem 1.12.

- (ii) Assume now $\Sigma$ is embedded. Then for every $y\in B_{Z}$ the points of $\Sigma$ lying in the $Z$ -fibre are distinct and $u^{Z}_{1}<u^{Z}_{2}<\dots<u^{Z}_{Q}$ on $B_{Z}$ , so that each $u^{Z}_{j}$ is smooth on $B_{Z}$ . The same removability argument as above (since $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma_{Z})=0$ ) implies that the $u^{Z}_{j}$ are globally smooth, and weak ordering is preserved. Strict ordering is also preserved by the strong maximum principle for the minimal surface equation in the interior and by the corresponding boundary strong maximum principle (Hopf lemma) using the uniformly oblique boundary condition. Thus $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{3R/4}$ is a union of pairwise disjoint smooth graphs and $\mathcal{S}\cap\mathcal{N}_{\delta}^{Z}(P_{3R/4})=\emptyset$ . Finally, the gradient estimates follow from standard elliptic regularity theory as in (i).

## 5. Compactness

In this section we give a proof of Theorem 1.1. This roughly follows [38] and crucially uses Theorem 1.12 and Theorem 1.15, proven in the previous sections.

### 5.1. From height to tilt

We start by proving two propositions bounding the tilt excess by the $L^{2}$ and $L^{1}$ norms of the height. This will be used later in the proof of compactness to deduce from the varifold convergence smallness of the tilt, and consequently that we are in a regime in which we can apply the sheeting theorems. The Euclidean interior analogue is the standard tilt excess inequality (see e.g. [4, Remark 4.2]).

We start with the boundary parallel case and then move to the orthogonal one.

#### Proposition 5.1 (Tilt-excess estimate).

Let $M,P,\rho_{0},R_{0}$ be as in the statement of Theorem 1.11, and let $\delta\in(0,\rho_{0}),R\in(0,R_{0})$ . Suppose $\Sigma$ is a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Then, there exists $C(n,\Lambda)>0$ such that for $0<2r<R$ the following estimate holds

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\Sigma\cap C_{r}}g^{2}=\frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\Sigma\cap C_{r}}|\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}|^{2}\leq\frac{C(n,\Lambda)}{r^{n+2}}\int_{\Sigma\cap C_{2r}}\left(d_{\partial M}^{2}+r^{2}d_{\partial M}\right), $$

where $g$ is the tilt function in Definition 3.1.

#### Proof.

Consider the vector field $X(x)=d_{\partial M}(x)\varphi^{2}(x)\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}(x)$ , where $\varphi\in C_{c}^{1}(C_{2r})$ is a smooth cut-off taken to be identically $1$ on $C_{r}$ and satisfying $|\nabla\varphi|\leq C/r$ (for some absolute constant $C$ ). In particular, $X(x)\equiv 0$ on $\partial M$ so that we can test the first variation with it. In particular, by free-boundary stationarity

$$ 0=\int_{\Sigma}\divergence_{\Sigma}X=\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}g^{2}+2\varphi d_{\partial M}\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi,\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}\rangle+\varphi^{2}d_{\partial M}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}, $$

since the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ is assumed to vanish in $\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma$ by Definition 2.2. Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma\cap C_{r}}g^{2}\leq\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}g^{2}\leq 2\int_{\Sigma}|\varphi\nabla_{\Sigma}d_{\partial M}||d_{\partial M}\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|+\sqrt{n}\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}d_{\partial M}|\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}d_{\partial M}| $$

from which (5.1) follows by Young’s inequality and (1.2). ∎

#### Proposition 5.2 (Orthogonal tilt–height excess estimate).

Let $M,P,\rho_{1},\delta_{1},R_{1}$ be as in the statement of Theorem 1.14. Let $z_{P}$ and $Z$ be as in Definition 4.1, and let $\delta\in(0,\delta_{1}),R\in(0,R_{1})$ . Suppose $\Sigma$ is a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ such that $\overline{\Sigma}\subset\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ . Then, there exists $C(n,\Lambda)>0$ such that for $0<2r<R$ the following estimate holds

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}}\tau^{2}\leq\frac{C(n,\Lambda)}{r^{n+2}}\int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{2r}}\left(z_{P}^{2}+r^{2}|z_{P}|\right), $$

where $\tau$ is the adapted tilt function in Definition 4.7. Moreover, since $|\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P}|^{2}=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{2}\tau^{2},$ the same estimate holds, up to increasing the constant $C$ , with $|\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P}|^{2}$ in place of $\tau^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $W\coloneqq|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{-1}Z$ and notice that $1/2\leq|W|_{\mathrm{g}}\leq 2$ by Definition 4.1. For $0<2r\leq R$ choose a cutoff $\chi$ on $P_{R}$ which is compactly supported on $P_{2r}$ and such that $0\leq\chi\leq 1,$ and $\chi\equiv 1$ on $P_{r},$ as well as $|\nabla_{P}\chi|\leq C/r,$ where $C$ is an absolute constant. Then pick a compactly supported vertical cutoff $\xi\geq\mathds{1}_{[-\delta,\delta]}$ supported in $(-2\delta,2\delta)$ and let $\varphi=(\xi\circ\mathcal{t}_{Z})(\chi\circ\pi_{Z})$ , so that $\varphi\equiv 1$ on $\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}$ as well as $\operatorname{spt}(\varphi)\cap\Sigma\subset\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{2r}$ . Also, $\varphi$ satisfies $|\nabla\varphi|\leq C/r,$ where $C$ depends on $n,\Lambda,\rho_{1}$ only.

Consider then the vector field $Y=\varphi^{2}z_{P}W.$ Since $W$ is tangent to $\partial M$ along $\partial M\cap\mathcal{N}^{Z}_{\delta}(P_{R})$ , then $Y$ is an admissible vector field for free-boundary stationarity and $\int_{\Sigma}\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}Y=0.$ Notice that

$$ \langle\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P},W\rangle=\left\langle|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|Z^{T},\frac{Z}{|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|}\right\rangle=|Z^{T}|^{2}=\tau^{2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\divergence_{\Sigma}Y=\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}(\varphi^{2}z_{P}W) \displaystyle=\varphi^{2}\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P},W\rangle+2\varphi z_{P}\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi,W\rangle+\varphi^{2}z_{P}\,\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}W \displaystyle=\varphi^{2}\tau^{2}+2\varphi z_{P}|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{-1}\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi,Z^{T}\rangle+\varphi^{2}z_{P}\divergence_{\Sigma}W. $$

Notice that

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}W \displaystyle=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{-1}\divergence_{\Sigma}Z-\left\langle Z,|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{-2}\nabla_{\Sigma}|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|\right\rangle $$

so that $|\operatorname{div}_{\Sigma}W|\leq C(n)\bigl(|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}Z|+|\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}z_{P}|\bigr)\leq C(n)\Lambda$ by Definition 4.1 and Lemma 4.6. Combining all of the above, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}\tau^{2} \displaystyle\leq 4\int_{\Sigma}\varphi|z_{P}|\,|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|\,\tau+C(n)\Lambda\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}|z_{P}|. $$

By Young’s inequality, $4\varphi|z_{P}|\,|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|\,\tau\leq\frac{1}{2}\varphi^{2}\tau^{2}+8z_{P}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}.$ After absorbing the first term into the left-hand side, it follows that

$$ \int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}\tau^{2}\leq 16\int_{\Sigma}z_{P}^{2}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\varphi|^{2}+C(n)\Lambda\int_{\Sigma}\varphi^{2}|z_{P}|. $$

Using properties of $\varphi$ , we conclude that

$$ \int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{r}}\tau^{2}\leq\frac{C}{r^{2}}\int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{2r}}z_{P}^{2}+C(n,\Lambda)\int_{\Sigma\cap\mathcal{C}^{Z}_{2r}}|z_{P}|. $$

Dividing by $r^{n}$ proves (5.2).

Finally, $|\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P}|^{2}=|(\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P})^{T}|^{2}=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{2}|Z^{T}|^{2}=|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}z_{P}|^{2}\tau^{2}.$ Thus, $(1/4)\tau^{2}\leq|\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P}|^{2}\leq 4\tau^{2},$ which proves the corresponding estimate for $|\nabla_{\Sigma}z_{P}|^{2}$ . ∎

#### Remark 5.3.

The height–tilt estimate also admits a formulation using only $Z$ described in Remark 4.2, right after Definition 4.1. In that formulation, use the flow time $\mathcal{t}_{Z}$ as height. Since $Z(\mathcal{t}_{Z})=1$ and $\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal{t}_{Z}=Z$ on $P$ , the derivative and flow estimates give

$$ |\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal{t}_{Z}-Z|\leq C(n)\Lambda|\mathcal{t}_{Z}|. $$

Testing free-boundary stationarity with $\varphi^{2}\mathcal{t}_{Z}Z$ therefore yields (5.2) with $\mathcal{t}_{Z}$ in place of $z_{P}$ : the error in replacing $\langle\nabla_{\Sigma}\mathcal{t}_{Z},Z\rangle$ by $\tau^{2}$ is bounded by $C(n)\Lambda|\mathcal{t}_{Z}|\tau$ , and hence by the linear height term already present in the estimate.

### 5.2. Free-boundary stationary varifolds

Notice that Definition 2.6 implies that a singular properly embedded1010 10 Most of the results in this specific subsection do actually hold for singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma$ with minimal changes in the statements and proofs. free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ defines an integral varifold $V=|\Sigma|\coloneqq\mathbf{v}(\Sigma,\mathds{1}_{\Sigma})$ on $M$ . We refer to [43] for the definition and basic properties of varifolds.

We define the regular set $\operatorname{reg}V$ of such a varifold to be:

$$ \operatorname{reg}(V)\coloneqq\bigg\{x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|:\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{there exists $r>0$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap B_{r}(x)$ is a smooth }\\
\textrm{embedded hypersurface-with-(possibly empty) boundary in $\partial M$}\end{array}\bigg\}. $$

If $x\in\operatorname{reg}(V)$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap B_{r}(x)$ is a smooth embedded hypersurface-with-boundary $\Gamma$ , then we say $x$ is a regular interior point (denoted $x\in\operatorname{reg}_{i}(V)$ ) if $x\in\Gamma\setminus\partial\Gamma$ , and $x$ is a regular boundary point if $x\in\partial\Gamma$ (denoted $x\in\operatorname{reg}_{b}(V)$ ). Moreover, we define its complement to be the singular set $\operatorname{sing}(V)$ of $V$ by

$$ \operatorname{sing}(V)\coloneqq\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\operatorname{reg}(V). $$

As we mentioned in Remark 2.8, given a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ , its closure $\overline{\Sigma}$ in $M$ , $\mathcal{S}=\overline{\Sigma}\setminus\Sigma$ , and the corresponding multiplicity-one varifold $V=|\Sigma|$ , we can redefine $\mathcal{S}$ and $\Sigma$ so that

$$ \operatorname{reg}(V)=\Sigma,\quad\operatorname{reg}_{i}(V)=\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma,\quad\operatorname{reg}_{b}(V)=\partial\Sigma,\quad\operatorname{sing}(V)=\mathcal{S}. $$

By (1)-(2) in Definition 2.2 and the discussion in Appendix B, the multiplicity-one varifold $V$ associated to a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ also satisfies an additional variational property; indeed such a $V$ is free-boundary stationary in $M$ . See [26] for more details on free-boundary stationary varifolds. Some of the basic properties of free-boundary stationary varifolds which are needed in this paper are also briefly recalled in Appendix C.

For the multiplicity-one varifold $V$ associated to a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ , we can easily compute the first variation $\delta V(X)$ for all compactly supported vector fields $X\in\mathfrak{X}(M)$ .

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $\Sigma$ be a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and let $V=|\Sigma|$ be its associated multiplicity-one varifold. Then

$$ \delta V(X)=-\int_{\partial\Sigma}\mathrm{g}(X,\eta)\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\quad\text{for all }X\in\mathfrak{X}(M), $$

where $\eta$ denotes the inner unit conormal of $\partial\Sigma$ in $\Sigma$ . Hence, for all $K\Subset M$ , if $K\Subset\operatorname{int}K^{\prime}\Subset M$ , then

$$ \sup\left\{|\delta V(X)|:X\in\mathfrak{X}(M),|X|_{\mathrm{g}}\leq 1,\operatorname{spt}X\subset K\right\}\leq C(K)\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma\cap K^{\prime}), $$

i.e. the integral varifold $|\Sigma|$ has locally bounded first variation.

#### Proof.

Notice that for all vector fields $X$ supported away from the singular set $\mathcal{S}$ , (5.7) holds because of Definition 2.2. On the other hand, for a general $X\in\mathfrak{X}(M)$ , if we let $\{\chi_{j}\}$ be the sequence of test functions in Corollary B.6, then $X_{j}\coloneqq\chi_{j}X$ is supported away from the singular set, and the same excision argument as in the proof of Lemma 2.14 proves the general result. ∎

#### Remark 5.5.

Notice that our proof crucially uses the property that $V$ is induced by a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface. On the other hand, (5.8) holds in general for free-boundary stationary varifolds, albeit with a more involved proof. The proof under the assumption of integrality is in [12, Proposition 3.2], and in full generality in [10, Theorem 1.1].

The results that follow, although stated for varifolds induced by singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, hold for general free-boundary stationary integral varifolds and sequences thereof. See [27] for a detailed treatment at this level of generality.

In this paper, we chose to restrict our treatment to varifolds induced by singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces for the sake of simplicity and to offer a (more) self-contained presentation. Indeed, this special case will be sufficient for the applications in this paper, provided we supplement it with the following (elementary) observation.

#### Remark 5.6.

The conclusions of Proposition 5.7, Lemma 5.8, Proposition 5.11, and Proposition C.7 also hold for varifold limits of sequences of singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in $M$ with locally bounded mass. (This will be needed in Section 5.3 and Section 5.4.)

By Allard’s Compactness Theorem [1, 6.4] and Lemma 5.8, we have the following.

#### Proposition 5.7.

Let $(\Sigma_{k})$ be a sequence of singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in $M$ and, for each $k$ , let $V_{k}=|\Sigma_{k}|$ be the associated multiplicity-one varifold. Assume that for each $K\Subset M$

$$ \sup_{k}\|V_{k}\|(K)\leq C(K)<+\infty. $$

Then, up to a subsequence (not relabelled), there is a free-boundary stationary integral varifold $V_{\infty}$ on $M$ such that

$$ V_{k}\to V_{\infty}\quad\text{in the sense of varifolds.} $$

In particular, $\delta V_{k}\to\delta V_{\infty}$ and the limit has locally bounded first variation. Moreover,

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|V_{k}\|\to\operatorname{spt}\|V_{\infty}\| $$

locally in Hausdorff distance.

#### Proof.

The first variation hypothesis in [1, 6.4] is fulfilled, in view of Lemma 5.4; this yields the subsequential limit $V_{\infty}$ . The only conclusion that needs justification is (5.11), which follows from the standard proof for stationary integral varifolds (as remarked e.g. in [38, Remark 10]) once the following lemma is established. ∎

#### Lemma 5.8.

Let $\Sigma$ be a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and let $V=|\Sigma|$ be the associated multiplicity-one varifold in $M$ . Then for each compact $K\subset M$ there exist constants $c_{K}>0,C_{K},r_{K}>0$ such that

$$ c_{K}r^{n}\leq\|V\|(B_{r}(y))\leq C_{K}r^{n} $$

for all $y\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap K$ , $0<r<r_{K}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $K\subset M$ be compact and pick $r_{K}>0$ small enough that

- • if $K\subset M\setminus\partial M$ , $2r_{K}\leq\inf_{x\in K}\operatorname{inj}_{x}(M)$ ;

- • if $K\cap\partial M\neq\emptyset$ , $F_{\partial M}$ is a diffeomorphism of $(K\cap\partial M)\times[0,2r_{K})$ onto the collar neighbourhood $\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2r_{K}}(K\cap\partial M)$ and $2r_{K}\leq\inf_{x\in K\setminus\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2r_{K}}(K\cap\partial M)}\operatorname{inj}_{x}(M)$ .

Then notice that by [43, §17] and [18, Theorem 3.4] there exist constants $\Lambda^{\mathrm{int}}_{K},\Lambda^{\mathrm{bd}}_{K}$ depending on $\sup_{K}|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}}|$ and $\sup_{\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2r_{K}}(K\cap\partial M)}|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}|$ such that for all $y\in K$

$$ e^{\Lambda^{\mathrm{int}}_{K}\sigma}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\sigma}(y))}{\sigma^{n}}\leq e^{\Lambda^{\mathrm{int}}_{K}\rho}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(y))}{\rho^{n}}\quad\text{whenever }B_{\rho}(y)\cap\partial M=\emptyset,0<\sigma<\rho<r_{K}, $$

and

$$ e^{\Lambda^{\mathrm{bd}}_{K}\sigma}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\sigma}(y))}{\sigma^{n}}\leq e^{\Lambda^{\mathrm{bd}}_{K}\rho}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(y))}{\rho^{n}}\quad\text{whenever }y\in K\cap\partial M,0<\sigma<\rho<r_{K}. $$

For simplicity we shall prove the density ratio lower bound in (5.12). The proof of the upper bound follows a similar strategy. Choose $c_{K}=16^{-n}\omega_{n}e^{-2\max\{\Lambda^{\mathrm{int}}_{K},\Lambda^{\mathrm{bd}}_{K}\}r_{K}}>0$ , and consider first a regular point $y\in\Sigma$ . If $y\in\partial\Sigma$ , then $\Theta(\|V\|,y)=1/2$ and, by (5.14), we can conclude (5.12) holds for $0<r<r_{K}$ . Similarly if $y\in(\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma)\cap\partial M$ .

Now fix $r\in(0,r_{K})$ . Since $y\in\Sigma\setminus\partial\Sigma$ , then $\Theta(\|V\|,y)=1$ and $d\coloneqq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(y,\partial M)>0$ . If $d\geq r/4$ , then $B_{r/8}(y)\Subset M\setminus\partial M$ and (5.12) follows from (5.13). On the other hand, if $0<d<r/4$ , then let $\hat{y}=\pi_{\partial M}(y)$ be the nearest boundary point to $y$ . By interior monotonicity at $y$ at scale $d/2$ , $\|V\|(B_{d/2}(y))\geq c_{K}d^{n}$ . Since $B_{d/2}(y)\subset B_{2d}(\hat{y})$ , $\|V\|(B_{2d}(\hat{y}))\geq c_{K}(2d)^{n}$ . By boundary monotonicity (5.14) from scale $2d$ to scale $r/2$ ,

$$ \frac{\|V\|(B_{r/2}(\hat{y}))}{(r/2)^{n}}\geq c_{K}\frac{\|V\|(B_{2d}(\hat{y}))}{(2d)^{n}}\geq c_{K} $$

after absorbing exponential factors in the constant. Since $B_{r/2}(\hat{y})\subset B_{r}(y)$ , then (5.12) follows.

Finally, for a singular point $y\in\mathcal{S}$ , choose regular points $\Sigma\ni y_{\ell}\to y$ , and notice that for all sufficiently large $\ell$ , $B_{r/2}(y_{\ell})\subset B_{r}(y)$ , so (5.12) at $y$ follows from the statement for regular points we have just proven. ∎

#### Remark 5.9.

A quantitative version of the density lower bound in Lemma 5.8 follows from [33, Theorem 9.22].

#### Remark 5.10.

It is easy to see that the conclusion of Proposition 5.7 still holds if each $\Sigma_{k}$ is a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $(M,\mathrm{g}_{k})$ where the metrics $\mathrm{g}_{k}$ converge in $C^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to a smooth metric $\mathrm{g}$ on $M$ .
