The notion of a tangent cone will be central to our analysis. We shall provide the definition and recap the basic properties of tangent cones to free-boundary stationary varifolds in Appendix C. For the purposes of the proof of Theorem 1.1, the following proposition will suffice.

#### Proposition 5.11.

Let $\Sigma$ be a singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface in $M$ and let $V=|\Sigma|$ be the associated multiplicity-one varifold. If $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|=\overline{\Sigma}\subset M$ , then $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\neq\emptyset$ . Moreover,

- (1) if $x\in M\setminus\partial M$ and $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ , then $\mathbf{C}$ is a stationary integral cone in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ of density $\Theta(\|V\|,x)$ ;

- (2) if $x\in\partial M$ and $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ , then $\mathbf{C}$ is a free-boundary stationary integral cone in $(T^{+}_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ of density $\Theta(\|V\|,x)$ , and $\overline{\mathbf{C}}=\mathbf{C}+(\theta_{0})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}$ is a stationary integral cone in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ which is invariant under $\theta_{0}$ , where $\theta_{0}$ denotes the reflection across $T_{x}(\partial M)\subset T_{x}M$ in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ .

Finally, we shall need a version of Almgren’s stratification for free-boundary stationary integral varifolds $V$ . See Appendix C for the relevant notation and the statement of the relevant stratification result and [27] for a proof.

We can now proceed with the proof of the Compactness Theorem (Theorem 1.1). Fix a compact $K\subset M$ and assume without loss of generality (by Proposition 5.7) that the multiplicity-one varifolds $V_{k}$ associated with $\Sigma_{k}$ converge in $K$ to a free-boundary stationary varifold $V$ . We then begin by analysing the possible tangent cones of $V$ .

### 5.3. Top-dimensional stratum

We first analyse the top-dimensional part of the singular stratum of $V$ , i.e. those (a priori, singular) points such that at least one tangent cone $\mathbf{C}$ is such that $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}$ has a spine of dimension $n$ .

#### Proposition 5.12 (Regularity at flat tangent cones).

Let $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ and assume $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ is such that $\dim S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})=n$ . Then $x$ is a regular point of $V$ and $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)=\{\mathbf{C}\}$ , i.e. the tangent cone at $x$ is unique.

#### Proof.

For the sake of brevity, we shall focus on the case of $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M$ . The interior case is almost identical to (and, indeed, slightly simpler than) (1) in the dichotomy below. So, for the rest of this proof, let $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M$ , and, for simplicity, let $H=T_{x}M$ , $H_{+}=T^{+}_{x}M$ , and $T=\partial H_{+}=T_{x}\partial M$ .

By the constancy theorem [43], $\overline{\mathbf{C}}=Q|\Pi|$ for some $n$ -plane $\Pi$ . By Proposition 5.11, the doubled cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is invariant under the reflection $\theta_{0}$ across $T$ . Hence, we know that the normal to $\Pi$ is an eigenvector of the reflection map. Consequently, there are two options:

- (1) $\Pi=T_{x}\partial M$ , in which case $Q$ is even and $\mathbf{C}=(Q/2)|T_{x}\partial M|$ . Let the notation be as in Appendix C, so for $r>0$ the map $\Psi_{x,r}:H_{+}\cap B^{H}_{r^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)\to M$ is the rescaling map in (C.2) with inverse $\Phi_{x,r}$ , and $\mathrm{g}_{x,r}=r^{-2}\Psi_{x,r}^{*}\mathrm{g}$ as a metric on (a subset of) $H_{+}$ . By definition (see Section C.2 together with Remark 5.6), there exist positive numbers $r_{i}\to 0$ such that the free-boundary stationary integral varifolds $W_{i}\coloneqq(\Phi_{x,r_{i}})_{\sharp}V$ in $(H_{+},\mathrm{g}_{i})$ converge locally to $(Q/2)|T|\subset H_{+}$ , where for simplicity we let $\mathrm{g}_{i}\coloneqq\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i}}$ . Let $d_{i}$ denote the $\mathrm{g}_{i}$ -distance function to $T$ in $(H_{+},\mathrm{g}_{i})$ . Moreover, for each $i$ and $R>0$ , let $P^{i}_{R}$ be the intrinsic ball in $(T,\mathrm{g}_{i}|_{T})$ of radius $R$ centred at $0$ and $P_{R}$ the Euclidean ball in $T$ . Since $\mathrm{g}_{i}\to\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ locally smoothly, given any $\rho_{0}>0$ , there exists $i_{0}\geq 1$ such that (5.15) the normal exponential map of $T_{x}(\partial M)$ is a diffeomorphism of $P^{i}_{8\rho_{0}}\times[0,8\rho_{0})$ and $|\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}d_{i}|^{2}+|\nabla^{3}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}d_{i}|+|\operatorname{Rm}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}|\leq 1$ for all $i\geq i_{0}$ . By Proposition 5.7 (and Remark 5.6), $\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\to T$ locally in Hausdorff distance. As $\mathrm{g}_{i}\to\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ , for any compact set $K\subset H_{+}$ , we have (5.16)

$$ \sup_{\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap K}d_{i}\to 0\quad\text{as }i\rightarrow\infty. $$

Fix $\rho_{0}\in(0,1]$ and the corresponding $i_{0}\geq 1$ , and notice that by (5.15), the threshold radius $R_{0}$ and the threshold normalised tilt excess $\varepsilon_{0}$ in Theorem 1.12 can be chosen to hold uniformly for all $i\geq i_{0}$ . By varifold convergence to $(Q/2)|T|$ , we can assume that for all $i\geq i_{0}$ we have (5.17)

$$ \|W_{i}\|(\mathcal{N}^{+}_{4\rho_{0}}(P^{i}_{4\rho_{0}}))\leq C(n,Q). $$

For fixed $R\in(0,R_{0}/2)$ , by (5.17), we can choose $\delta\in(0,\rho_{0}/2)$ such that the right hand side of (5.1) with $r=2R$ is strictly less than $\varepsilon_{0}^{2}/2$ for all $i\geq i_{0}$ . By (5.16) with $K=\overline{\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}}(P_{2R})$ , by possibly increasing $i_{0}$ , we can guarantee that for all $i\geq i_{0}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}(P^{i}_{2R})\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta/2}(P^{i}_{2R}) $$

Now fix the scale $r_{*}=r_{i_{0}}$ and write $\mathrm{g}_{*}\coloneqq\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i_{0}}}$ , $P^{*}_{R}\coloneqq P^{i_{0}}_{R}$ , $W^{*}=W_{i_{0}}$ , and $W^{*}_{k}\coloneqq(\Phi_{x,r_{i_{0}}})_{\sharp}V_{k}$ . $$ \operatorname{spt}\|W^{*}_{k}\|\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}(P^{*}_{2R})\subset\mathcal{N}^{+}_{\delta}(P^{*}_{2R}), $$

and $W^{*}_{k}$ satisfies a mass bound analogous to (5.17). Therefore, by Proposition 5.1, we obtain that, for all sufficiently large $k$ , we have

$$ E_{W^{*}_{k},P^{*}}(2R)^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{0}^{2}/2, $$

and Theorem 1.12 applies. In particular, (ii) of Theorem 1.12 applies and for all sufficiently large $k$ (by uniform equivalence of the metrics) (5.18)

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|W^{*}_{k}\|\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{2\rho_{0}}(P_{R/2})=\bigcup_{j=1}^{Q_{k}}F_{\partial M}(\operatorname{graph}(u_{k,j})) $$

Each $u_{j}$ satisfies the $\mathrm{g}_{*}$ -minimal surface equation on $P_{R/4}$ , so if any two graphs touch they must coincide. After shrinking the neighbourhood further if needed, this shows that the support of $W^{*}$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ is given by a single smooth embedded minimal hypersurface, possibly with multiplicity, which must then be given by the density $Q/2$ at $0$ . After undoing all the rescalings, this shows that $x$ is a regular point of $V$ , and that the tangent cone is unique. It also gives local smooth graphical convergence of the hypersurfaces $\Sigma_{k}$ .

- (2) $\Pi\subset T_{x}M$ is an $n$ -plane invariant under reflection across $T_{x}\partial M$ and $\Pi\neq T_{x}\partial M$ . Notice that then $\mathbf{C}=Q|\Pi^{+}|$ . $$ \sup_{\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap K}|z_{i}|\to 0\quad\text{as }i\rightarrow\infty. $$

### 5.4. Excluding boundary classical cones: slicing argument

We can now move to the $(n-1)$ -dimensional part of the singular stratum. We will use the argument of [38]. Since the interior case is completely analogous to [38], we shall focus on the boundary case, i.e. $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M$ . Again, as in the proof of Proposition 5.12, we let $H=T_{x}M$ , $H_{+}=T^{+}_{x}M$ , and $T=\partial H_{+}=T_{x}\partial M$ .

Before we proceed with the argument we need the following elementary lemma, which shows that if $\mathbf{C}$ is a tangent cone of a stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ at some $x\in\overline{\Sigma}=\operatorname{spt}|\Sigma|$ , then the regular part of $\mathbf{C}$ is a stable free-boundary minimal cone (for the Euclidean metric on $T_{x}M$ ). Similarly for tangent cones to varifold limits of stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces.

#### Lemma 5.13.

Let $V$ be the multiplicity-one varifold induced by a stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ , or the varifold limit of a sequence of such objects. Let $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ and let $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ . Then $\operatorname{reg}(\mathbf{C})$ is a stable smooth (possibly free-boundary) minimal hypersurface in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ .

#### Proof.

Let the notation be as in Appendix C and the proof of Proposition 5.12. For simplicity, let us assume $V=|\Sigma|$ for a stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurface $|\Sigma|$ and $x\in\overline{\Sigma}\cap\partial M$ . By definition, there exists a sequence $r_{i}\to 0$ such that the multiplicity-one varifolds $|\Sigma_{i}|$ induced by stable singular free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces $\Sigma_{i}=\Phi_{x,r_{i}}(\Sigma)$ in the rescaled metrics $\mathrm{g}_{i}$ converge locally to $\mathbf{C}$ . By tracking how the geometric quantities involved transform, we see that, for every $\varphi\in C_{c}^{0,1}(\Sigma_{i})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma_{i}}|\nabla^{\mathrm{g_{i}}}_{\Sigma_{i}}\varphi|^{2}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}- \displaystyle r_{i}^{2}\left((|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}+\operatorname{Ric}_{\mathrm{g}}(\nu_{\Sigma},\nu_{\Sigma}))\circ\Psi_{x,r_{i}}\right)\varphi^{2}\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}^{n} \displaystyle-r_{i}\int_{\partial\Sigma_{i}}(\mathrm{I\!I}^{\mathrm{g}}_{\partial M}(\nu_{\Sigma},\nu_{\Sigma})\circ\Psi_{x,r_{i}})\varphi^{2}\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{i}}^{n-1}\geq 0. $$

By Corollary B.6, (5.20) holds for all compactly supported ambient Lipschitz test functions.

Now let $y\in\operatorname{reg}(\mathbf{C})$ . Then any tangent cone $\mathbf{D}$ to $\mathbf{C}$ at $y$ is a constant multiplicity hyperplane or orthogonal half-plane. Therefore, after applying Proposition 5.12 to a diagonal sequence converging to $\mathbf{D}$ , we see that the free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in the diagonal sequence converge smoothly and graphically to $\mathbf{D}$ on a neighbourhood of $y$ . In particular, we can pass (5.20) to the limit in a neighbourhood of $y$ and obtain that $\operatorname{reg}(\mathbf{C})$ satisfies the (Euclidean) stability inequality

$$ \int_{\operatorname{reg}(\mathbf{C})}|A_{\mathbf{C}}|^{2}\varphi^{2}\leq\int_{\operatorname{reg}(\mathbf{C})}|\nabla\varphi|^{2} $$

for all compactly supported Lipschitz test functions $\varphi$ .

Finally, the case where $V$ is a varifold limit of stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces follows from the same proof after taking a further diagonal subsequence. ∎

We are now ready to prove the main result in this subsection, namely that for a varifold limit $V$ of a sequence of stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces the $(n-1)$ -dimensional part of the singular stratum $\mathscr{S}_{n-1}\setminus\mathscr{S}_{n-2}$ is empty. Another way to formulate this is that if $\mathbf{C}$ is a tangent cone to such a varifold $V$ and $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})\geq n-1$ , then actually $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})=n$ and Proposition 5.12 applies.

#### Proposition 5.14.

Let $V$ be a varifold limit of a sequence $\{\Sigma_{k}\}_{k}$ of stable singular properly embedded free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in $M$ . Then the $(n-1)$ -dimensional part of the singular stratum $\mathscr{S}_{n-1}\setminus\mathscr{S}_{n-2}$ of $V$ is empty.

#### Proof.

As we stated above, we shall focus on the case where $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M$ . As in the proof of Proposition 5.12, we let $H=T_{x}M$ , $H_{+}=T^{+}_{x}M$ , $T=\partial H_{+}$ , and $H_{+}^{\circ}=H_{+}\setminus T$ .

Let $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ and assume that $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ has an $(n-1)$ -dimensional spine, denoted by $L$ . Since $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is invariant under reflection $\theta_{0}$ across $T=\partial H_{+}$ , then $L$ is invariant under $\theta_{0}$ . As the $(-1)$ -eigenspace of the reflection is one-dimensional, exactly one of the following occurs: either $L\subset T$ , or $\mathbf{n}_{x}\in L$ , where $\mathbf{n}_{x}$ is the inward unit normal to $T$ .

If $\mathbf{n}_{x}\in L$ , choose a nonzero point $z\in H_{+}^{\circ}\cap L$ . In a sufficiently small ball centred at $z$ , the reflected part of the cone lies outside $H_{+}$ , and hence $\mathbf{C}$ agrees with the full cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ there. Since $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is invariant along $L$ , its tangent cone at $z$ is again a classical cone with $(n-1)$ -dimensional spine. The usual interior slicing argument of [38] gives the contradiction. Hence, it remains to treat the genuinely free-boundary case $L\subset T$ .

Choose coordinates on $H\cong\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ so that $H_{+}=\{x_{1}\geq 0\}$ and $T=\partial H_{+}=\{x_{1}=0\}$ . After rotation, assume that $L$ is given by $\{x_{1}=x_{n+1}=0\}=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\{0\}\subset T$ . Write a point as $X=(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})$ , where $y=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ . For $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$ , define the $n$ -dimensional half-hyperplane

$$ H^{+}_{\alpha}=\{(r\sin(\alpha),y,-r\cos(\alpha))\;\colon\;r\geq 0,\,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\}. $$

Then $\partial H^{+}_{\alpha}=L$ for every $\alpha$ . Furthermore, $H^{+}_{0},H^{+}_{\pi}\subset T$ (actually $T=H^{+}_{0}\cup H^{+}_{\pi}$ ), while $H^{+}_{\pi/2}=\{x_{n+1}=0,x_{1}\geq 0\}$ meets $T$ orthogonally. Set $\omega_{\alpha}=\sin(\alpha)e_{1}-\cos(\alpha)e_{n+1}$ , so that $\omega_{\alpha}$ points from $L$ into $H_{\alpha}^{+}$ . A choice of unit normal to $H^{+}_{\alpha}$ is given by $\nu_{\alpha}=\cos(\alpha)e_{1}+\sin(\alpha)e_{n+1}$ , while the outward conormal of $H^{+}_{\alpha}$ along $L$ is $\eta_{\alpha}=-\omega_{\alpha}=-\sin(\alpha)e_{1}+\cos(\alpha)e_{n+1}$ . Consequently, since the cone is invariant along $L$ , it has the form

$$ \mathbf{C}=q_{0}|H^{+}_{0}|+\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}|H^{+}_{\alpha_{i}}|+q_{\pi}|H^{+}_{\pi}|, $$

with $0<\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\ldots<\pi$ , $p_{i}\in\mathbb{N}$ , $q_{0},q_{\pi}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ . Because $\mathbf{C}$ is only free-boundary, we do not have the full vector balancing equation. However, testing the first variation near $L$ with a vector field equal to $e_{n+1}$ which is tangent to $T$ gives the identity $q_{0}-q_{\pi}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}\cos(\alpha_{i})=0$ . There is no corresponding balancing condition for the $e_{1}$ -component.

We first prove that $\alpha_{i}=\pi/2$ for every $i$ . Choose a diagonal sequence realising the tangent cone $\mathbf{C}$ . Thus, after relabelling, $\Sigma_{j}=\Phi_{x,r_{j}}(\Sigma_{k_{j}})$ and $V_{j}=(\Phi_{x,r_{j}})_{\sharp}V_{k_{j}}$ ; then $V_{j}\to\mathbf{C}$ locally as varifolds. We also have the corresponding sequence of Riemannian metrics as in Proposition 5.12. Every point of $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\setminus L$ has a planar tangent cone. On the one hand, at points of $H^{+}_{\alpha_{i}}\setminus L$ , with $0<\alpha_{i}<\pi$ , we are in the interior of $H$ , and hence interior sheeting [38] applies. On the other hand, at points of $(H^{+}_{0}\cup H_{\pi}^{+})\setminus L$ , boundary sheeting (cf. Theorem 1.12) applies. Consequently, $\Sigma_{j}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}$ smoothly and graphically on compact subsets of $\overline{H}_{+}\setminus L$ . In other words, on every fixed annulus around the spine $L$ , the graphical sheets, their tangent planes, and their unoriented normals converge (locally) uniformly to those of $\mathbf{C}$ .

For $\tau>0$ , define the following $\tau$ -tubular neighbourhood $\mathcal{L}_{\tau}$ of the spine by

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\tau}=\{(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})\in B_{3/2}^{+}\;\colon\;x_{1}^{2}+x_{n+1}^{2}<\tau^{2},|y|<1\}. $$

Choose $\zeta\in C_{c}^{1}(B_{2})$ such that $0\leq\zeta\leq 1,$ $\zeta\equiv 1$ on $B_{3/2},$ and $|D\zeta|\leq 3.$ Since the metrics are converging locally in $C^{2}$ , applying the stability inequality (5.20) for $\Sigma_{j}$ , reabsorbing the boundary terms using Lemma 2.14, and then using uniform equivalence of $\mathrm{g}_{j}$ to $\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ gives a uniform bound $\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap B_{3/2}^{+}}|A_{j}|^{2}\leq C$ . Furthermore, cover $L\cap\{|y|<1\}$ by at most $C\tau^{1-n}$ balls of radius $2\tau$ with centres on $L\subset T$ . Boundary-centred monotonicity and the uniform mass bound give mass at most $C\tau^{n}$ in each corresponding ball of radius $4\tau$ . Hence $\mathcal{H}^{n}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}(\Sigma_{j}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau})\leq C\tau$ , uniformly for all sufficiently large $j$ and $0<\tau<\tau_{0}$ . Therefore, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}|A_{j}|\leq\left(\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap B_{3/2}^{+}}|A_{j}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{n}\bigl(\Sigma_{j}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}\bigr)\right)^{1/2}\leq C\tau^{1/2}. $$

Let now $\pi:H_{+}\rightarrow L$ be given by $\pi(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})=y.$ For $y\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ , define $P^{+}_{y}\coloneqq\pi^{-1}(y)=\left\{(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})\,\colon x_{1}\geq 0\right\}$ and $D_{\tau,y}^{+}=\{(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})\in P_{y}^{+}\,\colon x_{1}^{2}+x_{n+1}^{2}\leq\tau^{2}\}$ . We denote the curved boundary of this half-disk by $\Lambda_{\tau,y}=\{(x_{1},y,x_{n+1})\,\colon x_{1}\geq 0,\ x_{1}^{2}+x_{n+1}^{2}=\tau^{2}\}$ . Since $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ has locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ measure, we have $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_{j})=0,$ and hence, since $\pi$ is Lipschitz, $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\bigl(\pi(\mathcal{S}_{j})\bigr)=0.$ Consequently, for almost every $y\in B_{1/2}^{n-1}$ , the point $y$ does not belong to $\pi(\mathcal{S}_{j})$ and, by Sard’s theorem, is a regular value of both $\pi|_{\Sigma_{j}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{j}}$ and $\pi|_{\partial\Sigma_{j}}.$ Additionally, the intersection with $\Lambda_{\tau,y}$ is transverse for all sufficiently large $j$ . For all such $y$ , the slice $\Gamma_{j,y}\coloneqq\Sigma_{j}\cap D_{\tau,y}^{+}$ is a one-dimensional, smooth manifold with $\partial\Gamma_{j,y}\subset(\Sigma_{j}\cap\Lambda_{\tau,y})\cup(\partial\Sigma_{j}\cap D_{\tau,y}^{+})$ . Notice that a point of $(\Sigma_{j}\setminus\partial\Sigma_{j})\cap T$ is an interior point of $\Gamma_{j,y}$ rather than an endpoint. In particular, every connected component of $\Gamma_{j,y}$ is either a smooth embedded circle, or a smooth embedded arc with exactly two endpoints. In the latter case, the unordered pair of endpoint types is one of $\{\Lambda_{\tau,y},\Lambda_{\tau,y}\}$ , $\{\Lambda_{\tau,y},\partial\Sigma_{j}\}$ , or $\{\partial\Sigma_{j},\partial\Sigma_{j}\}$ . No other case arises: the slice does not meet $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ or the curved part of $\partial B_{3/2}^{+}$ , while properness prevents connected components from terminating or accumulating in the interior of $D_{\tau,y}^{+}$ .

Let $N_{j}$ denote a continuous choice of Euclidean unit normal to $\Sigma_{j}$ , and regard $[N_{j}]\colon\Sigma_{j}\rightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{n}$ as the unoriented Gauss map. For a curve $\gamma\subset\Sigma_{j}$ , write

$$ \mathrm{osc}_{\gamma}[N_{j}]=\sup_{a,b\in\gamma}d_{\mathbb{RP}^{n}}([N_{j}(a)],[N_{j}(b)]). $$

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $\alpha_{i_{0}}\neq\pi/2$ for some $i_{0}$ . For every regular slice, choose one of the outer endpoints $a_{j,y}\in\Sigma_{j}\cap\Lambda_{\tau,y}$ corresponding to the ray $H^{+}_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}$ , and let $\gamma_{j,y}\subset\Gamma_{j,y}$ be the connected component containing it. Since $\gamma_{j,y}$ has an endpoint, it is an arc. Denote its other endpoint by $b_{j,y}$ . Let $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbf{C}}\coloneqq\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m}\}\cup\{0:q_{0}>0\}\cup\{\pi:q_{\pi}>0\}$ and define

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{\mathbf{C}}\coloneqq\min\Bigl\{d_{\mathbb{RP}^{n}}\bigl([\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}],\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\perp})\bigr),d_{\mathbb{RP}^{n}}\bigl([\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}],[\nu_{\alpha}]\bigr):\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathbf{C}},\ \alpha\neq\alpha_{i_{0}}\Bigr\}, $$

where the latter family is omitted if empty. Since $d_{\mathbb{RP}^{n}}([\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}],\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\perp}))=|\alpha_{i_{0}}-\pi/2|>0$ , and we have finitely many rays, $\delta_{\mathbf{C}}>0$ . We now have three cases for $b_{j,y}$ :

- (i) If $b_{j,y}\in\partial\Sigma_{j}$ , then the free-boundary condition gives $d_{\mathbb{RP}^{n}}\bigl([N_{j}(b_{j,y})],\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\perp})\bigr)=o_{j}(1),$ while smooth convergence at the outer endpoint gives $[N_{j}(a_{j,y})]\rightarrow[\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}].$ Hence, for all sufficiently large $j$ , $\operatorname{osc}_{\gamma_{j,y}}[N_{j}]\geq\delta_{\mathbf{C}}/2$ .

- (ii) If $b_{j,y}\in\Lambda_{\tau,y}$ corresponds to a ray $H_{\alpha}^{+}$ with $\alpha\neq\alpha_{i_{0}}$ , then $[N_{j}(a_{j,y})]\rightarrow[\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}],$ and $[N_{j}(b_{j,y})]\rightarrow[\nu_{\alpha}].$ Therefore, for all sufficiently large $j$ , $\operatorname{osc}_{\gamma_{j,y}}[N_{j}]\geq\delta_{\mathbf{C}}/2.$

- (iii) Suppose finally that $b_{j,y}\in\Lambda_{\tau,y}$ corresponds to the same ray $H_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}^{+}$ . Set $E=\operatorname{span}\{e_{1},e_{n+1}\}$ , and let $N_{j}$ be as above. Since $y$ is a regular value of $\pi|_{\Sigma_{j}}$ , we have $T_{p}\gamma_{j,y}=\ker D(\pi|_{\Sigma_{j}})_{p}=T_{p}\Sigma_{j}\cap E,$ and $\dim T_{p}\gamma_{j,y}=1.$ In particular, $\operatorname{proj}_{E}N_{j}\neq 0$ along $\gamma_{j,y}$ : otherwise $N_{j}\in E^{\perp}$ , and hence $E\subset N_{j}^{\perp}=T_{p}\Sigma_{j}$ , contradicting the fact that the kernel above is one-dimensional. Thus, $\widehat{N}_{j,y}\coloneqq|\operatorname{proj}_{E}N_{j}|^{-1}\operatorname{proj}_{E}N_{j}$ is a unit normal to the planar curve $\gamma_{j,y}$ . Orient this curve from $a_{j,y}$ to $b_{j,y}$ , and let $T_{j,y}$ denote its Euclidean unit tangent. Smooth convergence at the two outer endpoints gives, for all sufficiently large $j$ , $\langle T_{j,y}(a_{j,y}),\omega_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}\rangle<-1/2,$ and $\langle T_{j,y}(b_{j,y}),\omega_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}\rangle>1/2,$ since the curve enters $D_{\tau,y}^{+}$ at the first endpoint and leaves it at the second. If $\operatorname{osc}_{\gamma_{j,y}}[N_{j}]$ were sufficiently small, then $[\widehat{N}_{j,y}]$ would remain close to $[\nu_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}]$ , and hence the tangent line would remain close to $[\omega_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}]$ . In particular, for some fixed $c>0$ , $\big|\langle T_{j,y},\omega_{\alpha_{i_{0}}}\rangle\big|\geq c$ along $\gamma_{j,y}.$ This contradicts the intermediate value theorem, since the scalar product is negative at $a_{j,y}$ and positive at $b_{j,y}$ . Therefore, $\operatorname{osc}_{\gamma_{j,y}}[N_{j}]\geq\delta_{\mathrm{turn}}$ , for some $\delta_{\mathrm{turn}}>0$ independent of $j,y,\tau$ .

Taking $\beta\coloneqq\min\{\delta_{\mathbf{C}}/2,\delta_{\mathrm{turn}}\}>0,$ we conclude that $\operatorname{osc}_{\gamma_{j,y}}[N_{j}]\geq\beta$ for all sufficiently large $j$ and almost every regular $y\in B_{1/2}^{n-1}$ .

Next, there exists a sequence $\varepsilon_{j}\rightarrow 0$ such that, along every $\mathrm{g}_{j}$ -unit speed curve in $\Sigma_{j}$ , there holds $|\partial_{s}N_{j}|\leq C(|A_{j}|+\varepsilon_{j})$ . Thus, we obtain

$$ \beta\leq C\int_{\gamma_{j,y}}(|A_{j}|+\varepsilon_{j})\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{1},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\beta\leq C\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap P^{+}_{y}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}(|A_{j}|+\varepsilon_{j})\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{1}, $$

for almost every $y\in B_{1/2}^{n-1}$ . Integrating and using coarea, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\beta\mathcal{L}^{n-1}\bigl(B_{1/2}^{n-1}\bigr) \displaystyle\leq C\int_{B_{1/2}^{n-1}}\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap P^{+}_{y}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}\bigl(|A_{j}|+\varepsilon_{j}\bigr)\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{1}\,dy\leq C\int_{\Sigma_{j}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}|A_{j}|\,d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{n}+C\varepsilon_{j}\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{g}_{j}}^{n}\bigl(\Sigma_{j}\cap\mathcal{L}_{\tau}\bigr), $$

where we have used the uniform bound $J_{n-1}(\pi|_{\Sigma_{j}})\leq C$ . We conclude that $\beta\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(B_{1/2}^{n-1})\leq C\tau^{1/2}+C\varepsilon_{j}\tau.$ First let $j\to\infty$ , with $\tau>0$ fixed. We obtain $\beta\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(B_{1/2}^{n-1})\leq C\tau^{1/2}.$ Letting $\tau\downarrow 0$ , the right-hand side tends to zero, whereas the left-hand side is strictly positive. This contradiction proves that $\alpha_{i}=\pi/2$ for every $i$ .

We have proven that $\mathbf{C}=q_{0}|H^{+}_{0}|+p|H^{+}_{\pi/2}|+q_{\pi}|H^{+}_{\pi}|,$ where $p=\sum_{i}p_{i}.$ Appealing to the free-boundary balancing equation, we infer $q_{0}-q_{\pi}=0.$ Consequently, $q_{0}=q_{\pi}=q$ and $q|H^{+}_{0}|+q|H^{+}_{\pi}|=q|T|.$ Thus, $\mathbf{C}=p|H_{\pi/2}^{+}|+q|T|$ .

A completely analogous argument allows us to treat the mixed case $p,q\geq 0$ . More precisely, one can show that $pq=0$ , in which case either $\mathbf{C}=q|T|$ , or $\mathbf{C}=p|H_{\pi/2}^{+}|$ . Doubling and appealing to Theorem 1.12, or Theorem 1.15, we conclude. ∎

We can finally conclude the proof of Theorem 1.1 by a simple and (by now) rather standard argument using dimension reduction and Simons’ classification of stable regular cones in low dimensions.

### 5.5. Conclusion

The key result is the following spine-increase result, which allows the reduction to the aforementioned Simons’ classification of stable regular cones in low dimensions. Let $\mathbf{D}$ be a cone and let $S(\mathbf{D})$ be its spine. If $y\in\mathrm{spt}\|\mathbf{D}\|$ and $\mathbf{E}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(\mathbf{D},y)$ , then $S(\mathbf{D})+\mathrm{span}\{y\}\subset S(\mathbf{E})$ . In particular, if $y\not\in S(\mathbf{D})$ , then $\dim S(\mathbf{E})\geq\dim S(\mathbf{D})+1$ . Using this and appealing to Simons’ classification of stable regular cones of codimension one, we conclude that $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{S}\leq n-7$ . In particular, when $n\leq 6$ , $\mathcal{S}=\emptyset$ , while in the case $n=7$ , we can additionally prove that $\mathcal{S}$ is discrete. For the sake of contradiction, assume there are distinct singular points $z_{j}\in\mathcal{S}$ converging to $z$ , and set $\rho_{j}=d_{\mathrm{g}}(z_{j},z)$ . Blow up $V$ around $z$ at scale $\rho_{j}$ to obtain, after passing to a subsequence, a tangent cone $\mathbf{C}$ . Furthermore, the rescaled points $\rho_{j}^{-1}\exp_{z}^{-1}(z_{j})$ converge to a point $z^{*}\in S^{n}$ satisfying $z^{*}\in\operatorname{sing}(\mathbf{C})$ . Since $\mathbf{C}$ is a cone, $\{tz^{*}\colon\;t>0\}\subset\operatorname{sing}(\mathbf{C})$ , which is impossible since we have established that for $n=7$ , $\mathcal{H}^{\gamma}(\mathcal{S})=0$ for all $\gamma>0$ .

### 5.6. Stability of the limit

As in [38, Section 5], the previous steps have already established the dimension bound on the singular set $\mathcal{S}$ and local smooth graphical convergence to $\Sigma$ on $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ .

Notice that by stationarity in the interior and the constancy theorem, the density of the limit varifold is constant on each connected regular component.

Now let $\Gamma$ be a connected component of $\Sigma$ . For $x\in\Gamma$ , $y\in\partial\Gamma\subset\partial M$ define

$$ a_{\Gamma}(x)\coloneqq|A_{\Gamma}(x)|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\nu(x),\nu(x)),\quad b_{\Gamma}(y)\coloneqq\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\nu(y),\nu(y)), $$

where $\nu(x)$ is any choice of unit normal to $\Gamma$ at $x$ , and similarly for $\nu(y)$ . Notice that $a_{\Gamma}$ , $b_{\Gamma}$ are well-defined on $\Gamma$ and $\partial\Gamma$ respectively, since each term is invariant under $\nu\mapsto-\nu$ . Now define

$$ Q_{\Gamma}(\varphi,\varphi)=\int_{\Gamma}\bigl(|\nabla_{\Gamma}\varphi|^{2}-a_{\Gamma}\varphi^{2}\bigr)-\int_{\partial\Gamma}b_{\Gamma}\varphi^{2} $$

for $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Gamma)$ .

Let $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Gamma)$ be arbitrary. Since $\Gamma$ is embedded, there is a relatively open neighbourhood $U\Subset M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ of the support of $\varphi$ which does not intersect any other component of $\Sigma$ , and an extension $\hat{\varphi}\in C^{0,1}_{c}(U)$ of $\varphi$ to $U$ . By (iv) in Theorem 1.1, if $\varphi_{k}\coloneqq\hat{\varphi}|_{\Sigma_{k}}$ , then

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{k}}|\nabla_{\Sigma_{k}}\varphi_{k}|^{2}-\int_{\Sigma_{k}}\big(|A_{\Sigma_{k}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\nu_{\Sigma_{k}},\nu_{\Sigma_{k}})\big)\varphi_{k}^{2}-\int_{\partial\Sigma_{k}}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\nu_{\Sigma_{k}},\nu_{\Sigma_{k}})\varphi_{k}^{2}\geq 0 $$

for all $k$ . As $|\Sigma_{k}|\to\theta|\Sigma|$ in the sense of varifolds, and $\Sigma_{k}$ converges locally smoothly to $\Sigma$ on $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ , then, after taking the limit as $k\to\infty$ in (5.25), we obtain that $mQ_{\Gamma}(\varphi,\varphi)\geq 0$ , where $m$ is the positive constant $\theta|_{\Gamma}$ . Therefore $Q_{\Gamma}(\varphi,\varphi)\geq 0$ .

For the one-sided case, we adapt the even–odd argument in the proof of [3, Lemma A.1] to the free-boundary setting. If $\Gamma$ is two-sided, the condition $Q_{\Gamma}(\varphi,\varphi)\geq 0$ for all $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Gamma)$ says exactly that the stability inequality (1.1) is satisfied with $\Gamma$ in place of $\Sigma_{k}$ and therefore that $\Gamma$ is stable.

Now suppose that $\Gamma$ is one-sided, and consider the orientable double cover $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ of $\Gamma$ in the normal bundle $N\Gamma$ defined by

$$ \widetilde{\Gamma}=\{(x,v):x\in\Gamma,v\in N_{x}\Gamma,|v|_{\mathrm{g}}=1\}. $$

Equip $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ with the induced pullback metric. The immersion $\tilde{\iota}:\widetilde{\Gamma}\to M$ given by $\tilde{\iota}(x,v)=x$ is free-boundary minimal and has a globally defined unit normal $\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(x,v)=v$ . Let

$$ Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi,\phi)\coloneqq\int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|\nabla_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\phi|^{2}-\int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\big(|A_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\big)\phi^{2}-\int_{\partial\widetilde{\Gamma}}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\phi^{2} $$

for all $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ .

If $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ is even, i.e. $\phi(x,-v)=\phi(x,v)$ , then it descends to a function $\varphi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\Gamma)$ defined by $\varphi(x)=\phi(x,v)$ for either unit normal $v\in N_{x}\Gamma$ , and, by definition,

$$ Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi,\phi)=2Q_{\Gamma}(\varphi,\varphi)\geq 0. $$

If $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ is odd, i.e. $\phi(x,-v)=-\phi(x,v)$ , then $|\phi|$ is an even compactly supported Lipschitz function on $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ such that $|\nabla_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|\phi||^{2}=|\nabla_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\phi|^{2}$ almost everywhere. Then

$$ Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi,\phi)=Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(|\phi|,|\phi|)\geq 0. $$

Finally, an arbitrary $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ decomposes into the sum $\phi=\phi_{\mathrm{e}}+\phi_{\mathrm{o}}$ of an even and an odd function and it is easy to check that by definition of $Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}$ , we have $Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi_{\mathrm{e}},\phi_{\mathrm{o}})=0$ . Therefore, for every $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$

$$ Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi,\phi)=Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi_{\mathrm{e}},\phi_{\mathrm{e}})+Q_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}(\phi_{\mathrm{o}},\phi_{\mathrm{o}})\geq 0. $$

Therefore,

$$ \int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|\nabla_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\phi|^{2}-\int_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}\big(|A_{\widetilde{\Gamma}}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}_{M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\big)\phi^{2}-\int_{\partial\widetilde{\Gamma}}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial M}(\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\tilde{\nu}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}})\phi^{2}\geq 0, $$

for all $\phi\in C^{0,1}_{c}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$ .

## Appendix A Removability of singularities

We now prove the simple PDE result that is needed in the proofs of the sheeting theorems, namely Theorem 1.12 and Theorem 1.15. The result is somewhat standard, and we state it here in the exact form we need in the paper.

Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a bounded open domain and let $E$ be a (possibly empty) relatively open smooth subset of $\partial D$ .

#### Lemma A.1.

Let $\Gamma$ be a relatively closed subset of $D\cup E$ and assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma)=0$ . For every compact set $K\subset D\cup E$ there exist $\chi_{j}\in C^{\infty}(D\cup E)$ with $0\leq\chi_{j}\leq 1$ , each $\chi_{j}$ vanishing on a relative neighbourhood of $\Gamma\cap K$ in $D\cup E$ such that $\chi_{j}\to 1$ locally on $(D\cup E)\cap K\setminus\Gamma$ and $\int_{D\cap K}|\nabla\chi_{j}|\to 0$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from [13, Theorem 4.15(v)]. ∎

Let $C_{0},C_{1}>0$ be fixed and let $\mathcal{L}:(D\cup E)\times(-C_{0},C_{0})\times B^{n}_{C_{1}}(0)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function. Assume there are constants $0<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}<+\infty$ such that for every $(y,z,q)\in(D\cup E)\times(-C_{0},C_{0})\times B^{n}_{C_{1}}(0)$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$

$$ \lambda_{1}|\xi|^{2}\leq\partial_{q_{i}q_{j}}\mathcal{L}(y,z,q)\xi^{i}\xi^{j}\leq\lambda_{2}|\xi|^{2}. $$

#### Lemma A.2.

Let $\Gamma$ be a relatively closed subset of $D\cup E$ and assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Gamma)=0$ . Let $u$ be a Lipschitz function on $D\cup E$ such that

$$ \|u\|_{L^{\infty}(D\cup E)}\leq c_{0}<C_{0},\quad\operatorname{Lip}(u;D\cup E)\leq c_{1}<C_{1}, $$

and suppose that the identity

$$ \int_{D}\bigl(D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\varphi+\partial_{z}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\varphi\bigr)\,dy=0 $$

holds for every test function $\varphi\in C^{1}(D\cup E)$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\varphi\Subset(D\cup E)\setminus\Gamma$ . Then (A.3) holds for every $\varphi\in C^{1}(D\cup E)$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\varphi\Subset(D\cup E)$ and $u\in C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D\cup E)$ . In particular, $u$ is a classical solution of

$$ -\partial_{y_{i}}(\partial_{q_{i}}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u))+\partial_{z}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)=0 $$

and

$$ D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\cdot\eta_{D}=0\quad\text{on $E$} $$

where $\eta_{D}$ is the outward unit normal to $D$ along $E$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\varphi\in C^{1}(D\cup E)$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\varphi\Subset(D\cup E)$ and let $K=\operatorname{spt}\varphi$ . Then let $\chi_{j}$ be the cutoff functions provided by Lemma A.1. Then $\chi_{j}\varphi$ is an admissible test function for (A.3), so that

$$ 0=\int_{D}\chi_{j}\bigl(D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\varphi+\partial_{z}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\varphi\bigr)\,dy+\int_{D}\varphi D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\chi_{j}\,dy. $$

By (A.2) and smoothness of $\mathcal{L}$ , there is some large constant $C<+\infty$ such that

$$ \|D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\|_{L^{\infty}(D\cap K)}+\|\partial_{z}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\|_{L^{\infty}(D\cap K)}\leq C<+\infty. $$

Hence,

$$ \left|\int_{D}\varphi D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,u,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\chi_{j}\,dy\right|\leq C\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{D\cap K}|\nabla\chi_{j}|\to 0 $$

by Lemma A.1. The first integral in (A.6) converges by the dominated convergence theorem. Therefore (A.3) holds for $\varphi$ , and, hence, by arbitrariness of $\varphi$ for all compactly supported $C^{1}$ functions on $D\cup E$ .

Smoothness of $u$ in the interior then follows from elliptic regularity theory since the divergence form operator associated to (A.3) is uniformly elliptic by (A.1), the coefficients of $\mathcal{L}$ are assumed to be smooth and $u$ is Lipschitz. Along $E$ , the natural boundary operator is $\mathcal{B}(y,z,q)\coloneqq D_{q}\mathcal{L}(y,z,q)\cdot\eta_{D}(y)$ . Notice that it is uniformly oblique as

$$ D_{q}\mathcal{B}(y,z,q)\cdot\eta_{D}=\partial_{q_{i}q_{j}}\mathcal{L}(y,z,q)\eta_{D}^{i}\eta_{D}^{j}\geq\lambda_{1}|\eta_{D}|^{2}=\lambda_{1}>0. $$

By [31, Theorem 1], there exists $\alpha\in(0,1)$ such that $u\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D\cup E)$ . By standard elliptic theory, smoothness follows from $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity, which is a consequence of the boundary Schauder estimates of [30]. ∎

#### Remark A.3.

Notice that Lemma A.2 is considerably weaker and more elementary than Simon’s removable singularity theorem in [41]. Indeed, in Lemma A.2 the function $u$ is already defined and Lipschitz across the deleted set $\Gamma$ , so only the weak Euler–Lagrange identity must be extended. Simon on the other hand assumes no a priori boundedness or continuity of the solution near $\Gamma$ and proves the existence of a classical extension. However, Simon’s theorem as formulated in [41] does not cover integrands having $z$ -dependence or oblique boundary conditions.

## Appendix B Capacity and extension of stationarity

We elaborate on Remark 2.7. In particular, we prove that under the assumptions of Definition 2.6 we can extend stationarity across $\mathcal{S}$ . The proof uses some ideas introduced by Harvey–Lawson in [21] and employs some tools from classical potential theory. The case $n=2$ of Proposition B.5 is due to Simon [42] (without assuming local finiteness a priori).

The following lemma provides the basic analytic construction behind Proposition B.5, and is based on [21, Propositions 10.2–10.4]. For the sake of completeness, we provide a detailed proof.

#### Lemma B.1.

Let $n\geq 2$ , and let $E\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be compact with $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(E)<\infty.$ Then there exists an upper semicontinuous function $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\rightarrow[-\infty,\infty)$ such that

$$ \{\psi=-\infty\}=E,\qquad\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus E), $$

and

$$ \mathrm{tr}_{P}D^{2}\psi(x)\geq 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus E\text{ and }P\in G(n,n+1). $$

#### Proof.

Let $K$ be the fundamental solution of the Laplacian in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , so that $K(r)\sim r^{2-n}$ for $n\geq 3$ and $K(r)\sim-\log r$ for $n=2$ . We first consider $n\geq 3$ . Define $U_{n-2}^{\sigma}(x)\coloneqq\int K(|x-y|)\,d\sigma(y)$ for a finite positive measure $\sigma$ . We shall use the following elementary fact (see [14, Theorem 4.13(a)]).

#### Fact B.2.

Let $F\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be Borel, and let $\sigma$ be a nonzero finite positive measure supported on $F$ . If

$$ I_{n-2}(\sigma)\coloneqq\iint K(|x-y|)\,d\sigma(x)d\sigma(y)<\infty, $$

then $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(F)=\infty.$

Let now $\lambda\coloneqq\mathcal{H}^{n-2}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}E,$ which is a finite positive measure by hypothesis. Set $Z\coloneqq\{x\in E:U_{n-2}^{\lambda}(x)<\infty\},$ and $Z_{m}\coloneqq\{x\in E:U_{n-2}^{\lambda}(x)\leq m\},$ so that $Z_{m}\subset Z$ and $Z=\bigcup_{m}Z_{m}$ . We claim that $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(Z)=0.$ Indeed, if $\lambda(Z_{m})>0$ for some $m$ , then the nonzero measure $\sigma\coloneqq\lambda\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}Z_{m}$ satisfies

$$ I_{n-2}(\sigma)=\int_{Z_{m}}U_{n-2}^{\sigma}\,d\lambda\leq\int_{Z_{m}}U_{n-2}^{\lambda}\,d\lambda\leq m\lambda(Z_{m})<\infty, $$

and Fact B.2 would then imply $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(Z_{m})=\infty$ , contradicting $Z_{m}\subset E$ and $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(E)<\infty$ . Hence $\lambda(Z_{m})=0$ for every $m$ , and therefore $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(Z)=\lambda(Z)=0.$

Thus $U_{n-2}^{\lambda}(\cdot)=+\infty$ at every point of $E\setminus Z$ . To conclude the argument, we shall now construct another finite positive measure $\nu$ such that $U_{n-2}^{\nu}(x)=+\infty$ for all $x\in Z$ as well. In the end, we shall define $\mu\coloneqq\lambda+\nu$ and take $\psi=-U^{\mu}_{n-2}$ , which, as we will show, has the desired properties.

Since $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(Z)=0$ , for each $k\geq 1$ we may choose a countable cover

$$ Z\subset\bigcup_{i}B_{r_{k,i}}(a_{k,i}),\qquad a_{k,i}\in Z, $$

such that $\sum_{i}r_{k,i}^{n-2}<2^{-k}.$ Define $\nu_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{i}r_{k,i}^{n-2}\,\delta_{a_{k,i}}$ , and $\nu\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\nu_{k}$ . Then $\nu$ is a finite positive measure supported on $E$ , since $\nu(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})\leq\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}<\infty$ . For every $x\in Z$ and every $k$ , there is an $i$ such that $|x-a_{k,i}|<r_{k,i}$ , from which we deduce $U_{n-2}^{\nu_{k}}(x)\geq|x-a_{k,i}|^{2-n}r_{k,i}^{n-2}\geq 1.$ It follows that

$$ U_{n-2}^{\nu}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}U_{n-2}^{\nu_{k}}(x)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }x\in Z. $$

Consequently, the finite positive measure $\mu\coloneqq\lambda+\nu$ is supported on $E$ and satisfies $U_{n-2}^{\mu}(x)=+\infty$ for every $x\in E$ . Define now $\psi(x)\coloneqq-U_{n-2}^{\mu}(x)$ so that $\psi=-\infty$ on $E$ . If $x\notin E$ , then $\operatorname{dist}(x,E)>0,$ and hence $U_{n-2}^{\mu}(x)<\infty$ . Thus $\{\psi=-\infty\}=E.$ Moreover, on every compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus E$ , the kernel and all of its derivatives are uniformly bounded for $y\in E$ ; differentiation under the integral therefore gives $\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus E).$

It remains to verify the Hessian inequality. For $z\neq 0$ , writing $e=z/|z|$ , one computes

$$ D^{2}\bigl(-|z|^{2-n}\bigr)=(n-2)|z|^{-n}\bigl(I-n\,e\otimes e\bigr). $$

Hence, for every $P\in G(n,n+1)$ , we have $\mathrm{tr}_{P}D^{2}\bigl(-|z|^{2-n}\bigr)=(n-2)|z|^{-n}\bigl(n-n|\pi_{P}e|^{2}\bigr)=n(n-2)|z|^{-n}\bigl(1-|\pi_{P}e|^{2}\bigr)\geq 0$ . It follows that, for $x\notin E$ ,

$$ \begin{split}\mathrm{tr}_{P}D^{2}\psi(x)&=\frac{n}{\omega_{n}}\int_{E}\frac{1-|\pi_{P}e_{x-y}|^{2}}{|x-y|^{n}}\,d\mu(y)\geq 0,\end{split} $$

where $e_{x-y}\coloneqq(x-y)/|x-y|$ .

If $n=2$ , then $\mathcal{H}^{0}(E)<\infty$ , so that $E=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\}$ is finite. In this case take

$$ \mu\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{a_{j}},\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(x)\coloneqq\int K(|x-y|)\,d\mu(y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\log|x-a_{j}|. $$

Clearly $\{\psi=-\infty\}=E$ and $\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus E)$ . Since $D^{2}\log|z|=|z|^{-2}\bigl(I-2e\otimes e\bigr),$ for every $P\in G(2,3)$ , $\mathrm{tr}_{P}D^{2}\log|z|=2|z|^{-2}\bigl(1-|\pi_{P}e|^{2}\bigr)\geq 0.$ ∎

#### Remark B.3.

The function $\psi$ , extended by $-\infty$ on $E$ , is $n$ -plurisubharmonic in the sense of [21, §9]. Consequently the set $E$ is $C^{\infty}$ $n$ -pluripolar (again, see [21, §9]).

Let us now adapt the basic construction of Lemma B.1 to the setting of Riemannian manifolds (with and without boundary). For $r>0$ , let

$$ B_{r}\coloneqq B^{n+1}_{r}(0),\quad C_{r}\coloneqq B^{n}_{r}(0)\times[0,r),\quad\partial_{0}C_{r}\coloneqq B^{n}_{r}(0)\times\{0\}\subset C_{r}. $$

#### Lemma B.4.

Let $n\geq 2$ .

- (a) Let $\mathrm{g}$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on a neighbourhood of $\overline{B}_{2}$ . There exists $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ such that for every compact set $E\subset\overline{B}_{r_{0}}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(E)<\infty$ there is a function $v\in C^{\infty}(B_{2r_{0}}\setminus E)$ , $v\geq 1$ such that $v(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to E$ and $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}v(x)\leq 0$ for all $x\in B_{2r_{0}}\setminus E$ and every $P\in G(n,n+1)$ .

- (b) Let $\mathrm{g}$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on a neighbourhood of $\overline{C}_{2}$ of the form $\mathrm{g}=dt^{2}+h_{ij}(y,t)dy^{i}dy^{j}$ , where $(h_{ij})$ is smooth and positive-definite for all $t\in[0,2]$ . There exists $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ such that for every compact set $E\subset\overline{B}^{n}_{r_{0}}\times\{0\}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(E)<\infty$ there is a function $v\in C^{\infty}(C_{2r_{0}}\setminus E)$ , $v\geq 1$ such that $v(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to E$ and $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}v(x)\leq 0$ for all $x\in C_{2r_{0}}\setminus E$ and every $P\in G(n,n+1)$ , and $\partial_{t}v=0$ on $\partial_{0}C_{2r_{0}}\setminus E$ .

In both cases, the extension of $v$ by $+\infty$ on $E$ is lower semicontinuous on $B_{2r_{0}}$ and $C_{2r_{0}}$ , respectively.

#### Proof.

In order to deal with the errors arising from the Riemannian metric $\mathrm{g}$ , it is convenient to introduce a strictly superharmonic (with respect to the Euclidean metric) perturbation of the Riesz kernel in Lemma B.1. For $\lambda>0$ , choose $r_{*}>0$ such that $\lambda r_{*}<n$ , and define

$$ K_{\lambda}(r)\coloneqq\int_{r}^{r_{*}}s^{1-n}e^{\lambda s}\,ds\quad\text{for }0<r<r_{*}, $$

and notice that, as $r\downarrow 0$ , $K_{\lambda}$ has the same leading order behaviour as the Riesz kernel in Lemma B.1.

Now, for (a), by shrinking $r_{0}$ , let us assume that $B_{3r_{0}}$ is strongly $\mathrm{g}$ -convex and for $a\in B_{r_{0}}$ the distance $r_{a}(\cdot)=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(\cdot,a)$ is smooth on $B_{2r_{0}}\setminus\{a\}$ and satisfies $|\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}r_{a}-r_{a}^{-1}(\mathrm{g}-dr_{a}\otimes dr_{a})|\leq Cr_{a}$ (which is a consequence of the Hessian comparison theorem in [25, Theorem 11.7]). Then, if $P\in G(n,n+1)$ and $\alpha=|\pi^{\mathrm{g}}_{P}\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}r_{a}|_{\mathrm{g}}^{2}\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}K_{\lambda}(r_{a})\leq K^{\prime\prime}_{\lambda}(r_{a})+\frac{n-1}{r_{a}}K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(r_{a})+Cr_{a}|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(r_{a})|\leq(-\lambda+Cr_{a})|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(r_{a})|. $$

Take $\lambda=1$ and reduce $r_{0}$ so that $Cr_{a}<1$ ; then $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}K_{1}(r_{a})\leq 0$ for all $P\in G(n,n+1)$ .

If we let $\mu$ be the finite positive measure given in the proof of Lemma B.1, and

$$ v(x)\coloneqq 1+\int_{E}K_{1}(\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(x,y))\,d\mu(y), $$

then it is easy to check that, after shrinking $r_{0}$ if needed, $v$ has all the required properties, since $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}$ is uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean distance on $B_{3r_{0}}$ with constants going to 1 as $r_{0}\to 0$ . In particular, the integral diverges on $E$ . Its extension by $+\infty$ on $E$ is lower semicontinuous by Fatou’s lemma, which gives $v(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to E$ .

For (b), write $h_{t}\coloneqq h_{ij}(y,t)dy^{i}dy^{j}$ on $C_{2}$ and let $\hat{\mathrm{g}}\coloneqq dt^{2}+h_{0}(y)$ on the doubled cylinder $\hat{C}_{2}\coloneqq B^{n}_{2}(0)\times(-2,2)$ . For $a=(a^{\prime},0)\in E$ , let $\hat{r}_{a}(y,t)\coloneqq\operatorname{dist}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}((y,t),(a^{\prime},0))=(\operatorname{dist}_{h_{0}}(y,a^{\prime})^{2}+t^{2})^{1/2}$ . Then notice that $\partial_{t}\hat{r}_{a}(y,0)=0$ for $y\neq a^{\prime}$ .

The interior computation in (B.2) implies that for every $P\in G(n,n+1)$ , we have $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})\leq(-\lambda-C\hat{r}_{a})|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|$ . By smoothness of $h_{t}$ in $t$ we have $|h_{t}-h_{0}|=O(|t|)$ , $|\mathrm{g}-\hat{\mathrm{g}}|_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}\leq C|t|$ , $|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}-\nabla^{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}|_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}\leq C$ . Then,

$$ \mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})\leq\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})+C\left(|t||\nabla^{2}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}+|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|\right). $$

If $\lambda\hat{r}_{a}\leq n/2$ , then $|\nabla^{2}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}\leq C\hat{r}_{a}^{-1}|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|$ , so that using $|t|\leq\hat{r}_{a}$

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})\leq(-\lambda+C_{0}+C_{1}\hat{r}_{a})|K^{\prime}_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})|. $$

Choose first $\lambda>2C_{0}+1$ and then $r_{0}<r_{*}$ so small that $\lambda r_{*}<n/2$ , and $C_{1}\hat{r}_{a}\leq 1$ . Then $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}K_{\lambda}(\hat{r}_{a})\leq 0$ for all $P\in G(n,n+1)$ .

Finally, if we define

$$ v(x)\coloneqq 1+\int_{E}K_{1}(\operatorname{dist}_{\hat{\mathrm{g}}}(x,y))\,d\mu(y), $$

for the finite positive measure $\mu$ in the proof of Lemma B.1, then it is easy to check that it satisfies all the required properties. Divergence of the integral at $E$ follows as in (a), and $\partial_{t}v=0$ on $\partial_{0}C_{2r_{0}}\setminus E$ follows from $\partial_{t}\hat{r}_{a}(y,0)=0$ . ∎

We can now state and prove the main result of this appendix.

#### Proposition B.5.

Let $n\geq 2$ , and let $(M^{n+1},\mathrm{g})$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold-with-boundary with (possibly empty) boundary $\partial M$ . Let $\mathcal{S}\subset M$ be a relatively closed subset with locally finite $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ measure, i.e. $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{S}\cap K)<+\infty$ for every $K\Subset M$ . Let $V$ be an $n$ -dimensional rectifiable varifold in $M$ such that

$$ \delta V(X)=0\qquad\text{for every $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M\setminus\mathcal{S})$}. $$

Then $V$ is free-boundary stationary in $M$ , that is

$$ \delta V(X)=0\qquad\text{for every $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M)$}. $$

Consequently, if $\Sigma$ is a smooth proper minimal free-boundary immersion in $M\setminus\mathcal{S}$ and $|\Sigma|$ has locally finite mass, then $|\Sigma|$ is free-boundary stationary in $M$ .

#### Proof.

Let $U\Subset M$ be a subset of the domain of a coordinate chart such that $U$ is either a metric ball or a metric half-cylinder in Fermi coordinates with respect to $\partial M$ as in Lemma B.4, and let $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(U)$ . The global statement then follows from this local one after covering $\operatorname{spt}X$ by finitely many sufficiently small metric balls or half-cylinders.

Choose $\operatorname{spt}X\Subset U_{0}\Subset U_{1}\Subset U$ and set $E=\mathcal{S}\cap\overline{U}_{1}$ , so that $E$ is compact and satisfies $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}(E)<\infty$ by hypothesis. By Lemma B.4, there is a function $v\in C^{\infty}(U\setminus E)$ such that $v\geq 1$ on $\overline{U}_{1}\setminus E$ , $v(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to E$ and $\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}v\leq 0$ for all $P\in G(n,n+1)$ . In particular, $v$ is superharmonic.

We now prove a logarithmic Caccioppoli estimate. Let $\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}(U_{1})$ satisfy $\eta\equiv 1$ on $U_{0}$ , and let

$$ q_{\ell}(v)\coloneqq\left(\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{\ell}\right)_{+},\qquad\text{for $\ell>1$}. $$

Extend $v$ by $+\infty$ on $E$ . Lower semicontinuity and the fact that $\operatorname{spt}\eta$ is compact imply that $\operatorname{spt}\eta\cap\{v\leq\ell\}$ is a compact subset of $U_{1}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ . Thus $Y_{\ell}\coloneqq\eta^{2}q_{\ell}(v)\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}v$ is supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ and is tangent to $\partial M$ in the boundary case. Free-boundary stationarity away from $\mathcal{S}$ gives

$$ 0=\delta V(Y_{\ell})=\int_{G_{n}(U_{1})}[\eta^{2}q_{\ell}(v)\mathrm{tr}_{P}\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{g}}v+\langle\nabla_{P}(\eta^{2}q_{\ell}(v)),\nabla_{P}v\rangle]\,dV(x,P). $$

The first term is non-positive, thus implying

$$ \int_{G_{n}(U_{1})}\langle\nabla_{P}(\eta^{2}q_{\ell}(v)),\nabla_{P}v\rangle\,dV(x,P)\geq 0. $$

Now, on $\{v<\ell\}$ , there holds $\nabla_{P}q_{\ell}(v)=-v^{-2}\nabla_{P}v$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle A_{\ell}\coloneqq\int_{\{v<\ell\}}\eta^{2}|\nabla_{P}\log(v)|^{2}\,dV \displaystyle\leq 2\int_{\{v<\ell\}}\eta\left(1-\frac{v}{\ell}\right)\langle\nabla_{P}\eta,\nabla_{P}\log(v)\rangle\,dV \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}A_{\ell}+2\int|\nabla_{P}\eta|^{2}\,dV. $$

Rearranging,

$$ A_{\ell}\leq 4\int|\nabla_{P}\eta|^{2}\,dV\leq 4\|D\eta\|_{\infty}^{2}\|V\|(\mathrm{spt}\eta)<+\infty. $$

The last quantity is finite because $V$ has locally finite mass by assumption. Letting $\ell\rightarrow\infty$ gives

$$ \int_{U_{0}}|\nabla_{P}\log(v)|^{2}\,dV<+\infty. $$

We now construct the cut-off. Choose $\vartheta\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $0\leq\vartheta\leq 1$ , $\vartheta\equiv 1$ on $(-\infty,1]$ and $\vartheta\equiv 0$ on $[2,\infty)$ . Define then $\chi_{j}\coloneqq\vartheta\left(j^{-1}\log(v)\right).$ For every fixed $j$ , the function $\chi_{j}$ vanishes in an ambient neighbourhood of $E$ , so that $\chi_{j}X$ is an admissible test vector field supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ . Moreover, $\chi_{j}\rightarrow 1$ pointwise on $U_{0}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ . Lastly,

$$ \int_{U_{0}}|\nabla_{P}\chi_{j}|^{2}\,dV\leq\frac{\|\vartheta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}^{2}}{j^{2}}\int_{U_{0}}|\nabla_{P}\log(v)|^{2}\,dV\rightarrow 0, $$

as $j\rightarrow\infty$ . Consequently, from the stationarity condition

$$ 0=\delta V(\chi_{j}X)=\int\chi_{j}\mathrm{div}_{P}X\,dV+\int\langle\nabla_{P}\chi_{j},X\rangle\,dV, $$

we can use dominated convergence to pass the first term on the right-hand side to the limit, while for the second term we have

$$ \left|\int\langle\nabla_{P}\chi_{j},X\rangle\,dV\right|\leq\|X\|_{\infty}\|V\|(\mathrm{spt}X)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\mathrm{spt}X}|\nabla_{P}\chi_{j}|^{2}\,dV\right)^{1/2}\rightarrow 0, $$

as $j\rightarrow\infty$ . Thus, $V$ satisfies $\delta V(X)=0$ in $U$ meaning that it is free-boundary stationary across $\mathcal{S}$ . ∎

We record the following consequence of Proposition B.5 which will be the form we shall use for excision arguments (see 2.5 for the notational convention in the integrals).

#### Corollary B.6.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be as in Definition 2.6. Then for every compact $K\subset M$ there exists a sequence of smooth cutoff functions $\{\chi_{j}\}_{j}$ on $M$ , each supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ , such that $0\leq\chi_{j}\leq 1$ , $\chi_{j}\to 1$ on $\Sigma\cap K$ , and $\int_{\Sigma\cap K}|\nabla_{\Sigma}\chi_{j}|^{2}\to 0.$ This will sometimes be denoted by $\operatorname{cap}_{2}(\mathcal{S})=0$ and referred to as having vanishing relative $2$ -capacity in $\Sigma$ (see below).

#### Remark B.7.

A weaker hypothesis suffices for extending stationarity when a local area-growth bound is already available. Namely, assume $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\mathcal{S})=0$ and $\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Sigma\cap B_{r}(c))\leq Cr^{n}$ for $x\in\mathcal{S}$ and all sufficiently small radii for some constant $C$ uniform on compact sets. Then stationarity away from $\mathcal{S}$ extends across $\mathcal{S}$ .

Indeed, fix $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(U)$ and choose a compact $K\Subset U$ whose relative interior contains $\operatorname{spt}X$ . Since $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\mathcal{S}\cap K)=0$ , for every $\varepsilon>0$ we may cover $\mathcal{S}\cap K$ by finitely many balls $B_{r_{i}}(x_{i})$ , with $r_{i}<\varepsilon$ and $\sum_{i}r_{i}^{n-1}<\varepsilon$ . Choose $0\leq\eta\leq 1$ , equal to $0$ near $\bigcup_{i}B_{r_{i}}(x_{i})$ and to $1$ outside $\bigcup_{i}B_{2r_{i}}(x_{i})$ , with $|D\eta|\leq C\sum_{i}r_{i}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_{B_{2r_{i}}(x_{i})}$ . The Euclidean growth bound $\|V\|(B_{r}(x))\leq Cr^{n}$ at $x\in\mathcal{S}$ gives

$$ \int|\nabla_{P}\eta|\,dV\leq C\sum_{i}r_{i}^{n-1}\leq C\varepsilon,\qquad\|V\|(\{\eta\neq 1\})\leq C\sum_{i}r_{i}^{n}\leq C\varepsilon^{2}. $$

Since $\eta X$ is supported away from $\mathcal{S}$ , $0=\delta V(\eta X)$ ; hence

$$ |\delta V(X)|\leq\|DX\|_{\infty}\|V\|(\{\eta\neq 1\})+\|X\|_{\infty}\int|\nabla_{P}\eta|\,dV\leq C\bigl(\|DX\|_{\infty}\varepsilon^{2}+\|X\|_{\infty}\varepsilon\bigr). $$

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ proves that $\delta V(X)=0$ .

## Appendix C Tangent cones and stratification for free-boundary stationary varifolds

### C.1. Free-boundary stationary varifolds

An integral1313 13 It is actually not necessary to assume integrality, but, for the purposes of this paper, we shall not need to consider any larger classes of varifolds. varifold $V$ on $M$ is said to be free-boundary stationary if its first variation vanishes for all compactly supported vector fields on $M$ which are tangential to $\partial M$ along $\partial M\subset M$ , i.e.

$$ \delta V(X)=0\quad\text{for all }X\in\mathfrak{X}^{\mathrm{tan}}(M). $$

In particular, nothing is assumed on the first variation of $V$ in the direction of vector fields that are not tangential to $\partial M$ . Notice that by Definition 2.6, it is easy to see that if $\Sigma$ is a singular properly embedded (or properly immersed) free-boundary minimal hypersurface, then the multiplicity-one varifold $|\Sigma|$ induced by it is a free-boundary stationary varifold.

#### Remark C.1.

Note that if $\Gamma$ is a boundary component of $M$ , then the varifold $|\Gamma|$ is free-boundary stationary, independently of whether the mean curvature of $\Gamma$ in $M$ vanishes, even though $\Gamma$ is a smooth hypersurface. On the other hand, notice that $\Gamma$ would not be a free-boundary minimal hypersurface according to our Definition 2.2. Therefore, free-boundary stationary varifolds are strictly more general than free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, even if we restrict to smooth objects.

Although it is not apparent from the definition, free-boundary stationary integral varifolds have locally bounded first variation by [12, Proposition 3.2]1414 14 This is true even without assuming integrality by [10].. From this, Edelen manages to deduce a compactness theorem for sequences of free-boundary stationary integral varifolds with locally uniformly bounded mass [12, Theorem 3.5] from Allard’s Compactness theorem [1, 6.4]. In our simplified setting of singular free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces, the full first variation can be computed rather directly as in Lemma 5.4, so compactness can be reduced immediately to Allard’s result.

If we consider free-boundary stationary varifolds in a Euclidean half-space, then we have the following rather useful reflection principle.

#### Lemma C.2 (Reflection principle, [29, Lemma 2.2]).

Let $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be a unit vector and let $P^{+}$ be the closed half-space $\{u:u\cdot v\geq 0\}$ . Let $\theta:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be the reflection map across $T=v^{\perp}$ given by $\theta(u)=u-2(u\cdot v)v$ . If $V$ is a free-boundary stationary integral varifold in $P^{+}$ , then the doubled varifold

$$ \overline{V}\coloneqq V+\theta_{\sharp}V $$

is a stationary integral varifold in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and it is invariant under $\theta$ , i.e. $\theta_{\sharp}\overline{V}=\overline{V}$ .

Now let $V$ be a free-boundary stationary integral varifold and let $x\in M$ .

- • If $x\in M\setminus\partial M$ , then clearly for any open set $U\Subset M\setminus\partial M$ containing $x$ , $V$ is stationary in $U$ and therefore the usual interior monotonicity formula (see [43, §17]) holds for balls $B_{r}(x)\subset U$ .

- • If $x\in\partial M$ , then [18, Theorem 3.4] provides a boundary monotonicity formula for balls centred at $x$ .

The combination of these two monotonicity formulas implies existence of density and of tangent varifolds at every point. It also allows us to show that any tangent varifold to $V$ at a point $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ is a cone. (See Section C.2 for the exact definition in the manifold setting and some properties.)

On the other hand, some standard properties of stationary integral varifolds do not hold directly for free-boundary stationary integral varifolds. As an example, upper semicontinuity of density does not hold, even in the smooth setting (think of a sequence of interior points converging to a boundary point). In order to have a quantity that does not distinguish interior balls from balls centred at the boundary and satisfies a uniform monotonicity formula, it is possible to introduce the so-called reflected density (see [16, Section 3] for the Euclidean case) which turns out to be upper-semicontinuous. As the adaptation to the manifold setting is somewhat involved, we shall avoid introducing the reflected density, and work with the two distinct monotonicity formulas above, which will suffice for our purposes.

### C.2. Tangent cones

Let $V$ be a free-boundary stationary integral varifold in $M$ , let $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ , and $r_{i}\to 0$ be a sequence of positive numbers. We shall consider two cases.

- (1) If $x\in M\setminus\partial M$ , let $0<\rho_{x}<\min\{\operatorname{inj}_{x}(M),\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(x,\partial M)\}$ so that the exponential map of $M$ at $x$ is a diffeomorphism of $B^{T_{x}M}_{\rho_{x}}(0)\subset T_{x}M$ onto its image $B^{M}_{\rho_{x}}(x)$ , and let $\Psi_{x,r_{i}}:B^{T_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)\to M$ be given by

$$ \Psi_{x,r_{i}}(v)\coloneqq\exp_{x}(r_{i}v). $$

Let $\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i}}\coloneqq r_{i}^{-2}\Psi_{x,r_{i}}^{*}\mathrm{g}$ . Then, notice that

$$ (B^{T_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0),\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i}})\to(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})\quad\text{ locally smoothly}. $$

- (2) If $x\in\partial M$ , let $0<\rho_{x}<\min\{\operatorname{inj}_{x}(\partial M),\operatorname{inj}_{x}(M)\}$ be such that the exponential map of $\partial M$ at $x$ is a diffeomorphism of $B^{T_{x}(\partial M)}_{\rho_{x}}(0)\subset T_{x}(\partial M)$ onto its image $B^{\partial M}_{\rho_{x}}(x)\subset\partial M$ and the normal exponential map $F_{\partial M}$ of $\partial M$ is a diffeomorphism of $B^{\partial M}_{\rho_{x}}(x)\times[0,\rho_{x})$ onto its image. Then let $\Psi_{x,r_{i}}:B^{T^{+}_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)=T_{x}^{+}M\cap B^{T_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)\to M$ be given by (C.2)

$$ \Psi_{x,r_{i}}(v+t\mathbf{n}(x))\coloneqq F_{\partial M}(\exp^{\partial M}_{x}(r_{i}v),r_{i}t), $$

for $v\in B^{T_{x}(\partial M)}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)$ , $t\geq 0$ , $v+t\mathbf{n}(x)\in B^{T^{+}_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0)$ . Again, let $\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i}}\coloneqq r_{i}^{-2}\Psi_{x,r_{i}}^{*}\mathrm{g}$ , and notice that

$$ (B^{T^{+}_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0),\partial_{0}B^{T^{+}_{x}M}_{r_{i}^{-1}\rho_{x}}(0),\mathrm{g}_{x,r_{i}})\to(T^{+}_{x}M,T_{x}(\partial M),\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})\quad\text{ locally smoothly}. $$

In either case, let $\Phi_{x,r_{i}}$ denote the inverse map $\Psi_{x,r_{i}}^{-1}$ .

If we apply Edelen’s Compactness theorem [12, Theorem 3.5] to the sequence $V_{i}\coloneqq(\Phi_{x,r_{i}})_{\sharp}V$ 1515 15 It is easy to see that [12, Theorem 3.5] applies to a sequence of metrics converging in $C^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ ., then, up to a subsequence (not relabelled), there exists an integral varifold $V_{\infty}$ such that $V_{i}\to V_{\infty}$ locally in the sense of varifolds. By convergence of the first variation, we can pass the variational property of $V$ to the limit. More precisely, we have the following.

- (1) If $x\in M\setminus\partial M$ , then $V_{\infty}$ is a stationary integral varifold in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})\cong(\mathbb{R}^{n+1},\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ . The usual monotonicity formula for stationary varifolds applies and one deduces that $V_{\infty}$ is a stationary integral cone of density $\Theta(\|V\|,x)$ .

- (2) If $x\in\partial M$ , then $V_{\infty}$ is a free-boundary stationary integral varifold in $(T^{+}_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})\cong(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n+1},\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ . The monotonicity formula for free-boundary stationary varifolds of [18] applies, and one deduces that $V_{\infty}$ is a free-boundary stationary integral cone of density $\Theta(\|V\|,x)$ . Moreover, if we denote by $\theta_{0}$ the map on $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ given by reflection in $T_{x}(\partial M)\subset T_{x}M$ , then, by the reflection principle in [29, Lemma 2.2], the doubled cone (C.3)

$$ \overline{V}_{\infty}\coloneqq V_{\infty}+(\theta_{0})_{\sharp}V_{\infty} $$

is a stationary integral cone in $(T_{x}M,\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ , which is also invariant under $\theta_{0}$ .

Any varifold $V_{\infty}$ that arises in this way is said to be a tangent cone to $V$ at $x$ . The set of all tangent cones to $V$ at $x$ is denoted by $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ .

### C.3. Singular set and stratification for free-boundary stationary integral varifolds

In order to analyse the regularity of a free-boundary stationary integral varifold $V$ , we need to introduce some further definitions.

#### Definition C.3 (Regular and singular set).

Let $V$ be a free-boundary stationary integral varifold in $M$ . We define the regular set $\operatorname{reg}(V)$ of $V$ to be

$$ \operatorname{reg}(V)\coloneqq\bigg\{x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|:\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{there exists $r>0$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap B_{r}(x)$ is a smooth }\\
\textrm{embedded hypersurface-with-(possibly empty) boundary in $\partial M$}\end{array}\bigg\}. $$

Similarly, we define the singular set $\operatorname{sing}(V)$ of $V$ by

$$ \operatorname{sing}(V)=\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\operatorname{reg}(V). $$

We shall now subdivide the singular set into pieces according to the possible tangent cones that can occur. In order to state the results of this stratification procedure, we need some more definitions and notation about cones. Let $\eta_{v,\lambda}$ be the map $x\mapsto\lambda^{-1}(x-v)$ .

#### Definition C.4 (Spine of a cone).

Let $\mathbf{C}$ be an $n$ -dimensional cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ . We define the spine $S(\mathbf{C})$ of $\mathbf{C}$ to be the translation invariance set of $\mathbf{C}$ , namely

$$ S(\mathbf{C})\coloneqq\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:(\eta_{v,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}\}, $$

which is a vector subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ .

For $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ and $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ let

$$ \widehat{\mathbf{C}}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{C}&\text{if }x\in M\setminus\partial M,\\
\mathbf{C}+(\theta_{0})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}&\text{if }x\in\partial M.\end{cases} $$

#### Definition C.5 ( $j$ -stratum).

For $j\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ , we define the $j$ -stratum $\mathscr{S}_{j}$ as follows:

$$ \mathscr{S}_{j}\coloneqq\{x\in\operatorname{sing}(V):\mathrm{dim}(S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}}))\leq j\text{ for all }\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\}. $$

#### Remark C.6.

Clearly,

$$ \mathscr{S}_{0}\subset\mathscr{S}_{1}\subset\dots\subset\mathscr{S}_{n}=\operatorname{sing}(V). $$

The usefulness of this stratification of the singular set is due to the following result, which was first proved by Almgren in the setting of area-minimising currents.

#### Proposition C.7 ([27, Proposition 3.30]).

Let $V$ be a free-boundary stationary integral varifold in $M$ . Then, for all $j\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$

$$ \dim_{\mathcal{H}}\mathscr{S}_{j}\leq j, $$

where $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}$ denotes the Hausdorff dimension.

## Appendix D Non-emptiness of the boundary

We expand on Remark 1.10. In particular, we first provide an example of a compact Riemannian manifold-with-boundary $(M,\mathrm{g})$ where the one-parameter min-max construction of Theorem 1.8 yields a stationary integral varifold $V$ which is supported on an optimally regular minimal hypersurface entirely contained in the interior of $M$ , then show that this cannot happen under the additional assumption that $\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0$ on $M$ and $\partial M$ is strictly mean-convex.

### D.1. $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial M=\emptyset$

For sufficiently large $L>0$ , let the manifold $M_{L}$ be the following truncated ellipsoid

$$ E_{L}=\left\{(x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{R}:|x|^{2}+\frac{z^{2}}{L^{2}}=1\right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+2},\quad M_{L}=E_{L}\cap\{z\leq L/2\}, $$

endowed with the induced metric coming from the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ . The latitude sweepout $t\mapsto M_{L}\cap\{z=L/2-t\}$ for $t\in[0,3L/2]$ implies that the first free boundary min-max width $W_{1}(M_{L},\partial M_{L})$ of $M_{L}$ is at most $\mathcal{H}^{n}(\mathbb{S}^{n})$ , independently of $L$ .

For $t\in[0,L/2)$ , the level sets $M_{L}\cap\{z=L/2-t\}$ have mean curvature vector pointing towards $\partial M_{L}$ . In particular, by White’s varifold maximum principle [48], if $\Sigma$ is a singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface with $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\partial M_{L}\neq\emptyset$ , then $\overline{\Sigma}$ must intersect every level set $M_{L}\cap\{z=t\}$ for $t\in[0,L/2]$ . On the other hand, by applying interior monotonicity to $\Sigma\cap\{L/8\leq z\leq 3L/8\}$ , we obtain $\mathcal{H}^{n}(\overline{\Sigma})\geq c_{n}L$ whenever $\overline{\Sigma}\cap\partial M_{L}\neq\emptyset$ , where $c_{n}>0$ is independent of $L$ . Consequently, for $L$ sufficiently large, every singular free-boundary minimal hypersurface realising $W_{1}(M_{L},\partial M_{L})$ must be disjoint from $\partial M_{L}$ .

### D.2. $\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0$ on $M$ and strictly mean-convex boundary

Let us then give a quick proof of the following simple fact.

#### Lemma D.1.

If $(M,\mathrm{g})$ is a compact connected Riemannian manifold-with-boundary with $\partial M\neq\emptyset$ such that $\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0$ and $\partial M$ is strictly mean-convex (namely $H_{\partial M}>0$ ), and the free boundary stationary integral varifold $V$ in $M$ is induced by a non-empty singular properly immersed free-boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ , then $\partial\Sigma\neq\emptyset$ .

#### Proof.

We shall argue by contradiction. Notice that $\overline{\Sigma}=\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . By compactness of $M$ , there is $c>0$ such that $H_{\partial M}\geq c$ , so that, by [7, Lemmas 2.1–2.2], the distance function $d_{\partial M}$ from $\partial M$ satisfies $\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}d_{\partial M}\leq-c$ in the barrier sense1616 16 This is stated clearly in Lemma 2.1 of [7] for the region where $d_{\partial M}$ is smooth, and it follows from the proof of Lemma 2.2 (in the barrier sense) outside this region. This statement also appears (without proof) as Proposition 5 in [47]. A similar barrier construction appears in [34, Proof of Theorem 1.1].. Now suppose $x\in\overline{\Sigma}$ is such that $d_{\partial M}(x)=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{g}}(\overline{\Sigma},\partial M)>0$ . For $\varepsilon\in(0,c/2)$ , the construction in the proof of [7, Lemma 2.2], applied to the strictly mean-convex hypersurface $\partial M$ , gives a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ in $M$ and a smooth upper barrier function $u:U\to\mathbb{R}$ for $d_{\partial M}$ such that $|\nabla^{\mathrm{g}}u|=1$ on $U$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}u(x)\leq-c+\varepsilon\leq-c/2<0$ . For $y\in U\cap\overline{\Sigma}$ , we have

$$ u(x)=d_{\partial M}(x)\leq d_{\partial M}(y)\leq u(y) $$

since $u$ is an upper barrier for $d_{\partial M}$ and $x$ minimises distance to $\partial M$ . Therefore, $\overline{\Sigma}\cap U$ lies on one side of $S=\{u=u(x)\}$ and it touches $S$ at $x$ . Since $|\nabla_{\mathrm{g}}u|=1$ , it is easy to check that $H_{S}(x)=-\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}u(x)\geq c/2>0$ , and the domain $\{u\geq u(x)\}\supset\overline{\Sigma}\cap U$ is strongly $n$ -convex at $x$ . The contradiction then follows from White’s varifold maximum principle [48]. ∎
